Rug pull — An MCP server changing a tool's definition after you reviewed and approved it. Defended by pinning and hashing tool definitions and blocking on drift. (first taught in C8)

Rule of Two (Agents) — Meta's rule that an agent session should combine no more than two of untrustworthy input, sensitive data or systems, and state changes or external communication; with all three, require human approval or redesign. (first taught in C9)

docs.title: S
docs.text:
Saga — Modelling a long-running plan as steps each with a compensation, run in reverse on failure. Irreversible steps go last and behind approval. (first taught in D2)

Security trimming — Applying permissions as a retrieval filter before content reaches the model, never by instructions in the prompt. (first taught in C7)

Semantic cache — A cache that returns a stored answer when a new prompt is semantically close to a cached one (APIM llm-semantic-cache-*, backed by Azure Managed Redis). Only safe for answers that are not user-, time- or permission-specific, and keyed by tenant, role and language. (first taught in C15)

Semantic layer — Curated database views with business names, definitions, units and owners (for example an analyst schema) that the text-to-SQL agent queries instead of raw tables. (first taught in C10)

SFT (supervised fine-tuning) — Training on prompt and ideal-response demonstrations. (first taught in C1)

Shadow deployment — Running a new version on mirrored or sampled traffic without showing its output to users, then comparing offline. No user impact, double cost. (first taught in C15)

SLO (service level objective) — A target for a service level indicator over a window. For agents the course separates behavioural SLOs (task success, safety) from infrastructure SLOs (availability, latency). (first taught in C15)

Slopsquatting — Registering package names that AI models predictably hallucinate. A USENIX 2025 study found 19.7% of 2.23M AI code samples referenced non-existent packages; defended by allow-lists, lockfiles and package-age rules. (first taught in C4)

Spec-driven development — Using written specs to drive agent implementation. The course position is spec-anchored with an executable anchor (human-written acceptance tests and eval cases), and ceremony proportional to the change. (first taught in C4)

Spotlighting — Marking untrusted input so the model can tell it is data (delimiting, datamarking or encoding). It lowers attack success cheaply but is never the only control. (first taught in C3)

STRIDE — The threat-modelling categories Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service and Elevation of privilege, applied per element of an AI system's data-flow diagram. (first taught in C16)

Structured outputs — Schema-constrained generation (JSON Schema, constrained decoding) that guarantees the output conforms to a schema, but not that its values are correct. Make unknowns representable and validate in code anyway. (first taught in C3)

Sub-agent — A separate agent session with its own context, tools and permissions, used for isolation (for example a diagnostics sub-agent returning a short finding) or for specialist work in coding agents. (first taught in C4)

Synthetic data (dimension tuples) — Generating test cases by defining dimensions, hand-writing about 20 tuples, generating more, then turning each tuple into natural language in a separate step. Synthetic data shows coverage, not production frequency. (first taught in C5)

System card — A per-system document of what the system does and does not do, models, evaluation summary, limitations, oversight, data handling and contact, written for non-technical readers. (first taught in A6)

docs.title: T
docs.text:
Tau-bench (τ-bench) — A benchmark of tool-agent-user interaction with simulated users, domain policies and database end-state checks, which introduced pass^k; τ²-bench adds dual control. (first taught in C5)

Temperature — A sampling parameter that rescales logits: low is near-greedy, high is flatter. Not a creativity dial for facts; reasoning models often ignore it. (first taught in C1)

Text-to-SQL — Generating SQL from a natural-language question. In the course it is a read-only, validated tool over a semantic layer, with parser validation, row-level security, row caps and execution-accuracy evals. (first taught in C10)

Threat register — The output of threat modelling: per threat, the element, STRIDE class, OWASP mapping, trifecta flag, mitigation, the test that proves it, and residual risk with an owner. (first taught in C16)

Token — The unit models read, generate and bill. Context windows, rate limits, prices and output limits are all in tokens; the provider's reported usage is the bill. (first taught in C1)

Tool calling — The model returning a structured request to call a tool, which your code validates and executes before returning the result. The model never executes anything. (first taught in C3)

Tool definition pinning — Hashing each MCP tool's name, description and schema at approval time and blocking or alerting when a live definition changes. (first taught in C8)

Tool poisoning — Malicious instructions hidden in a tool's description, visible to the model but usually not to the user. (first taught in C8)

Top-p (nucleus sampling) — Sampling from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p. Tune temperature or top-p, not both. (first taught in C1)

TPM (tokens per minute) — The rate limit on a model deployment and the hard ceiling on model spend you control; budgets only alert. (first taught in C0)

TPR / TNR — True positive rate and true negative rate of an LLM judge against human labels. Course convention: Pass is the positive class, so TNR is the "catches failures" number. Reported separately because classes are imbalanced. (first taught in C5)

Track-critical area — A competency area in which a track requires Expert level at graduation (marked ● in the competency matrix). (see Competency matrix)

Trajectory eval — Evaluating an agent's path (right tools, valid arguments, order, forbidden actions, efficiency) from its spans, preferably by asserting invariants rather than exact paths. (first taught in C9)

Trakia Freight — The fictional Plovdiv logistics company (about 400 trucks, 600 drivers, depots in Plovdiv, Sofia and Varna) for which you build Fleet Ops Copilot. All data is synthetic. (first taught in C0)

TrakiaBench — The internal coding-agent benchmark you build in D6 from your own repository's history, with hidden tests, contamination control and pass^k. (first taught in D6)

TrakiaOps — The product's SQL Server 2025 database of vehicles, pseudonymised drivers, trips, telematics events, work orders, customers and shipments. (first taught in C0)

TrakiaSim — The τ-bench-style simulation harness (simulated users, policies, resettable environment, end-state graders) you build in D7 to measure agent reliability. (first taught in D7)

Transparency Note — A document explaining a system's capabilities, limitations and appropriate use, in the style Microsoft publishes for its services; you write one for your own system. (first taught in C18)

TTFT (time to first token) — The delay before the first output token, driven by network, prefill of uncached input and provider queueing. Streaming improves perceived latency, not total time or cost. (first taught in C1)

docs.title: U
docs.text: Unaided segment — The short, proctored part of each gate done without AI assistance, such as predicting behaviour from traces or writing a design note. (see Assessment and gates)

docs.title: V
docs.text:
VECTOR type (SQL Server 2025) — The SQL vector data type and VECTOR_DISTANCE function, GA, keeping vectors next to rows with transactional consistency and row-level security. Exact search is recommended below about 50k vectors after predicates. (first taught in C6)

Voice Live — Azure's managed voice orchestration (speech recognition, turn detection, interruption, speech synthesis) around a model or agent; Voice Live prompt agents and hosted agents with Voice Live are GA. (first taught in D3)

Volatility tag — The Low, Med or High tag in each module header indicating how quickly its content dates. (see Course overview)

docs.title: W
docs.text:
WAF for AI workloads — The Azure Well-Architected Framework's AI guidance, with ten design areas mapped to the five pillars and an Assessment Review Tool used as the review instrument for every architecture package. (first taught in A2)

Workflow — LLMs and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths (prompt chaining, routing, parallelization, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer). The default for known processes, with autonomy confined to bounded nodes. (first taught in C9)

Worktree — A separate Git working directory on its own branch, used to run parallel coding agents on independent tasks without interfering. (first taught in C4)

  • NIST AI Risk Management Framework (C18, A6)

docs.title: C0 — Orientation, setup & toolchain
docs.text: Level: Part 0 — Orientation · Duration: 6h (theory 30% / labs 70%) · Prerequisites: Git, HTTP/REST, SQL, one unit-test framework in any language; an Azure subscription where you can create resource groups; a GitHub account · Volatility: High (tool versions, portal UX, SDK names)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Trakia Freight's IT lead gives you a laptop, a GitHub org and an Azure subscription on Monday and expects a working "Ask Fleet Ops" prototype by Friday. Teams that skip setup discipline lose that week in predictable ways: one developer is on .NET 9 and another on .NET 10; someone pastes an API key into appsettings.json and pushes it; a forgotten test deployment of a frontier reasoning model runs a load test over the weekend and burns the quarter's budget; a sample copied from a 2025 blog targets the retired Assistants API and a hub-based project that only exists in "Foundry (classic)". None of these are AI problems, but in AI projects they cost more because every call is metered and the platform renamed half of itself in 2025–2026.

This course is long (~475h) and the platform moves monthly. You will rebuild your environment several times (new laptop, Codespaces, a colleague joining your capstone team, a CI runner, a coding agent's sandbox). The only sustainable answer is environment as code: a devcontainer, pinned SDKs and packages, configuration-only model selection, keyless authentication, and budget alerts created by script, not by memory. That same environment is what your coding agents (C4) will run in, so its reproducibility directly limits how much you can safely delegate.

Experts also set up feedback on day one: a cost alert that fires before damage is done, an Aspire dashboard that shows every model call, and a CI job that builds and tests the empty solution. In this course you are graded on how you direct and verify agents (from C4 on); the factory you start here is the foundation of that grade.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of C0 you can:

  1. Provision a reproducible dev environment (devcontainer or local) with .NET 10, Aspire 13.x, Node.js LTS and Python, and prove it with a scripted doctor check.
  2. Create a Microsoft Foundry resource and project (new resource/project model, not hub-based), deploy two model roles ("fast small model", "frontier reasoning model") and call them with keyless (Entra ID) authentication.
  3. Configure Azure cost guardrails: a resource-group budget with actual and forecast alerts, and per-deployment rate limits as a hard ceiling.
  4. Run a model locally with Foundry Local and explain when local inference is the right lab default.
  5. Explain the lab repo structure, tagging scheme and version-pinning policy (global.json, central package management, models.json), and find the start state of any lab.
  6. Read the C#, Python and Node.js you will meet in this course well enough to modify samples (non-.NET developers: C# crash-course checkpoints passed).
  7. Describe how mastery gates (G1–G3) work: hidden eval suites, code review, design defense.

docs.title: The course workflow: Product + Factory, gated by evals
docs.text:
You grow one product, Fleet Ops Copilot for the fictional Plovdiv logistics company Trakia Freight (~400 trucks, ~600 drivers, depots in Plovdiv, Sofia and Varna), and in parallel your Factory — your own agentic SDLC (memory files, custom agents, hooks, eval gates, CI agents). Every module ends with a product increment and a factory increment. From C4 onward, product work is done through the factory: you specify, constrain and verify; agents type.

Vehicle identifiers (course-wide convention). Two vehicle identifiers recur in every module and must not be confused: the fleet/vehicle ID (VehicleId, e.g. TRK-0471), assigned by TrakiaOps and stable for the vehicle's life — the key that tools, traces and logs use; and the registration plate (VehicleReg, canonical form Cyrillic with spaces, e.g. РВ 4471 АК), which drivers type in Cyrillic or Latin look-alikes, is normalised to Cyrillic in code (C1, C3), can change over a vehicle's life and is resolved to the fleet ID by lookup. Tools return and accept both, but joins, logs and approvals use the fleet ID.

Each lab follows Learn → Do → Break → Fix → Explain: a working baseline, an induced failure, a fix, and a short written explanation (ADR, postmortem or eval report). The explanation is graded.

Gates. After Level 1 you sit Gate G1 (specified separately). Gates use (a) hidden eval suites run against your product branch, (b) a code review against a rubric (correctness, security, observability, cost, eval coverage), and from G2 (c) a design defense. Passing means your evals clear thresholds on cases you have not seen, so overfitting prompts to your own golden set does not help. You can resit; feedback is specific.

docs.title: Environment as code
docs.text:
• Devcontainer (.devcontainer/devcontainer.json): the same image runs in VS Code Dev Containers, GitHub Codespaces and the CI runner. Coding agents (Copilot cloud agent, Claude Code in Actions) get an equivalent environment, which is why their test runs mean something.
  • Pinned SDK (global.json) with rollForward: latestFeature within .NET 10 — allows patch/feature-band updates, blocks an accidental major jump.
  • Central Package Management (Directory.Packages.props, ManagePackageVersionsCentrally=true): one place where every NuGet version is pinned. Nightly CI (run by the course team, and later by you in C19) bumps versions on a branch and runs all lab solutions; that is how the course keeps up with preview churn without breaking you mid-module.
  • Model config, not model code: labs reference model roles. models.json / appsettings.json maps roles (chat-fast, chat-reasoning, embedding) to deployment names. Model names change monthly (GPT-6 Sol/Luna/Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 all shipped in September 2026); your code must survive that as a config change. Foundry GA models are deprecated at 12 months and retired at 18 (partner models typically 12), with ≥60 days notice, and retired models return 410 Gone — so hard-coded names are a production defect, not a style issue.

docs.title: Microsoft Foundry, as of October 2026
docs.text:
• "Azure AI Foundry" is now Microsoft Foundry; "Azure AI Services" is now Foundry Tools.
  • One Foundry resource contains projects. Hub-based projects survive only in the "Foundry (classic)" portal. Do not follow tutorials that create a hub.
  • Endpoints you will use:
  • Project endpoint: https://<resource>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project> (Responses API, agents, evaluations) via Azure.AI.Projects 2.0 GA family.
  • OpenAI v1 endpoint: https://<resource>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/ via the plain OpenAI .NET package — no dated api-version query strings.
  • The Assistants API retired on 26 Aug 2026; use the Responses API.
  • Do not install the preview Azure.AI.Projects.OpenAI alongside Azure.AI.Extensions.OpenAI — Microsoft warns of ambiguous types.

docs.title: Keyless authentication from the start
docs.text: Use Microsoft Entra ID (DefaultAzureCredential locally via az login; managed identity in Azure; OIDC federated credentials in GitHub Actions). Assign yourself the minimal data-plane role on the Foundry resource (the role name for calling models in the new Foundry RBAC model — verify against current documentation; Foundry evaluations require Entra ID and do not accept API keys). API keys are allowed only for Foundry Local / local OpenAI-compatible endpoints. Rule: no secret ever lands in a tracked file; dotnet user-secrets for anything unavoidable, GitHub secret scanning on.

docs.title: Cost guardrails: three layers
docs.text:
1. Budgets with alerts (Cost Management) on the course resource group: e.g. €40/month, alerts at 50% actual, 80% actual, 100% forecast. Budgets alert; they do not stop spend.
  2. Deployment rate limits (tokens-per-minute quota per deployment): the only hard ceiling you control at the model layer. Set the frontier model deployment low (a few thousand TPM is plenty for labs).
  3. Habits: default to the fast small model or Foundry Local; use the frontier role only when a lab says so; delete load-test deployments; MEAI.Evaluation response caching (C5) for repeated eval runs.

Rough numbers to calibrate intuition (list prices from research notes; verify against the Azure pricing page before quoting to learners): a "fast small" class model at ~$0.10/$0.50 per million input/output tokens vs a frontier class at ~$10/$50 is a 100× spread. A 50-case eval suite × 3 runs × ~2k tokens per case ≈ 300k tokens: cents on the small model, a few dollars on the frontier model, much more with high reasoning effort. Per-token price is not per-task cost (C1).

docs.title: Foundry Local
docs.text: Foundry Local went GA on 9 Apr 2026: on-device inference on Windows, macOS (Apple silicon) and Linux x64; ONNX Runtime with automatic GPU/NPU/CPU selection; OpenAI-compatible API including the Responses format; C# SDK Microsoft.AI.Foundry.Local; curated models (Phi, Qwen, gpt-oss, Mistral, DeepSeek, Whisper). Use it for offline work, cheap iteration and as the "swap" target that proves your code is provider-agnostic (C2). Caveat: small local models are weaker at tool calling and structured output — that is a lesson, not a bug.

docs.title: Why Python and Node.js in a .NET course
docs.text: Everything is C# except a bounded, declared set marked [Python]: PyRIT / AI Red Teaming Agent local scans (C14, C16), Foundry cloud-evaluation authoring samples (azure-ai-evaluation), fine-tuning data prep and the interactive-training preview (D1), Agent Framework "Labs" packages, RAGAS. Node.js is needed for Playwright test agents (npx playwright init-agents, C11), AG-UI/React front-ends (D4), and many MCP servers and CLIs. The certification market also matters: AI-103 (the AI-102 successor) assumes Python, so reading fluency is a career asset.

docs.title: Misconceptions to unlearn
docs.text:
• "Budgets cap my spend." They alert. Quotas/rate limits and deleting deployments cap spend.
  • "A key in user-secrets is safe enough for CI." CI uses OIDC federation; no long-lived secrets.
  • "The latest preview package is better." Labs pin versions; you upgrade deliberately, behind a green eval suite.
  • "Any Foundry tutorial works." Hub-based, Assistants-API and api-version-dated samples are legacy as of 2026.

docs.title: Tools & versions (as of Oct 2026)
docs.text: Tool / package Purpose Status Notes .NET 10 SDK, C# Primary runtime/language GA (LTS) Pin in global.json Aspire 13.6 Local orchestration, OTel dashboard GA Renamed from ".NET Aspire"; dashboard marks LLM calls when MEAI UseOpenTelemetry is on Visual Studio 2026 (v18.x) / VS Code IDE GA VS 2026 has Copilot @Test agent (GA v18.3) and "Agent (Preview)" built on the Copilot CLI SDK Dev Containers / GitHub Codespaces Reproducible env GA Same image locally, in Codespaces and CI GitHub + GitHub Actions Source, CI, agents GA Azure DevOps interop covered in C19 Azure CLI, azd Provisioning GA Bicep for IaC from C17 Microsoft Foundry (resource + project) Models, agents, evals, tracing GA Hub projects = "Foundry (classic)" only Azure.AI.Projects / .Agents / Azure.AI.Extensions.OpenAI 2.0.0 Foundry .NET SDK GA Don't mix with preview Azure.AI.Projects.OpenAI OpenAI .NET package /openai/v1/ endpoint GA Some APIs need #pragma warning disable OPENAI001 Azure.Identity Entra auth GA DefaultAzureCredential Foundry Local (Microsoft.AI.Foundry.Local) Local inference GA (9 Apr 2026) Learn page carries no GA label — verify against current documentation Foundry Toolkit for VS Code Model playground, local models GA Appears to supersede "AI Toolkit" (rename unconfirmed) Node.js LTS Playwright agents, MCP servers, front-ends GA Pin via .nvmrc / devcontainer feature (course choice: current LTS line — verify) Python 3.12+ with uv [Python] red-teaming, cloud evals, fine-tuning prep GA Course choice; pinned in scripts/python/pyproject.toml GitHub Copilot (agent mode), Claude Code, Codex Coding agents (C4) GA Paid plan needed for some features

docs.title: Lab 1 — Environment as code (≈1.25h)
docs.text:
• Goal: A devcontainer-based environment that builds and tests the empty Fleet Ops solution, identical on your machine, in Codespaces and in CI.
  • Start state: lab repo trakia-fleetops, tag c0/lab1-start (solution skeleton, no devcontainer).
  • Steps:
  • Clone and inspect the repo layout: 
    trakia-fleetops/
  .devcontainer/           # you create in this lab
  .github/workflows/       # ci.yml (build+test), nightly.yml (course team)
  data/                    # TrakiaOps SQL scripts, docs corpus (BG+EN), mock API OpenAPI specs
  docs/adr/                # ADRs; template + checklist in README.md (you write from C1)
  evals/                   # golden datasets, error-analysis notes (C5)
  prompts/                 # versioned prompt templates (C3)
  scripts/doctor.sh        # environment check
  scripts/python/          # the only Python in the repo [Python]
  src/FleetOps.AppHost/    # Aspire AppHost
  src/FleetOps.ServiceDefaults/
  src/FleetOps.Core/       # domain + AI services
  src/FleetOps.Api/        # minimal API
  src/FleetOps.Cli/        # console client
  tests/FleetOps.Tests/    # xUnit unit tests
  tests/FleetOps.Evals/    # eval tests (C5)
  global.json  Directory.Packages.props  models.json  AGENTS.md (C4)
  • Create .devcontainer/devcontainer.json: 
    {
  "name": "trakia-fleetops",
  "image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/dotnet:10.0", // verify current tag
  "features": {
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/node:1": { "version": "lts" },
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/python:1": { "version": "3.12" },
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/azure-cli:1": {},
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/github-cli:1": {},
    "ghcr.io/devcontainers/features/docker-in-docker:2": {}   // Aspire containers, SQL Server
  },
  "postCreateCommand": "dotnet restore && dotnet tool restore && ./scripts/doctor.sh",
  "forwardPorts": [17000, 5080],
  "customizations": { "vscode": { "extensions": ["ms-dotnettools.csdevkit", "GitHub.copilot-chat"] } }
}
  • Pin the SDK and packages: 
    // global.json
{ "sdk": { "version": "10.0.100", "rollForward": "latestFeature" } }  // set to the course release's SDK

    <!-- Directory.Packages.props (excerpt) -->
<Project>
  <PropertyGroup><ManagePackageVersionsCentrally>true</ManagePackageVersionsCentrally></PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageVersion Include="Microsoft.Extensions.AI" Version="10.5.0" />  <!-- course release pin; verify -->
    <PackageVersion Include="Azure.Identity" Version="..." />
    <PackageVersion Include="OpenAI" Version="..." />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>
  • Write scripts/doctor.sh that prints and asserts: dotnet --version major = 10, node --version ≥ pinned LTS major, python --version ≥ 3.12, az account show succeeds, aspire --version or the Aspire templates are installed (verify the current Aspire CLI install path), docker info succeeds. Exit non-zero on any failure.
  • Run dotnet new is not needed — the skeleton exists. Run dotnet build and dotnet test inside the container.
  • Add .github/workflows/ci.yml that uses the same devcontainer (e.g. devcontainers/ci action) to run ./scripts/doctor.sh --ci && dotnet test.
  • Break it: Change global.json to 9.0.100 with rollForward: disable and rebuild. Then add a package with a floating version (Version="10.*") to a project file directly. Observe the CPM error (NU1008-style) and the SDK resolution failure.
  • Acceptance criteria: ./scripts/doctor.sh exits 0 in the container; ci.yml green on your fork; Directory.Packages.props is the only place versions appear (CI step grep -R "Version=" src tests --include=*.csproj returns nothing).
  • Stretch: Open the repo in a Codespace and time from "Create" to green dotnet test. Add a prebuild configuration to cut it.

docs.title: Lab 2 — Foundry resource, project, two deployments, keyless call (≈1.25h)
docs.text:
• Goal: A Foundry resource + project in an EU region with a "fast small" and a "frontier reasoning" deployment, called from C# with Entra ID.
  • Start state: c0/lab2-start.
  • Steps:
  • Create a resource group rg-trakia-<you> in an EU region that offers your chosen models (check model/region availability; Sweden Central and France Central frequently appear in Microsoft regional lists — verify for the current models).
  • Create the Foundry resource and a project in the new portal (ai.azure.com), not a hub. Optional IaC path: Bicep Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts (kind AIServices) with project management enabled and a child projects resource — verify exact properties against current docs before teaching.
  • Deploy two models, recording only roles in config: 
    // models.json
{
  "roles": {
    "chat-fast":      { "provider": "foundry", "deployment": "fleet-fast",      "notes": "cheap/fast class" },
    "chat-reasoning": { "provider": "foundry", "deployment": "fleet-reasoning", "notes": "frontier reasoning class" },
    "chat-local":     { "provider": "foundry-local", "model": "phi-family-alias" }
  }
}
    Use Global/Data Zone Standard deployments; set the reasoning deployment's TPM limit low.
  • Assign your user the data-plane role required to call models (verify role name), then az login.
  • Call the OpenAI v1 endpoint with a bearer token: 
    #pragma warning disable OPENAI001
using Azure.Identity;
using OpenAI;
using System.ClientModel.Primitives;

var credential = new DefaultAzureCredential();
var client = new OpenAIClient(
    new BearerTokenPolicy(credential, "https://ai.azure.com/.default"), // token scope: verify against the SDK overview
    new OpenAIClientOptions { Endpoint = new Uri($"https://{resource}.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/") });

var chat = client.GetChatClient("fleet-fast");
var result = await chat.CompleteChatAsync("Reply with exactly: Trakia Freight online.");
Console.WriteLine(result.Value.Content[0].Text);
Console.WriteLine($"in={result.Value.Usage.InputTokenCount} out={result.Value.Usage.OutputTokenCount}");
    (C2 wraps this in IChatClient; here you only prove connectivity and auth.)
  • Break it: (a) Remove your role assignment and re-run — read the 401/403 body. (b) Call a deployment name that does not exist — 404. (c) Put a fake key in appsettings.json, commit to a branch and push to your fork; observe GitHub secret scanning / push protection (if enabled on your plan) and then rotate — the lesson is the rotation, not the detection.
  • Acceptance criteria: dotnet run --project src/FleetOps.Cli -- ping --role chat-fast and --role chat-reasoning both print a reply and token usage; git grep -nE "(api[-_]?key|Ocp-Apim)" -- ':!*.md' finds nothing; no key-based auth configured on the Foundry resource client path.
  • Stretch: Disable local (key) auth on the Foundry resource and confirm everything still works.

docs.title: Lab 3 — Cost guardrails by script (≈0.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Budget alerts and rate limits created reproducibly.
  • Start state: c0/lab3-start (contains scripts/budget.sh skeleton).
  • Steps:
  • Create a monthly resource-group budget with notifications at 50% and 80% actual and 100% forecasted to your email, via az consumption budget create or Bicep (Microsoft.Consumption/budgets) — verify current CLI command group; portal fallback documented in the script header.
  • Tag every resource with course=trakia, owner=<you>, module=c0 so Cost Management can group spend by module.
  • Record deployment TPM limits in docs/cost-guardrails.md: what each role costs per 1M tokens (list price, date-stamped), current TPM limit, who may raise it.
  • Write scripts/teardown.sh that deletes load-test deployments and lists anything tagged ephemeral=true.
  • Break it: Compute (on paper, then with a 30-line C# script) what a runaway loop calling the reasoning deployment at its TPM limit would cost in 48 hours at list price. Compare with your budget. This is why the rate limit, not the budget, is the real control.
  • Acceptance criteria: az consumption budget list -g rg-trakia-<you> (or equivalent) shows the budget with three notifications; all resources carry the three tags (checked by scripts/doctor.sh --azure); docs/cost-guardrails.md exists with a date stamp.
  • Stretch: Add an Azure Policy assignment that denies resources without the owner tag in the course resource group.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Foundry Local and the language primers (≈1.25h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Run a small model locally behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint; pass the C#, Python and Node reading checkpoints.
  • Start state: c0/lab4-start.
  • Steps:
  • Install Foundry Local (Windows/macOS/Linux x64) and run a small Phi-family or Qwen model from the curated catalog (CLI command names: verify against current Foundry Local docs). Note which execution provider (CPU/GPU/NPU) it picked.
  • Point the same OpenAIClient code from Lab 2 at the local endpoint (local endpoints accept a dummy key). Compare latency and answer quality for the prompt "Summarize in one sentence: Truck РВ 4521 КН reported a coolant leak near Stara Zagora." in English and Bulgarian.
  • C# crash-course checkpoints (for non-.NET developers; ~30 min with the pointers below): records and init; nullable reference types; async/await, IAsyncEnumerable<T> and await foreach; LINQ; generics; System.Text.Json with source generation; dependency injection (IServiceCollection, lifetimes); minimal APIs (app.MapPost); options pattern (IOptions<T>); xUnit [Fact]/[Theory]. Exercise: make the provided TripSummaryTests pass by implementing a record and an async method.
  • Python primer [Python] (~15 min): create the env with uv sync in scripts/python/, run hello_eval.py (reads a JSONL file, prints pass rate). Learn to read: virtual envs, pyproject.toml, async def, type hints, Pydantic models, pytest.
  • Node primer (~10 min): npm ci in tools/node/, run npx playwright --version; understand package.json, package-lock.json, npx.
  • Break it: Ask the local model for a JSON object with three fields for 10 different incident sentences. Count invalid JSON outputs. Keep the number — you will reduce it in C3.
  • Acceptance criteria: dotnet run --project src/FleetOps.Cli -- ping --role chat-local succeeds offline (network disabled); dotnet test --filter Category=C0Primer green; scripts/python/hello_eval.py prints a pass rate.
  • Stretch: Measure tokens/s locally vs cloud for a 300-token answer; record in docs/local-vs-cloud.md.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text: "Fresh machine in 20 minutes" (20–30 min, repeat 3×). Start from a clean Codespace (or a teammate's laptop) and reach: devcontainer up, doctor.sh green, ping succeeding against chat-fast and chat-local, Aspire dashboard reachable. Variations: (1) a different Azure subscription (forces you to parameterize resource names); (2) no Azure access at all — local-only path; (3) a CI runner — make ci.yml do it unattended with OIDC. Track your time; target < 15 min on the third run.

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text: Nothing user-facing yet: the solution skeleton builds, FleetOps.Cli ping reaches every model role, and models.json defines the roles that every later module uses. The TrakiaOps SQL Server 2025 database and the BG/EN document corpus are restored locally (Aspire runs SQL Server in a container) and verified by doctor.sh --data.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text: Dev environment as code (devcontainer, pinned SDK and packages), CI building and testing inside the same container, keyless auth for humans and CI, cost alerts and rate limits, a teardown script. This is the sandbox your coding agents inherit in C4 — a coding agent can only verify its work if dotnet test behaves identically for it.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Reproducibility Works only on own machine Devcontainer builds; manual steps remain Devcontainer + CI green; versions centrally pinned Codespace-to-green < 15 min, prebuilds, doctor checks data + Azure Security of credentials Keys in config Keys in user-secrets Entra ID everywhere except local endpoints Local auth disabled on resource; OIDC in CI; push protection verified Cost control No alerts Budget exists Budget + TPM limits + tags Budget + limits + tags + policy + teardown script, with a written runaway-cost estimate Platform currency Uses hub/Assistants samples New resource/project model Correct endpoints and SDK families Can explain why each legacy pattern is legacy and how to detect it in a sample Gate readiness (outcome 7) Thinks gates re-run the visible tests Names the three gate components (hidden suite, code review, design defense from G2) Explains hidden suites, 3-run nondeterminism handling (mean for quality, pass^3 for safety), the unaided segment and the ownership rule Explains the gate-sensitivity check and why thresholds are relative to the reference plus an absolute floor

Auto-checked: doctor.sh (env, Azure, data), CI status on the c0 branch, absence of secrets (gitleaks step), tag compliance, presence of docs/cost-guardrails.md.

Gate-readiness check (10 min, auto-marked quiz, pass 5/6, retake allowed): six short questions answered from gates.md: (1) what the three G1–G3 assessment components are; (2) why overfitting prompts to your own golden set does not help; (3) how the hidden suite handles nondeterminism (mean of 3 runs vs pass^3 for safety items); (4) what is allowed in the unaided segment; (5) what the ownership rule means for code your agent wrote; (6) what the gate-sensitivity check does to your CI eval gate. Misconceptions are revisited in the C5 debrief before G1.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Creating a hub-based project from an old tutorial; it lands in "Foundry (classic)" and later labs' endpoints won't match.
  • Choosing a region where your models aren't offered, then scattering deployments across regions.
  • Leaving rollForward unset and silently picking up a different SDK on the CI runner.
  • Assuming the budget will stop spend; it won't.
  • Mixing Azure.AI.Projects.OpenAI (preview) with Azure.AI.Extensions.OpenAI (GA) — ambiguous type compile errors.
  • Running Docker-dependent Aspire resources without Docker-in-Docker in the devcontainer.
  • On Apple silicon or ARM Windows, assuming an x64-only container image works; check image architectures.

docs.title: C1 — How generative AI works: an engineer's mental model
docs.text: Level: 1 — Foundations (Beginner) · Duration: 10h (theory 30% / labs 70%) · Prerequisites: C0 (environment, chat-fast/chat-reasoning/chat-local roles working) · Volatility: Low for mechanics; High for the model landscape and prices

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Trakia Freight's CFO asks a simple question: "If 600 drivers each ask the copilot ten questions a day, what does it cost, and can we trust the answers?" An engineer without a mental model of LLMs answers with a per-token price from a vendor page and a demo. Three months later the bill is 4× the estimate (Bulgarian text is token-heavier, the reasoning model spends hidden thinking tokens, the system prompt is resent with every turn), the regression tests are flaky ("but we set temperature to 0"), and a dispatcher acted on a confidently invented regulation.

Every one of those failures follows from mechanics you can learn in a day: text is billed and limited in tokens, not words; the model outputs a probability distribution and something samples from it; serving infrastructure is not batch-invariant, so even greedy decoding varies; input, output and reasoning tokens share one context budget; training and benchmarks reward guessing over abstaining, so hallucination is structural; and price per token is not cost per task. Experts don't memorize transformer math — they predict system behavior from these facts and then measure it.

This module is deliberately "predict → run → explain". For every claim you will first predict the outcome, then measure it against Trakia data with your own .NET harness, then explain the gap. The harness you build becomes the seed of the eval infrastructure in C5.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of C1 you can:

  1. Explain the pipeline text → tokens → embeddings → attention/MLP (or MoE) layers → next-token distribution → sampling, and predict how each stage affects cost, latency and failure modes.
  2. Measure token counts for the same content in English and Bulgarian with Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers and reconcile them with provider-reported usage.
  3. Demonstrate nondeterminism at temperature 0 and choose test strategies (schemas, graders, pass rates) that tolerate it.
  4. Compare reasoning effort levels on accuracy, latency and cost for a Trakia task, and justify a default.
  5. Calculate cost per task (not per token) for a feature, including system-prompt resend, reasoning tokens and caching.
  6. Describe pretraining vs post-training (SFT, RLHF, DPO, RLVR) and use that to explain knowledge cutoffs, refusal behavior and why fine-tuning does not teach fresh facts.
  7. Classify current models by capability class and choose a class (not a name) for a requirement.
  8. Decide when not to use an LLM (classical ML, OCR/document models, rules) and defend the choice with evidence.
  9. Apply the minimal ML vocabulary (loss, gradient descent, overfitting, train/val/test) to prompt iteration and eval sets.

docs.title: 1. Minimal ML you actually need
docs.text:
• Supervised learning loop: data → model with parameters → loss (a scalar measuring error) → gradient descent updates parameters to reduce loss → evaluate on held-out data. LLM pretraining minimizes next-token cross-entropy — self-supervised, labels come from the text itself.
  • Train / validation / test: fit on train, tune on validation, report once on test. The same discipline governs prompts: if you tweak a prompt until your 50 golden cases pass, those 50 cases are now training data; you need a held-out set (Gate G1's hidden suite exists for exactly this reason).
  • Overfitting: a model (or prompt) that memorizes its training examples and degrades on new ones. In LLM land: a prompt full of special cases for your eval set; a fine-tune on 20 examples that loses general capability.
  • Parameters and memory: weights are numbers; memory ≈ params × bytes/param (FP16 = 2, INT8 = 1, INT4 ≈ 0.5) plus KV cache. Fine-tuning changes weights; prompting and RAG do not. That single distinction drives most architecture decisions.

docs.title: 2. Tokens and BPE
docs.text:
LLMs see token IDs, produced by subword tokenizers such as byte-pair encoding (BPE): frequent character sequences become single tokens, rare ones split into several. Consequences:

  • Cost and limits are in tokens. Context windows, rate limits (TPM), prices and max output are all token-denominated.
  • Language skew. Tokenizer vocabularies are trained on corpora dominated by English; Cyrillic Bulgarian typically needs more tokens per word. No published measurement for current tokenizers was found, so you will produce Trakia's number in Lab 1. Expect it to matter for budgets, context limits and latency (output tokens are generated one at a time).
  • Quirks: spelling, character counting, arithmetic on long numbers, and look-alike characters (Bulgarian licence plates use Cyrillic letters that have Latin homoglyphs: "РВ 4521 КН" in Cyrillic vs "PB 4521 KH" in Latin are different token sequences and different strings to your database).
  • Different model families use different tokenizers; a local count is an estimate. The provider's reported usage is the bill.

docs.title: 3. Embeddings, attention, layers — at practitioner depth
docs.text:
• Embeddings: each token ID maps to a learned vector; geometry encodes meaning. Embedding models (C6) produce one vector per text for search.
  • Self-attention: each position computes queries, keys and values; output = softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V, i.e. every token mixes information from previous tokens weighted by relevance. Many heads, many layers, interleaved with feed-forward (MLP) blocks.
  • Position: rotary position embeddings (RoPE) encode order; context-extension tricks build on them, which is one reason quality degrades unevenly over very long contexts.
  • Practical consequences: attention cost grows with context length (FlashAttention and grouped-query attention make long contexts affordable, not free); prompt order matters; information in the middle of long contexts is used less reliably ("lost in the middle"); one irrelevant distractor measurably hurts (context rot — C13).

docs.title: 4. Context window and KV cache
docs.text:
• One budget. On Azure, current GPT-5.x/GPT-6 models have a 1,050,000-token window (922,000 input, 128,000 output). Microsoft: "Input tokens, generated output tokens, and reasoning tokens share the available context budget"; max output is "an upper limit, not a guaranteed output size." Claude 5.5-generation models: 1M context, 128K max output.
  • KV cache: during generation the model stores keys/values for prior tokens so it doesn't recompute them. This explains TTFT (time to first token: processing the whole prompt, "prefill") vs inter-token latency (decode, roughly constant per token), why long prompts cost memory, and why prompt caching works: providers reuse the KV cache of an identical prefix at a discount. Example (Claude Opus 5.5 list): base input $4/MTok, cache read $0.20/MTok, cache write $5/MTok (5-min TTL), minimum cacheable prompt 512 tokens (cache-write price, TTL and minimum: verify against current documentation); Batch API −50%. Consequence for design: static content first (system prompt, tool schemas, policies), dynamic content last (C3).
  • "1M context" ≠ "use 1M". Cost scales linearly, latency grows, and quality on long inputs degrades; focused ~300-token inputs beat ~113k-token inputs for every model family in Chroma's 2025 study.

docs.title: 5. Pretraining vs post-training
docs.text:
• Pretraining: next-token prediction on huge corpora → a base model that continues text. Knowledge is frozen at the cutoff.
  • Post-training turns it into an assistant:
  • SFT — supervised fine-tuning on (prompt, ideal response) demonstrations.
  • RLHF — reward model trained on human rankings, then RL (InstructGPT). RLAIF/Constitutional AI replaces much human labeling with AI feedback against written principles.
  • DPO — optimize directly on preferred/rejected pairs, no separate reward model.
  • RLVR — RL with verifiable rewards (unit tests, math checkers); DeepSeek-R1 showed long chain-of-thought reasoning emerging from it.
  • These are now your tools too: Foundry offers managed SFT, DPO and RFT (reinforcement fine-tuning with a grader) — D1. Microsoft's own guidance: fine-tuning benefit "isn't guaranteed" (compare against a baseline with held-out evaluation) and it "doesn't replace retrieval for current information."

docs.title: 6. Reasoning models and test-time compute
docs.text:
As of October 2026, effectively every frontier model is a reasoning model: it spends extra (often hidden) reasoning tokens before answering, and you control depth with an effort parameter. Claude 5.5-generation models use adaptive thinking with effort (Opus 5.5 default medium); Azure GPT models expose reasoning_effort, except gpt-chat-latest, which uses a fixed level you cannot set. MAI-Thinking-1 (preview) ships encrypted chain-of-thought — billed, not readable. Test-time compute can substitute for model size on some tasks, but:

  • reasoning tokens are billed and consume the context budget;
  • they inflate latency (and TTFT perceived by users);
  • higher effort helps multi-step reasoning, rarely helps lookup or extraction;
  • many reasoning endpoints restrict or ignore sampling knobs (temperature/top-p) — your abstraction layer must tolerate provider-specific parameters (C2).

docs.title: 7. Mixture-of-Experts and multimodality
docs.text:
• MoE: a router activates a few expert feed-forward blocks per token. Memory follows total parameters; compute follows active parameters. A "35B-A3B" model needs memory for 35B weights but computes like ~3B per token — vital when sizing local or self-hosted models (D1). Reported 2026 extremes: ~2.8T total / ~104B active (Kimi K3, aggregator figure).
  • Multimodality: text+image input is standard at the frontier; Azure's catalog adds realtime speech-to-speech, transcription with diarization, TTS, image generation and (unstable) video. Each has distinct latency/cost profiles (D3).

docs.title: 8. Sampling
docs.text:
The model outputs logits → softmax → a probability distribution over the vocabulary. Then:

  • Temperature rescales logits: low = peaked (near-greedy), high = flatter. Low for extraction/classification, higher for ideation; it is not a "creativity dial for facts".
  • Top-p (nucleus) samples from the smallest set whose cumulative probability ≥ p; top-k keeps the k most likely. Tune temperature or top-p, not both.
  • Max output tokens, stop sequences, penalties. A truncated answer reports finish_reason = length; unhandled truncation is a common production incident (half a JSON object).
  • Seed: best-effort reproducibility only.

docs.title: 9. Nondeterminism even at temperature 0
docs.text: Temperature 0 is not deterministic in production serving. Thinking Machines Lab showed the main cause is that inference kernels are not batch-invariant: your request's numerics depend on what else is in the batch (server load), not merely "GPU floating-point randomness". Batch-invariant kernels can fix it at a performance cost, but you don't control the provider's kernels. Engineering rule #1 of this course: never assert exact strings. Assert schemas, properties, grader verdicts, and statistical pass rates over N runs (C5).

docs.title: 10. Why models hallucinate
docs.text: Hallucinations are structural: next-token training and accuracy-only benchmarks reward guessing over "I don't know" (OpenAI, 2025). Types: factual fabrication, unfaithfulness to provided context (including lost-in-the-middle), and tool-call hallucination (invented tools or arguments). Mitigations are systemic: grounding/RAG with citations (C7), structured outputs and validation (C3), explicit permission and incentive to abstain, verification steps, and evals that reward abstention.

docs.title: 11. Token economics: price per token ≠ cost per task
docs.text:
Cost per task = Σ over calls of (input tokens × input price + cached input × cache price + (output + reasoning) tokens × output price). It depends on:

  • Prompt overhead resent every turn (system prompt + tool schemas + history).
  • Reasoning tokens (hidden, billed at output price).
  • Verbosity — a newer model at the same token price can cost more per task (Gemini 3.8 Flash vs 3.7 Flash) because it uses more tokens; vendor "per-task" savings claims are estimates.
  • Language (token inflation), retries, tool loops (each iteration resends context), caching hit rate, Batch discounts.

Illustrative list prices (research notes, Oct 2026; aggregator-sourced except Anthropic; verify against Azure pricing before teaching): GPT-6 Luna $0.10/$0.50; Claude Haiku 5.5 from $0.10/$0.50; GPT-6 Sol and Claude Sonnet 5.5 $2/$10; Claude Opus 5.5 $4/$20; GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 $10/$50; DeepSeek V4.1 Flash $0.30/$1.20.

docs.title: 12. The model landscape by capability class (Oct 2026)
docs.text:
Teach and design by class; names churn monthly.

Class Examples (Oct 2026) On Microsoft Foundry? Frontier reasoning GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable 5.1, Gemini 4 Argon GPT-6 yes; Opus 5.5 confirmed; Fable unverified; Gemini no Balanced workhorse GPT-6/6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5, Grok 4.7 GPT, Opus 5.5, Grok yes Cheap/fast high volume GPT-6 Luna, Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-5.4-nano GPT yes; Haiku unverified Open-weight large DeepSeek V4/V4.1, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8, Mistral Large 3, gpt-oss-120b DeepSeek V4, Kimi K2.x, Mistral Large 3, gpt-oss yes SLM / on-device Phi family, Qwen3.8-27B, gpt-oss-20b, Ministral-3B Via Foundry Local / catalog Specialists coding (GPT-5.x-codex), realtime voice (gpt-realtime-2.1), embeddings/rerank (text-embedding-3-*, Cohere v4), document/OCR (mistral-ocr-4-0, Cohere-parse-v5) Yes

Also: Microsoft Foundry is the most multi-vendor catalog; tool calling and JSON output are not universal (e.g., Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Llama-4-Maverick, mistral-medium-3-5 listed without tool calling); benchmarks are saturating and mostly vendor-run — your own eval set (C5) is the only benchmark that matters; "open-weight" ≠ "open-source" ≠ "free for any use" (licences range from MIT/Apache-2.0 to custom).

docs.title: 13. When NOT to use an LLM
docs.text:
Need Prefer non-LLM when… Prefer LLM when… Tabular prediction (e.g., Trakia breakdown risk from maintenance history) Almost always: gradient-boosted trees / ML.NET AutoML — cheaper, explainable Narrating the model's output Telematics anomaly detection / fuel forecasting Numeric, streaming, seasonal (ML.NET SSA, rules) Explaining anomalies, hypotheses Fixed-layout extraction (delivery notes, invoices) High volume, need per-field confidence/bounding boxes: Document Intelligence / Content Understanding Variable layouts, reasoning over content High-volume text classification Fine-tuned small model or typed "decision model"; ms latency Low volume, changing labels, zero-shot Deterministic rules (EU driving-time limits) Encode rules in code; they are law, not vibes Explaining a violation in plain language Batch speech transcription Azure Speech Conversational realtime agents

Decide per task on accuracy, cost, latency, explainability evidence — not on fashion. The tachograph rule check is the canonical Trakia example: the LLM explains, code decides.

docs.title: Misconceptions to unlearn
docs.text: "Tokens are words." "Temperature 0 is deterministic." "1M context means I can use 1M." "If it's in context the model uses it." "Fine-tuning teaches our latest facts." "The model executes tools" (it emits a structured request; your code executes — C3). "Cheaper per token = cheaper." "Benchmarks tell me which model is best for my app." "I can audit the chain of thought" (it may be hidden or encrypted). "MoE needs memory only for active params."

docs.title: Tools & versions (as of Oct 2026)
docs.text: Tool / package Purpose Status Notes Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers (+ data packages, e.g. o200k encoding) Local token counting GA Local counts are estimates for non-matching tokenizers; reconcile with API usage Microsoft.Extensions.AI 10.x Provider-agnostic calls (IChatClient) GA Full treatment in C2; used here via a provided harness OpenAI .NET package → /openai/v1/ Raw access incl. logprobs where supported GA Logprob support varies by model — verify per deployment Foundry deployments: fast, reasoning Experiments GA Roles from models.json Foundry Local Local model comparisons GA Small models; CPU/GPU/NPU auto ML.NET (+ AutoML) Classical ML baseline GA "When not to use an LLM" lab Polyglot Notebooks / dotnet run scripts Plotting results — Or export CSV to Excel nanoGPT / micrograd [Python] Optional deep-dive — Side reading only; not required

docs.title: Lab 1 — Tokens in two languages (≈1.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Produce Trakia's own number: tokens per word and per character for Bulgarian vs English, and its monthly cost impact.
  • Start state: c1/lab1-start (src/FleetOps.Lab.Tokens, corpus sample: 20 paired BG/EN paragraphs from the fleet policy handbook and driver code of conduct).
  • Steps:
  • Count locally: 
    using Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers;
Tokenizer tok = TiktokenTokenizer.CreateForModel("gpt-4o"); // o200k proxy; verify encoding for your deployment
foreach (var (id, bg, en) in pairs)
{
    int bgT = tok.CountTokens(bg), enT = tok.CountTokens(en);
    rows.Add(new(id, bgT, enT, Words(bg), Words(en), (double)bgT / enT));
}
  • Reconcile: send each paragraph to chat-fast with a trivial instruction and record usage.InputTokenCount. Subtract the fixed overhead (send an empty-content message to measure it). Compute the error of the local estimate.
  • Repeat for chat-local (different tokenizer) using its reported usage.
  • Plate-number homoglyphs: tokenize "РВ 4521 КН" (Cyrillic) and "PB 4521 KH" (Latin); write a 10-line normalizer and a unit test.
  • Cost projection: 600 drivers × 10 questions/day × 22 workdays; average question + answer sizes from the corpus; system prompt 1,200 tokens resent each call. Produce a table: EN-only vs BG-only, fast vs reasoning class, with and without prompt caching.
  • Break it: Prepend the full 3,000-word driver code of conduct to every request "for context". Recompute monthly cost and measure TTFT.
  • Acceptance criteria: dotnet test --filter Lab=C1.Tokens green (normalizer tests, reconciliation error < 5% for the matching tokenizer); docs/c1/token-report.md contains the BG/EN ratio with method, the reconciliation table and the cost projection.
  • Stretch: Add Bulgarian Latin transliteration ("шльокавица") inputs — how do token counts and answer quality change?

docs.title: Lab 2 — Sampling and nondeterminism (≈2h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Observe output distributions and design tests that survive them.
  • Start state: c1/lab2-start (SamplingHarness that runs a prompt N times and stores outputs as JSONL).
  • Steps:
  • Prompt: classify a Trakia incident note ("Шофьорът съобщава за силен шум от предната лява гума на АМ Тракия, км 142") into one of {tyre, brakes, engine, cargo, accident, other}; answer with the label only.
  • Run 20× each at temperature 0, 0.7 and 1.2 on chat-fast (where temperature is supported). Record distinct outputs, label distribution and invalid-label rate.
  • Run 20× at temperature 0 with a long free-text summary prompt. Count distinct outputs (string-exact) and semantically different outputs (compare extracted fields).
  • Try the same on chat-reasoning; record which parameters are rejected or ignored.
  • Force truncation with MaxOutputTokens = 20 on a summary; detect finish_reason = length and handle it (retry with higher limit or return a typed "truncated" result).
  • Optional (if the deployment returns logprobs): turn the classifier into a thresholded classifier — accept only if top-label probability ≥ 0.8, else route to a human.
  • Break it: Write an xUnit test that asserts the exact summary string. Run it 10 times in CI. Then rewrite it to assert (a) the label ∈ allowed set, (b) the summary mentions the km marker and the tyre, (c) pass rate ≥ 9/10.
  • Acceptance criteria: docs/c1/sampling-report.md with the three distributions and your explanation referencing batch invariance; the exact-string test is deleted; the property-based test passes in 3 consecutive CI runs; truncation handler has a unit test.
  • Stretch: Plot answer diversity (distinct outputs) vs temperature for 5 prompts.

docs.title: Lab 3 — Reasoning effort and context budget (≈2h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Quantify accuracy vs latency vs cost across effort levels and context sizes.
  • Start state: c1/lab3-start (12 driving-time questions with ground-truth answers computed by a deterministic C# rule engine from the EU driving-time summary; plus a "needle" document set).
  • Steps:
  • For each question, call chat-reasoning at effort low/medium/high (provider-specific option passed via the harness — verify the exact parameter name and its MEAI mapping for your deployment). Record correctness (compare to rule engine), latency, input/output/reasoning tokens, cost.
  • Compare with chat-fast (no or minimal reasoning).
  • Needle test: hide one fact ("Depot Varna's tyre supplier changed to Balkan Tyres on 3 Sept") at the start, middle and end of padded contexts of 2k, 20k and 100k tokens of policy text. Ask for it 5× per cell.
  • Break it: Set MaxOutputTokens low on high effort. Observe empty or truncated answers because reasoning consumed the budget.
  • Acceptance criteria: docs/c1/effort-report.md with an accuracy/latency/cost table per effort level and a one-paragraph recommended default for this task; needle grid (position × size) with recall; an ADR (docs/adr/0001-default-reasoning-effort.md) that cites your numbers. This is your first ADR: use the course template and checklist in docs/adr/README.md — context, ≥ 3 options considered (incl. "do nothing / status quo" where meaningful), decision, consequences, evidence links and a review date (the ADR linter enforces this from here on; here the options are effort levels plus the status-quo default).
  • Stretch: Replace the LLM for the driving-time questions with the rule engine plus an LLM that only explains the engine's output. Compare accuracy and cost.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Cost calculator and local vs cloud (≈1.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: A reusable cost-per-task calculator and an evidence-based local-vs-cloud comparison.
  • Start state: c1/lab4-start (pricing.json with date-stamped list prices per role).
  • Steps:
  • Implement CostCalculator.ForCall(UsageDetails usage, ModelPrice price) including cached-input and reasoning tokens (reasoning billed as output); unit-test it with hand-computed cases.
  • Run the incident-classification task (Lab 2) over 40 labeled incident notes on chat-fast, chat-reasoning and chat-local. Record accuracy, p50/p95 latency, cost per 1,000 tasks (local = €0 marginal; note hardware and energy as a footnote).
  • Train an ML.NET text classifier on 400 labeled historical incident notes (provided) and evaluate on the same 40. Build a confusion matrix for each approach.
  • Break it: Swap chat-fast for a model in the catalog listed without tool calling / JSON support and request JSON-mode output — record the failure.
  • Acceptance criteria: Calculator tests green; docs/c1/model-bakeoff.md with a 4-row table (fast, reasoning, local, ML.NET) × (accuracy, p95 latency, cost/1k, explainability) and a recommendation; pricing.json carries a "retrieved on" date.
  • Stretch: Model a cascade: ML.NET first, LLM only when classifier confidence < threshold; compute blended cost and accuracy.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text: "Predict, run, explain" (25–30 min, repeat with a new myth each time). Pick one misconception card (tokens = words; T=0 deterministic; 1M context usable; in-context = used; cheaper per token = cheaper; fine-tune = new facts; model executes tools). (1) Write your prediction and a falsifiable test in 3 sentences. (2) Run it with the harness on Trakia data (≤10 min). (3) Write a 5-sentence explanation citing the mechanism. Variation: switch model role or language (BG/EN) and predict whether the result changes.

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text: No new user feature. The product gains its economic and behavioral baseline: the token report (BG/EN ratio), the effort ADR, the cost calculator and pricing.json (consumed by C2's cost logging middleware), and the incident-classification labeled set that seeds the golden dataset in C5.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text: The SamplingHarness (run N times, store JSONL, compute pass rates) and the cost calculator become shared factory tools in tools/, used by eval tests from C5 on. Rule recorded in the repo's conventions for later agents: no exact-string assertions on model output.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Mechanistic explanation Repeats definitions Explains tokens, sampling, context correctly Predicts outcomes of experiments before running them Explains surprises (e.g., reasoning budget truncation, batch variance) and their engineering consequences Measurement rigor Single runs, anecdotes Repeated runs, basic tables N runs, distributions, reconciled with provider usage Confidence intervals, controlled variables, documented method others can rerun Cost reasoning Quotes per-token price Computes per-call cost Cost per task incl. overhead, reasoning, caching Cost model with sensitivity analysis (language mix, effort, cache hit rate) feeding an ADR Tool selection LLM for everything Knows alternatives exist Uses evidence to pick LLM vs ML.NET vs rules Designs hybrids/cascades and justifies on accuracy/cost/latency/explainability

Auto-checked: lab test filters (Lab=C1.*), presence and structure of the four reports and ADR-0001 (required headings, numeric tables), no exact-string assertions on model output (analyzer rule in tests/).

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Counting tokens with a tokenizer that doesn't match the deployment and treating it as truth.
  • Forgetting the system prompt and tool schemas in cost estimates — they are resent every call.
  • Comparing effort levels on a lookup task where reasoning can't help, and concluding "reasoning is useless".
  • Setting both temperature and top-p, or setting them on a reasoning endpoint that ignores them, then drawing conclusions.
  • Treating a single run as a measurement.
  • Quoting aggregator prices as facts; always date-stamp and cite.

docs.title: C2 — Your first AI feature in .NET
docs.text: Level: 1 — Foundations (Beginner) · Duration: 12h (theory 25% / labs 75%) · Prerequisites: C0 (env, Foundry project, model roles), C1 (tokens, sampling, cost per task) · Volatility: Med (MEAI 10.x is GA and stable; OpenAI/Foundry SDK surface and Responses adapters move quarterly)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Trakia's first copilot prototype was written in an afternoon: an HttpClient posting JSON to a model endpoint, a hard-coded model name, an API key in appsettings.json, string concatenation for the conversation, and no logging. It demoed well. Then the model was deprecated (60-day notice, 410 Gone after retirement), the security review rejected the key, the first load test produced a wall of 429 Too Many Requests that the code treated as fatal, and nobody could answer "what did that conversation cost?" because token usage was never captured.

The fix is not "more code" but the right abstraction. Microsoft.Extensions.AI (MEAI) gives .NET a provider-agnostic IChatClient with a composable middleware pipeline — the same shape ASP.NET Core developers know from HTTP middleware. Logging, OpenTelemetry, caching, tool invocation, cost accounting and guardrails become decorators you add in DI, and the provider (Foundry cloud model, Foundry Local, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) becomes configuration. Microsoft Agent Framework (C9) and the MCP SDK (C8) are built on these same abstractions, so everything you learn here carries forward.

Experts ship the boring parts on day one: keyless auth, retries that honor Retry-After, cancellation, streaming with back-pressure, usage capture per call, and traces that show every model call in the Aspire dashboard. That is what makes the later modules — evals, cost dashboards, model migrations — possible at all.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of C2 you can:

  1. Implement a chat feature on IChatClient with conversation state, ChatOptions and streaming (GetStreamingResponseAsync) in a console app and an ASP.NET Core minimal API.
  2. Connect to Foundry via the OpenAI v1 endpoint and via the Foundry project endpoint (Responses API), and justify which path to use.
  3. Compose a middleware pipeline with ChatClientBuilder: logging, OpenTelemetry, distributed caching, function invocation, plus a custom cost-logging/budget middleware.
  4. Register chat clients in DI (including keyed clients per model role) and orchestrate the app with Aspire, seeing GenAI spans in the dashboard.
  5. Swap providers (Foundry ↔ Foundry Local ↔ OpenAI-compatible local runner) by configuration only, and detect capability differences between them.
  6. Configure keyless authentication (Entra ID locally, managed identity in Azure) and keep secrets out of source.
  7. Handle 429s, timeouts and transient faults with bounded retries that honor Retry-After, plus cancellation and concurrency limits.
  8. Log token usage and cost per call and per conversation using the C1 cost calculator.

docs.title: The .NET AI stack, layered
docs.text: Microsoft's .NET AI decision guide: MEAI (IChatClient, IEmbeddingGenerator, ChatClientBuilder) for AI behavior; MEVD/MEDI for your own data (C6–C7); MCP SDK to share capabilities (C8); MAF or the Copilot SDK for agents (C9); Foundry / Foundry Local / Aspire for hosting. IChatClient and IEmbeddingGenerator<,> were extracted from Semantic Kernel into MEAI; Microsoft.Extensions.AI.Abstractions is at 10.5.0 (version-aligned with .NET 10).

docs.title: IChatClient in one screen
docs.text:
public interface IChatClient : IDisposable
{
    Task<ChatResponse> GetResponseAsync(IEnumerable<ChatMessage> messages,
        ChatOptions? options = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
    IAsyncEnumerable<ChatResponseUpdate> GetStreamingResponseAsync(IEnumerable<ChatMessage> messages,
        ChatOptions? options = null, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
    object? GetService(Type serviceType, object? serviceKey = null);
}
  • Messages carry a role (System, User, Assistant, Tool) and a list of AIContent items: TextContent, DataContent (images/audio bytes), UriContent, FunctionCallContent/FunctionResultContent (C3), and approval-request content for human-in-the-loop (C9).
  • ChatOptions: ModelId, Temperature, TopP, MaxOutputTokens, StopSequences, Seed, ResponseFormat, Tools, ToolMode, plus an escape hatch for provider-specific options (e.g. reasoning effort) via AdditionalProperties or a raw-representation factory — verify the current mechanism for effort on your provider adapter before teaching.
  • ChatResponse: Messages, Text, FinishReason, ModelId, Usage (InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, TotalTokenCount, plus provider extras in AdditionalCounts, where reasoning/cached tokens may appear — inspect per provider), RawRepresentation (the provider's object, for debugging).
  • Streaming yields ChatResponseUpdates; updates.ToChatResponse() reassembles a full response (including usage, if the provider sends it at the end).
  • Statelessness: with Chat Completions you send the whole history every call (and pay for it — C1). The Responses API can hold conversation state server-side; MEAI surfaces this via a conversation/response ID on options/response (verify property names in your MEAI version). Server-side state cuts payload size but couples you to the provider and its retention policy — a GDPR question (C18).

docs.title: Two endpoint paths to Foundry
docs.text:
OpenAI v1 endpoint Foundry project endpoint URL https://<res>.openai.azure.com/openai/v1/ https://<res>.services.ai.azure.com/api/projects/<project> .NET package OpenAI + Microsoft.Extensions.AI.OpenAI adapter Azure.AI.Projects 2.0 / Azure.AI.Extensions.OpenAI 2.0 (GA) Auth BearerTokenPolicy(cred, "https://ai.azure.com/.default") (token scope per the SDK overview at release time — some docs still use https://cognitiveservices.azure.com/.default; verify against current documentation) DefaultAzureCredential Use when Plain model calls; maximum portability (same code hits any OpenAI-compatible server incl. Foundry Local) You need project-scoped features: agents, connections, evaluations, tracing in the Foundry Control Plane

Both expose the Responses API (the successor to the Assistants API, retired 26 Aug 2026). Some OpenAI-package APIs require #pragma warning disable OPENAI001. Never mix the preview Azure.AI.Projects.OpenAI with GA Azure.AI.Extensions.OpenAI.

docs.title: The middleware pipeline
docs.text:
ChatClientBuilder wraps an inner client in delegating clients; order matters (outermost first in the builder chain):

IChatClient client = new ChatClientBuilder(innerClient)
    .UseLogging(loggerFactory)                 // outermost: sees every request incl. cache hits
    .UseDistributedCache(cache)                // identical requests served from cache (non-personal prompts only)
    .UseFunctionInvocation()                   // runs tool loops (C3); everything below sees each iteration
    .UseOpenTelemetry(sourceName: "FleetOps.AI", configure: o => o.EnableSensitiveData = false) // one span per model call
    .Use(inner => new CostTrackingChatClient(inner, pricing, costSink))  // custom; closest to the provider
    .Build(services);

Design rules (the first Use… call is the outermost wrapper; each wrapper only sees calls that pass through it):

  • Logging outside the cache if you want to observe cache hits; cost tracking inside the cache so cached responses cost €0.
  • Function invocation outside (above) per-call telemetry and cost tracking, so each tool-loop iteration is individually traced and costed. If you place UseFunctionInvocation() innermost, the outer middleware sees one aggregated call per user request ("tool loops show only one span" — kata below). Caching outside function invocation caches the final answer of a tool loop; never do that for answers built from live data (vehicle status).
  • Sensitive data (prompt/response content) is off by default in OTel; content capture in EU production must be justified in the DPIA. Turn it on in dev only.
  • Custom middleware subclasses DelegatingChatClient and overrides both the non-streaming and streaming methods — forgetting the streaming override is the most common bug.
  • Caching LLM responses is safe for deterministic, non-personal prompts (evals, static lookups). Never cache user- or time-specific answers across users (leakage).

docs.title: Observability with Aspire
docs.text: Aspire's AppHost starts the API, SQL Server container and any local resources; ServiceDefaults wire OpenTelemetry. Register your MEAI source name with the tracer/meter providers, and model calls appear as GenAI spans (the dashboard marks LLM calls with a "sparkles" indicator). Span/attribute names follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, which are still entirely at "Development" stability and moved to open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai in v1.42.0 — attribute names can change (gen_ai.system → gen_ai.provider.name already did). Pin package versions and don't build dashboards on attribute names you haven't verified (C15 goes deep).

docs.title: Provider swap and capability drift
docs.text: Foundry Local, Ollama, LLamaSharp and ONNX Runtime GenAI all plug into IChatClient (Foundry Local and Ollama via OpenAI-compatible endpoints or dedicated adapters). The code swaps by config; the behavior does not: small local models may lack tool calling, honor JSON schemas less reliably, ignore some options, report usage differently and have far smaller context windows. A provider swap without an eval run (C5) is an untested deployment. Use GetService<ChatClientMetadata>() to log provider and model identity on every call.

docs.title: Keyless auth and secrets
docs.text:
• Local: az login + DefaultAzureCredential (or AzureCliCredential for faster startup and fewer surprises).
  • Azure: managed identity of the hosting resource (Container Apps/App Service, C17) with a data-plane role on the Foundry resource.
  • CI: OIDC federated credential (C5).
  • Local OpenAI-compatible runners: dummy key from config; never a real key.
  • Config hierarchy: appsettings.json (non-secret), environment/Aspire parameters, user-secrets in dev; Key Vault references only for truly unavoidable secrets.

docs.title: Rate limits, 429s and retries
docs.text:
• Deployments have TPM (tokens per minute) and request-rate limits. Exceeding them returns 429 with a Retry-After header (Azure also returns remaining-quota headers — verify names before teaching).
  • The OpenAI/Azure SDK client pipeline retries transient failures (429, 5xx, timeouts) with exponential backoff by default; configure OpenAIClientOptions.RetryPolicy and NetworkTimeout explicitly rather than trusting defaults (verify default retry count for your package version).
  • Do not stack retry layers (SDK retries × your Polly retries × gateway retries = retry storms).
  • Retries are not free: a retried long prompt is re-billed for input; a streaming response that fails mid-way can't be resumed transparently.
  • Concurrency control: a SemaphoreSlim/System.Threading.RateLimiting limiter in front of the client keeps you under TPM rather than reacting to 429s.
  • Long-term fixes are architectural: APIM AI gateway with token limits and priority backends (C15, C17), Batch for offline work, smaller models for bulk.

docs.title: Misconceptions to unlearn
docs.text:
• "The SDK is the abstraction." The SDK is a provider; IChatClient is the abstraction your code depends on.
  • "Streaming makes it faster." It improves perceived latency (TTFT); total time and cost are unchanged.
  • "A provider swap is a config change." It's a config change plus an eval run.
  • "Retries fix 429s." Retries smooth bursts; sustained 429s mean capacity planning.
