docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Classification & roles Guesses tiers Correct tiers for clear cases Correct incl. grey zones, cites Art. 6(3)/profiling and roles Anticipates purpose drift; designs purpose-enforcing controls Risk file & GDPR Checklist copied Arts. 9–15 mapped Evidence linked to real artefacts; DPIA log design reconciles retention Evidence auto-refreshed; residual risks argued; counsel questions sharply framed Fairness Raw rates only Group metrics Exposure-normalised, stratified, CIs, small-n handled Confounders and proxies analysed; gate threshold justified Human oversight Approve button Evidence shown Anti-automation-bias design, second reviewer Oversight measured (honeypots, agreement) and acted upon Transparency Missing Generic text Channel-specific, BG/EN, tested Transparency Note with live metrics; readable by workers

Auto-checked: governance schema tests, aggregate-mode guardrail, content-capture regression, fairness gate, disclosure/marker UI tests. These artefacts form the RAI/compliance section of Gate G3.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Treating "internal tool" or "human in the loop" as automatic exemptions.
  • Classifying by technology ("it's just RAG") instead of by use and affected persons.
  • Choosing the non-high-risk design on paper without the technical controls that enforce it.
  • Logging everything for "AI Act compliance" and creating a GDPR problem; or logging nothing for "GDPR" and failing Art. 12/26.
  • Fairness by raw rates across depots that drive different roads.
  • Translating an English disclosure into Bulgarian with the same model you are disclosing, with no human review.
  • Teaching the 2 Aug 2026 high-risk date. The Omnibus moved Annex III to 2 Dec 2027.
  • Presenting the Bulgarian authority designation as settled.

docs.title: C19 — The automated SDLC: agents from issue to production
docs.text: Level: 3 — Production systems (Advanced) · Duration: 14h (theory 25% / labs 75%) · Prerequisites: C4 (agent-ready repo), C11 (test-first agents, Stryker.NET, Playwright agents), C14 (eval gates), C15 (tracing, cost), C16 (security gates), C17 (IaC, canary), C18 (governance checks) · Volatility: High (coding-agent features, names and billing change monthly; Azure DevOps agent support lags GitHub)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
You have built the Factory piece by piece: memory files and skills (C4), eval tests agents can run (C5, C14), test-first loops with mutation gates (C11), security agents (C16), IaC and canaries (C17), governance checks (C18). In this module the pieces become one closed loop. A dispatcher's complaint becomes a work item, the work item becomes a spec, the spec becomes a pull request written by an agent, and the PR passes a stack of automated gates and a human review before reaching a canary. Production telemetry then watches the canary, and when something degrades an SRE agent opens the next issue.

Getting this wrong is easy and expensive. Teams switch on a cloud agent, see dozens of PRs a week and declare a productivity win, while review queues grow, rework rises, tests pass because they were weakened, and nobody can explain the code in the incident review. The evidence is sobering. DORA 2025 found AI acts as a "mirror and a multiplier" of existing practices. METR's 2025 trial measured experienced developers ~19% slower while they believed they were faster, and its February 2026 update concedes developers are probably faster now but calls its own data "very weak evidence" of the size. Thoughtworks puts "coding throughput as a productivity measure" on Caution.

Experts build a governed delivery system. Verification is designed before implementation. Spec ceremony is matched to task size. Agents run in sandboxes with least-privilege tokens and cannot weaken their own gates. Humans act as spec owners, orchestrators and reviewers who can defend every merged line. Outcomes are measured (DORA keys, first-pass acceptance, rework, escaped defects, cost per merged PR), not output. This module assembles that system for Fleet Ops Copilot and prepares you for Gate G3, which audits both the product and this factory.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Choose the right level of spec ceremony (none / plan mode / spec-anchored / delta spec) for a given change, and justify it using Böckeler's spec-first / spec-anchored / spec-as-source distinction and its critiques.
  2. Configure an issue-to-PR flow with the Copilot cloud agent (from GitHub Issues and Azure Boards, with custom .agent.md agents) and with Claude Code in GitHub Actions, and compare them on the same task.
  3. Build an ordered gate stack (build, tests, mutation, evals, safety/ASR, CodeQL + agentic autofix, supply chain, architecture drift, governance, AI review, human approval, canary) where agents cannot weaken their own gates.
  4. Run parallel agents in git worktrees on decomposable work, and decide when parallelism hurts (coupled changes, review bandwidth).
  5. Operate maintenance agents: Copilot Upgrade agent for modernization, dependency agents, and a docs agent that keeps documentation and the Transparency Note current.
  6. Close the ops loop with Azure SRE Agent in Reader mode feeding issues back to coding agents, and specify when Privileged mode is acceptable.
  7. Measure the factory with DORA capabilities and agent-specific metrics, interpret them against the METR/DORA evidence, and write a governance policy for agents in the repo.

docs.title: 1. The reference loop
docs.text:
Azure Boards / GitHub issue ──► spec (right-sized) ──► coding agent (cloud or local, sandboxed)
        ▲                                                     │ draft PR on agent branch
        │                                                     ▼
 SRE Agent (Reader) ◄── canary + online evals ◄── human approval ◄── gate stack (+ AI review, autofix)

Each arrow has an owner. Humans own: the intent (issue), the acceptance tests (spec anchor), approval and the decision to promote. Agents own: implementation, first-pass review, mechanical fixes (autofix), diagnosis drafts and documentation drafts. Automation owns: the gates and the canary controller (C17). The architecture decision for .NET shops: Azure Boards can send a work item to the Copilot cloud agent, but the PR lands in a GitHub repository. No evidence was found that this flow targets Azure Repos, and Copilot Autofix for GitHub Advanced Security for Azure DevOps is only in limited preview (since 11 Jun 2026). Teams on Azure Repos get a less mature agent loop. That is a real trade-off for Trakia, whose legacy pipelines live in Azure DevOps; document it in ADR-0019.

docs.title: 2. Spec-driven development: useful, contested, right-sized
docs.text:
Birgitta Böckeler (martinfowler.com) distinguishes three levels: - Spec-first: write a spec, use it to generate code, then the spec drifts. - Spec-anchored: the spec is kept and maintained alongside the code for future changes. - Spec-as-source: humans edit only the spec; code is regenerated. Tessl's 1:1 spec-to-file mapping is the example, and regeneration gave non-deterministic output.

Tools: - GitHub Spec Kit: Constitution → Specify → Plan → Tasks, branch per spec, in practice spec-first. - Kiro: Requirements as user stories with GIVEN/WHEN/THEN criteria → Design → Tasks traced to requirements, with steering files product.md, structure.md, tech.md; its GA added property-based testing for spec correctness. - OpenSpec: propose/apply/archive with delta specs, suited to brownfield.

Thoughtworks Radar Vol. 34 rates Spec Kit and OpenSpec Assess and puts agent instruction bloat, coding agent swarms and MCP by default on Caution.

Böckeler's critiques are the reason for skepticism. Kiro turned a small bug into 4 user stories with 16 acceptance criteria. Reviewing verbose Markdown is more tedious than reviewing code. Agents still ignored specs, for example by duplicating existing classes. The approach echoes model-driven development's failure, now with non-determinism added. There is no rigorous comparative evidence that SDD beats plan-mode workflows.

Course position: spec-anchored, with the anchor executable. The durable artefact is the human-written acceptance test (xUnit + eval cases), not the prose. The ceremony ladder:

Change Ceremony One-line fix, typo, config Issue text only; agent must add a failing test first Multi-file change in one bounded context Plan mode; plan posted as PR description before code Feature Interview → specs/<id>/SPEC.md (≤1 page) + human-written acceptance tests + eval cases → fresh agent session implements Brownfield change across modules Delta spec (OpenSpec style) listing what changes against existing behaviour + characterization tests first

docs.title: 3. From issue to PR: the agents
docs.text:
GitHub Copilot cloud agent (docs now say "cloud agent" rather than "coding agent"; the URLs moved, but no official rename confirmation was found, so verify). You assign an issue to Copilot or prompt it from VS Code, the CLI or Azure Boards. It runs in an ephemeral GitHub Actions-powered environment with a firewall-controlled internet connection, runs tests and linters, runs Copilot code review on its own changes, and opens a draft PR on a copilot/ branch. It can push only to copilot/* branches, and Actions workflows on its PRs require human approval to run. Custom agents are .agent.md profiles (usually .github/agents/; org-wide in .github-private), each with its own instructions, tools, MCP servers and model; they appear in the Azure Boards agent picker. From Boards, "Create a pull request with Copilot" sends the work item's fields and last 50 comments. It requires a paid Copilot plan, the cloud agent enabled on the repo and the Azure Boards GitHub app. Environment preparation (restoring .NET 10 SDK, NuGet from the internal feed, starting SQL for integration tests) goes in the agent's setup workflow (copilot-setup-steps.yml per background knowledge; verify file name and schema).

---
# .github/agents/fleet-feature.agent.md  (frontmatter keys: verify against current docs)
name: fleet-feature
description: Implements one approved Fleet Ops spec, test-first, within one bounded context.
tools: ["read", "edit", "search", "terminal", "trakia-mcp/schema.*", "trakia-mcp/tickets.read"]
---
You implement exactly one spec in specs/<id>/. Rules:
1. Read SPEC.md and the acceptance tests in tests/Acceptance/<id>/. Never edit those tests or evals/ or .github/.
2. Run `dotnet test tests/Acceptance --filter Spec=<id>` first and confirm it fails for the right reason.
3. Implement; run `dotnet build -warnaserror`, unit tests, then `dotnet test tests/FleetOps.Evals --filter Category=Smoke`.
4. If a tool, prompt or MCP schema changes, update security/tool-manifest.yaml and explain why in the PR.
5. Stop and ask (comment on the issue) if the spec is ambiguous. Do not guess business rules.

Claude Code gives you a GitHub Actions integration, managed Code Review on PRs, Routines (cloud runs triggered by schedule, API or GitHub events) and headless claude -p with --output-format json|stream-json, --allowedTools and --permission-mode dontAsk for CI. Interactive sessions default to auto mode (a classifier reviews actions; since v2.1.283). CI runs should use explicit allow-lists, not auto mode. It reads AGENTS.md, so one memory file can serve both ecosystems.

OpenAI Codex (comparison): as of DevDay (29 Sep 2026) it has persistent configurable cloud environments, a CLI /agents view with worktree support, automatic initial PR reviews and Codex Security Cloud scanning. Thoughtworks rates Codex Trial versus Claude Code and Cursor Adopt.

Teach the transferable primitives: memory file, skills, subagents, hooks, MCP, headless mode, cloud agent → PR, AI reviewer. Then map them onto each vendor. Product walkthroughs date within months.

docs.title: 4. The gate stack: cheap and deterministic first
docs.text:
# Gate Tooling Blocking? Notes 1 Restore locked, format, analyzers, build dotnet restore --locked-mode, dotnet format --verify-no-changes, -warnaserror Yes Slopsquatting defense from C16 2 Unit + property tests xUnit, FsCheck/CsCheck Yes 3 Acceptance tests for the spec Human-owned tests/Acceptance Yes CODEOWNERS-protected 4 Mutation on changed code Stryker.NET (--since) Yes, ≥ threshold Catches hollow tests 5 Eval suite (cached) MEAI.Evaluation + dotnet aieval report Yes, per-failure-mode thresholds Uncached nightly run detects drift (C14) 6 Safety / ASR Lab 2 harness (C16), PyRIT nightly [Python] Yes for consequential ASR 7 Code scanning & secrets CodeQL, secret scanning push protection, dependency review, package allow-list Yes for high/critical Agentic autofix proposes fixes 8 Architecture drift NetArchTest / ArchUnitNET rules from ADRs Yes Agents ignore architecture without this 9 Governance C18 governance-check, tool-manifest test Yes 10 AI code review Copilot code review / Claude Code review Advisory (blocking only for high-precision categories) Track comment acceptance rate 11 Human approval CODEOWNERS, rulesets, required reviewers Yes Agent identities can't approve 12 Deploy → canary → promote azd deploy, C17 canary controller Automatic rollback Environment protection rules

Rule zero: agents cannot weaken their own gates. Put .github/, tests/Acceptance/, evals/, security/, release/canary-criteria.yaml and infra/ under CODEOWNERS with required code-owner review in a repository ruleset. Agent-authored commits that touch them need a human owner's approval and a PR label explaining why. Agent tokens are least-privilege (contents/PR write on agent branches only), secrets are not exposed to agent-triggered workflows until a human approves the run, and production deployment uses an environment with required reviewers and OIDC federation (no stored cloud secrets).

AI code review catches inconsistencies, missing tests, obvious bugs and security smells cheaply. It misses intent, cross-system effects and business rules. Anthropic notes that reviewers asked to find gaps will always find some, which pushes toward over-engineering. Make AI review advisory, give it a narrow checklist (the C16 threat register, tool-manifest rules, logging of personal data), and measure its precision (accepted comments / total).

docs.title: 5. Security autofix in the loop
docs.text: Agentic autofix for code scanning alerts went GA on 15 Oct 2026. Copilot explores the relevant files, proposes a fix, re-runs CodeQL to confirm the alert closes, iterates, then opens a draft PR with up to 25 alerts and the validation steps. Alerts can be assigned via REST (assignees: ["copilot-swe-agent[bot]"]). It requires GitHub Code Security or Advanced Security on Enterprise Cloud, with an enterprise policy plus an org/repo setting. Billing is Code Security AI credits plus Actions minutes, and it replaces the free "Generate Fix" button. For Azure DevOps, Copilot Autofix for GHAzDO is in limited preview (since 11 Jun 2026): CodeQL alerts on the default branch, including C#, at 1 AI credit = $0.01 billed to Azure. Autofix PRs go through the same gate stack; a fix that closes the alert but drops a mutation-killing test is still rejected.

docs.title: 6. Parallel agents and worktrees
docs.text: Claude Code supports git worktrees and /batch, which fans one change out to 5–30 subagents, each in its own worktree. Codex CLI added worktrees, and Cursor runs up to 8 background agents. Parallelism pays for independent, mechanical, well-tested work: migrate 14 MCP tools to the C# SDK 2.0 attribute style, add gen_ai.* attributes to every tool span, translate 40 UI strings into Bulgarian. It hurts for coupled writes, where agents with partial context make conflicting implicit decisions (Cognition's argument from C12), and it hits a hard limit at review bandwidth. If the team can review 6 PRs a day, launching 20 agents only grows the queue and the merge-conflict surface. Thoughtworks cautions against "coding agent swarms" and assesses small, role-specific "teams of coding agents". Pattern: one orchestrator session decomposes the work, N workers run in worktrees with the same gate stack locally (hooks), a reviewer subagent pre-reviews, and a human merges in dependency order.

docs.title: 7. Maintenance agents: upgrades, dependencies, docs
docs.text:
• Copilot Upgrade agent (GitHub Copilot app modernization for .NET): assess → plan → execute, writing assessment, plan and tasks files into the repo for review before execution. It runs in VS, VS Code, Copilot CLI and the cloud agent (which delivers PRs), and accepts custom skills for internal migration patterns. It covers ASP.NET Core, Blazor, Functions, WPF and libraries to .NET 10, and .NET Framework → modern .NET (Windows only). Review the plan like an ADR: it is where wrong decisions are cheap to fix.
  • Dependency agents: Dependabot PRs plus an agent that reads release notes, fixes breaking changes and runs the gate stack. Pin and allow-list as in C16.
  • Docs agents: keep docs/ consistent with code (API reference, ADR index, runbooks) and regenerate the metrics section of the Transparency Note (C18) from the latest eval artefacts. Constraints: docs agents cite the source file and line or artefact for every claim, never invent behaviour, and humans approve wording. DORA's AI capabilities model lists accessible internal knowledge as a precondition for AI benefit, and docs are context for the next agent run.

docs.title: 8. Operations: Azure SRE Agent
docs.text:
Azure SRE Agent investigates incidents and automates remediation. It queries Azure Monitor, Application Insights and Log Analytics, supports custom subagents and MCP connections, and integrates with GitHub and Azure DevOps. Modes: Reader (read-only) and Privileged (remediation). Network modes: Unrestricted, Limited or VNet. Regions: Sweden Central, East US 2, Australia East. Billing is in Azure Agent Units, and GA was reported in March 2026 by a secondary source (verify GA date and pricing from Microsoft).

Policy for Trakia: Reader by default. It diagnoses, correlates with recent deployments and agent versions, and opens a GitHub issue containing the KQL, trace IDs and suspected change. Privileged actions (restart a revision, roll back traffic, scale) are allowed only when they map to a pre-approved runbook, the action is reversible, and it is logged with the agent's identity (C16). The canary controller (C17) remains the primary rollback mechanism. SRE Agent adds diagnosis, not a second uncontrolled actuator.

docs.title: 9. Measuring the factory
docs.text:
DORA 2025: ~90% AI adoption (median ~2h/day). AI use is now linked to higher throughput, but ensuring software works before delivery remains a challenge, and AI is "a mirror and a multiplier". Its AI Capabilities Model lists seven practices: clear AI policy, healthy data ecosystem, accessible internal knowledge, strong version control and code review, user-centric focus, platform engineering, small batches. Larger changesets raise instability risk, which matters because agents happily produce large diffs. METR: the RCT slowdown and the 2026 update both show how hard measurement is, and that perceived speed is not measured speed. Thoughtworks: coding throughput on Caution, DORA metrics on Adopt; "lines of code generated is misleading; rework rate exposes blind spots"; codebase cognitive debt on Caution.

Factory scorecard (weekly, from GitHub/ADO APIs + App Insights):

Metric Definition Why Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, failed-deployment recovery time DORA keys Outcome Rework rate (DORA) Share of deployments that are unplanned fixes for production issues (verify current DORA definition) Instability hidden by throughput Code churn Lines changed again within 21 days of merge, by author type Hidden cost of fast agent merges First-pass acceptance Agent PRs merged with ≤1 human revision request Spec and context quality Iterations per PR Agent push cycles before green gates Feedback sensor quality Escaped defects Prod incidents/bugs traced to PRs, by author type Quality Mutation score (changed code) Stryker Test strength Agent cost per merged PR Premium requests / tokens / Actions minutes ÷ merged PRs Economics Review latency & load Time to first human review; open PRs per reviewer Bottleneck AI review precision Accepted AI comments ÷ total Reviewer trust calibration

Beware Goodhart's law. Never reward PR counts. Pair every speed metric with a quality metric, and compare agent-authored with human-authored PRs on the same task classes.

docs.title: 10. Governance of agents in the repo, and the human role
docs.text:
docs/governance/agent-policy.md is a short, enforced document. It covers: - which agents may run where (local, cloud, CI) and with which tools and MCP servers; - token scopes; - sandbox and egress allow-lists; - data classes agents may see (no production personal data in agent sandboxes; synthetic TrakiaOps only); - approved models and BYOK endpoints (Foundry, EU data zone); - protected paths; - attribution (an Agent-Id trailer in commits; Agent Trace, an open attribution spec, is on Thoughtworks Assess); - audit-log retention; - a kill switch (disable the agent app/identity) and an incident process for agent misbehaviour.

Every rule that matters is backed by a ruleset, hook or test. A policy that is not enforced is decoration.

The human role shifts to spec owner, orchestrator and reviewer. Expert habits: design the verification first; manage context deliberately (memory file vs skill vs subagent vs hook vs MCP); pick the ceremony; run unattended agents safely; measure outcomes; explain every merged line. To counter cognitive debt, the labs include "explain-the-diff" checks and occasional unaided implementations.

docs.title: Lab 1 — One feature, two agents, right-sized spec (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Deliver "Driving-time compliance check" (Fleet Assistant warns a dispatcher when a proposed maintenance trip would breach EU driving-time limits for the assigned driver) via the full loop, implemented once by the Copilot cloud agent and once by Claude Code in Actions.
  • Start state: tag c19/lab1-start (C18 increment plus specs/ and tests/Acceptance/ folders, CODEOWNERS).
  • Steps:
  • Create the work item in Azure Boards (or a GitHub issue form for GitHub-only cohorts). Choose the ceremony level and justify it in the issue: this is a feature → SPEC.md ≤1 page.
  • Run an interview session with your local agent to draft specs/0042-driving-time/SPEC.md. Then write the acceptance tests yourself: 8 xUnit cases over the rules summary in the corpus (daily limit, weekly limit, breaks), plus 6 eval cases (one per failure mode from C14 that applies, incl. a Bulgarian question).
  • Add .github/agents/fleet-feature.agent.md (Concepts §3) and the setup workflow (restore from internal feed, start SQL container).
  • From Boards, "Create a pull request with Copilot" with the fleet-feature agent. In parallel, trigger the Claude Code workflow on a twin issue: 
    # .github/workflows/claude-implement.yml (action inputs: verify against the pinned major version)
on:
  issues: { types: [labeled] }
jobs:
  implement:
    if: github.event.label.name == 'agent:claude'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: write, pull-requests: write, issues: write, id-token: write }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<pinned-sha>
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@<pinned-sha>
        with: { dotnet-version: '10.0.x' }
      - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@<pinned-sha>
        with:
          prompt: "Implement the spec referenced in issue #${{ github.event.issue.number }} following AGENTS.md. Never modify tests/Acceptance, evals, .github or security."
          claude_args: >-
            --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Grep,Glob,Bash(dotnet build:*),Bash(dotnet test:*)"
            --permission-mode dontAsk --max-turns 60
        # model access via Foundry/Bedrock/Vertex or API key secret per org policy (verify supported auth inputs)
  • Compare both PRs: gate results, iterations, cost, diff size, and whether either touched protected paths.
  • Break it: Write an ambiguous acceptance criterion ("long trips need a break") and observe which agent asks and which guesses. Then fix the spec, not the code.
  • Acceptance criteria: Both PRs exist and are linked to the work item; acceptance tests and eval smoke pass on at least one; a comparison table (docs/factory/agent-comparison-0042.md) with measured numbers; you can explain every line of the PR you merge (instructor spot-check of 3 random hunks).
  • Stretch: Re-run the same feature through Spec Kit (Constitution → Specify → Plan → Tasks) and record review time and spec length versus your one-page spec.

docs.title: Lab 2 — The gate stack, unweakenable (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: A single pr-gates workflow and repository ruleset implementing Concepts §4.
  • Start state: c19/lab2-start (separate workflows from earlier modules).
  • Steps:
  • Consolidate into pr-gates.yml with jobs ordered cheap → expensive and needs: dependencies: 
    name: pr-gates
on: { pull_request: { branches: [main] } }
permissions: { contents: read, pull-requests: write, security-events: write, id-token: write }
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<pinned-sha>
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@<pinned-sha>
        with: { dotnet-version: '10.0.x' }
      - run: dotnet restore --locked-mode
      - run: dotnet format --verify-no-changes
      - run: dotnet build -warnaserror --no-restore
      - run: dotnet test tests/FleetOps.Tests tests/Acceptance --no-build
      - run: dotnet test tests/Architecture tests/Governance tests/Security.ThreatModel --no-build
  mutation:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<pinned-sha>
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@<pinned-sha>
        with: { dotnet-version: '10.0.x' }
      - run: dotnet tool restore && dotnet stryker --since:main --break-at 70   # verify flag names for pinned Stryker.NET
  evals:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: evals            # OIDC federated credential to the eval Foundry project; no stored keys
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<pinned-sha>
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@<pinned-sha>
        with: { dotnet-version: '10.0.x' }
      - uses: azure/login@<pinned-sha>
        with: { client-id: '${{ vars.EVAL_CLIENT_ID }}', tenant-id: '${{ vars.TENANT_ID }}', subscription-id: '${{ vars.SUB_ID }}' }
      - run: dotnet test tests/FleetOps.Evals --filter "Category=Gate"   # cached responses; thresholds in evals/thresholds.json
      - run: dotnet aieval report --path ./eval-results --output ./eval-report   # verify CLI arguments
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@<pinned-sha>
        with: { name: eval-report, path: ./eval-report }
  asr:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<pinned-sha>
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@<pinned-sha>
        with: { dotnet-version: '10.0.x' }
      - run: dotnet run --project tools/AsrHarness -- --suite indirect --cached --fail-on-consequential
  • Enable CodeQL (C#) with default setup, secret scanning push protection, dependency review, and agentic autofix (enterprise policy + repo setting). Assign two seeded alerts to Copilot via REST.
  • Add NetArchTest rules derived from ADRs (e.g., FleetOps.Agents must not reference Microsoft.Data.SqlClient directly; data access only via the MCP server or repository layer).
  • Configure the repository ruleset: required status checks (all jobs), required code-owner review for protected paths, no bypass for bot actors, linear history.
  • Enable advisory AI review (Copilot code review or Claude Code review) with a checklist prompt referencing security/threat-register.csv and docs/governance/agent-policy.md.
  • Break it (three attacks): (a) ask the cloud agent to "make the failing eval pass" for an intentionally hard case and watch whether it edits evals/thresholds.json; (b) a PR that deletes an assertion, so mutation score drops; (c) an autofix PR that closes a CodeQL SQL-injection alert by removing the feature's validation test. All three must be blocked by gates or rulesets, not by luck.
  • Acceptance criteria: Ruleset export committed (.github/rulesets/main.json); the three attack PRs are blocked with the expected gate names; a clean PR goes green in under 20 minutes; autofix produced at least one validated draft PR that passed the full stack.
  • Stretch: Measure AI review precision on 15 PRs and tune its checklist.

docs.title: Lab 3 — Parallel agents and maintenance agents (≈2h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Use parallelism where it fits and run upgrade/docs agents under the same gates.
  • Start state: c19/lab3-start, including legacy/DepotKiosk (a .NET Framework 4.8 WinForms depot check-in app) and 14 MCP tools still using an older SDK attribute style.
  • Steps:
  • (≈45 min) Decompose the MCP tool migration into independent units, then migrate 4 of the 14 tools in parallel with Claude Code worktrees//batch (or 4 parallel cloud-agent issues), with a reviewer subagent pre-reviewing each PR. Merge in dependency order. The remaining 10 tools are stretch/homework.
  • (≈30 min, timeboxed) Deliberately try parallelism on a coupled change: two agents each adding a field to IncidentReport and its serializer and eval cases (UI out of scope). Record the conflicts and the inconsistent decisions; do not resolve them beyond the write-up.
  • (≈25 min) Run the Copilot Upgrade agent on legacy/DepotKiosk (Windows runner or VS 2026) through assessment and plan only. Review its assessment, plan and tasks files; reject or amend at least one plan step with a reason. Execution is stretch.
  • (≈20 min) Run the provided docs agent workflow (.github/workflows/docs-agent.yml, scheduled Action) once: it regenerates docs/api/, the ADR index and the Transparency Note metrics section from artefacts, with citations, as a PR. Review the PR; adding a Routine variant is stretch.
  • Break it: Give the docs agent a stale eval artefact. The staleness check from C18 must flag it rather than publishing old numbers.
  • Acceptance criteria: 4 migration PRs merged green, with human review time per PR logged; the coupled-change experiment write-up (≤300 words) with the conflict count; Upgrade agent plan review comments committed; docs PR with per-claim citations passes tests/Docs link/citation checks, and the stale-artefact run is flagged.
  • Stretch: Migrate the remaining 10 tools and compute review-queue time versus number of parallel agents to find your team's saturation point; execute the reviewed Upgrade plan on DepotKiosk; author the docs agent as a weekly Routine.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Ops loop: SRE Agent → issue → fix → canary (≈1.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Close the loop from production signal to agent-made fix.
  • Start state: c19/lab4-start, deployed prod-sim (C17) with SRE Agent connected in Reader mode (Sweden Central).
  • Steps:
  • The instructor ships a canary with a regression: a new SQL index hint in Fleet Analyst raises p95 latency 4× for Varna queries, and tool error rate rises.
  • SRE Agent investigates App Insights/Log Analytics and opens a GitHub issue with KQL, trace IDs, the suspected deployment and the agent version.
  • Triage as human: confirm, add an acceptance test reproducing the slow query plan (or an eval latency budget), and label it for the cloud agent.
  • The cloud agent fixes it; the full gate stack runs; the C17 canary controller promotes.
  • Break it: Temporarily switch SRE Agent to Privileged in a sandbox subscription and ask it to "fix it". Record exactly what it would change and argue whether that action fits the runbook policy.
  • Acceptance criteria: Issue created by the SRE Agent contains reproducible evidence; MTTR (detection → promoted fix) recorded; the fix PR includes a regression test; the agent-policy decision on Privileged mode is documented.
  • Stretch: Connect SRE Agent to the Trakia MCP server (read-only tools) and evaluate whether diagnosis improves.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Measure and govern the factory (≈1h)
docs.text:
• Goal: A factory scorecard and an enforced agent policy, ready for Gate G3.
  • Start state: c19/lab5-start with a script skeleton querying the GitHub/ADO APIs.
  • Steps:
  • Compute the scorecard (Concepts §9) for the last 4 weeks of your repo, split by agent- versus human-authored PRs.
  • Write docs/governance/agent-policy.md and link every rule to its enforcement (ruleset, hook, test, Azure Policy).
  • Present a one-slide interpretation: which metric would you act on, and which looks good but is misleading?
  • Break it: The instructor adds 30 trivial agent PRs (README edits). Show how PR count and throughput jump while first-pass acceptance and rework reveal nothing improved.
  • Acceptance criteria: Scorecard JSON + workbook committed; every policy rule has an enforcement link (checked by tests/Governance/PolicyEnforcementTests); the interpretation explicitly references DORA's amplifier finding or METR's measurement caveat.
  • Stretch: Add cost per merged PR from Copilot premium-request and Actions usage exports.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text: "Ceremony and gate call" (20 min, repeat 5×). Draw a change card (e.g., "rename a config key", "add a new MCP tool that sends SMS to drivers", "upgrade MEAI to the next minor", "change the incident triage prompt", "bump the frontier model version"). Decide: (1) ceremony level; (2) which agent (local, cloud, batch) or none; (3) which gates from the stack must run and which new ones are needed (e.g., the SMS tool needs a tool-manifest entry, HITL and an ASR scenario); (4) promotion path (direct, canary, shadow). Compare with a peer; disagreements must be resolved by citing a concept from C11–C18.

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text: Fleet Ops Copilot is now delivered by an end-to-end automated, governed SDLC: - the driving-time compliance feature, shipped through spec → agent PR → gates → human approval → canary; - the MCP tools migrated by parallel agents; - the legacy DepotKiosk on a reviewed upgrade path; - docs and the Transparency Note regenerated by a docs agent; - an SRE Agent (Reader) watching production and feeding issues back into the loop.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text:
The Factory is complete for the core: - Boards/Issues → Copilot custom agents and Claude Code Actions; - a consolidated pr-gates workflow (build, tests, acceptance, mutation, evals, ASR, CodeQL + agentic autofix, supply chain, architecture, governance, advisory AI review); - rulesets and CODEOWNERS that agents cannot bypass; - an OIDC-only deployment with environment approvals and the eval-gated canary; - parallel-agent and maintenance-agent playbooks; - an SRE Agent ops loop; - a factory scorecard and an enforced agent-policy.md.

D6 extends this with your own agent tooling; A7 governs it at team and programme level.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Spec & orchestration Prompts agents ad hoc Uses specs Right-sized ceremony; human-owned executable anchors Diagnoses spec ambiguity from agent behaviour; minimal specs, high first-pass acceptance Gate design Build + tests Most gates present Ordered stack, protected paths, OIDC, autofix in loop All three attack PRs blocked; gates fast (<20 min); measured AI-review precision Parallel & maintenance agents Sequential only Runs parallel agents Decomposes well, avoids coupled parallelism, reviews upgrade plans Finds review saturation point; agents' outputs cited and verifiable Ops loop Manual incident handling SRE Agent reads Reader-mode loop to fix PR with regression test Privileged-mode policy argued with runbooks and reversibility Measurement & governance PR counts DORA keys DORA + agent metrics split by author type Interprets against METR/DORA evidence; every policy rule enforced

Auto-checked: pr-gates status on clean and attack PRs, ruleset export, policy-enforcement tests, docs citation tests, scorecard schema. Gate G3 (see gates.md) lets you bring this factory into the operated environment (Blocks A–C) and draws Block D challenge questions from your evidence pack, including the governance artefacts. Learners must be able to demonstrate the full loop live.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Measuring success by agent PR volume.
  • Specs longer than the code they produce; prose specs without executable anchors.
  • Letting agents edit tests, eval thresholds or workflows "to get green".
  • Running CI agents in auto/permissive modes with broad tokens and secrets available before human approval.
  • Making AI review blocking for everything, which trains humans to ignore it, or for nothing, which wastes it.
  • Launching more parallel agents than the team can review.
  • Accepting upgrade-agent output without reviewing its plan files.
  • Giving SRE Agent Privileged mode "to save time" without runbooks.
  • Assuming Azure Repos has feature parity with GitHub for agent flows.
  • Merging code no human can explain, which builds cognitive debt that surfaces at the next incident.

docs.title: D1 — Model customization & small/local models
docs.text: Level: Expert (AI Solution Developer track) · Duration: 20h (theory 25% / labs 75%) · Prerequisites: Core C0–C19 and Gate G3; especially C1 (mechanics), C5/C14 (evals, judges), C15 (cost per task), C18 (data protection) · Volatility: High (fine-tunable model list, preview deployment options, local runtime APIs)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A proficient practitioner can run a fine-tuning job and serve a local model. An expert decides, with numbers, whether either should happen at all. The expert quantifies the gap a rung of the customization ladder must close, predicts its cost, and builds the before/after eval before touching training data. They know which failure each technique fixes (knowledge, behaviour, format, cost, latency, sovereignty). They catch leakage, forgetting and quantization loss before users do. They also treat a fine-tuned model as a versioned artifact with a retirement date, not as a one-off experiment.

Trakia Freight's depots in Plovdiv, Sofia and Varna triage engine fault codes (DTCs) for ~400 trucks. Today a frontier model answers mechanics' questions in Fleet Ops Copilot. Three things hurt: Varna's connectivity is unreliable, thousands of near-identical classification calls are billed at frontier prices, and a safety-relevant decision ("stop the truck now") depends on a cloud round trip.

"Fine-tune a small model and run it locally" fails in four predictable ways: - training data leaks across splits, so offline scores are great and production scores are not; - the student learns the teacher's mistakes; - INT4 quantization quietly erases the rare-but-critical class; - the fine-tuned base is retired 12–18 months later with no migration plan.

Experts therefore run customization as an experiment with a pre-registered success criterion. For Trakia: macro-F1 within 2 points of the frontier baseline, StopNow recall ≥ 0.97, p95 < 400 ms on depot hardware, and cost per 1,000 triages < 5% of baseline. If the experiment misses the bar, they stop and write down why.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this module you can:

  1. Choose and justify a rung on the customization ladder (prompting, few-shot, RAG, SFT, DPO, RFT, distillation, classical ML) for a given failure mode, using an explicit decision record with expected cost and eval delta.
  2. Construct a leakage-free fine-tuning dataset (grouped splits, dedup, label audit, PII handling) and diagnose leakage when offline and online scores diverge.
  3. Design and run a before/after evaluation matrix that measures target-task quality, safety-critical class recall, format adherence, general-capability regression and cost/latency.
  4. Execute SFT and teacher-to-student distillation on Microsoft Foundry, and explain when DPO or RFT would be the better training signal and what the grader or preference data must look like.
  5. Detect overfitting and catastrophic forgetting from loss curves and regression suites, and apply mitigations (epochs, rank, data mixing, early stopping).
  6. Explain LoRA/QLoRA/PEFT mechanics well enough to size trainable parameters, pick rank, and decide between merged and hot-swapped adapters.
  7. Size memory for a local or self-hosted model (weights + KV cache, dense vs MoE) and measure the quality cost of INT8/INT4 quantization on the critical class.
  8. Implement provider-swappable local inference (Foundry Local, ONNX Runtime GenAI, LLamaSharp, Ollama) behind IChatClient, with an offline-first fallback chain.
  9. Produce a cost/latency/accuracy comparison and an ADR that a reviewer can reproduce from pinned artifacts.

docs.title: 1. The customization ladder as decision rules, not a staircase
docs.text:
The ladder is a set of tools mapped to failure types. You do not climb it in order. Heuristic: knowledge → RAG; behaviour/format → fine-tune; cost/latency at volume → distil to a smaller model; gradeable quality with many valid answers → RFT; "better vs worse is easy to judge, hard to demonstrate" → DPO; everything → evals first. Microsoft's own guidance states the benefit of fine-tuning "isn't guaranteed", that teams must "compare against a baseline with held-out evaluation", and that fine-tuning "doesn't replace retrieval for current information".

Decision rules experts apply:

Observed failure (from error analysis, C14) First lever Escalate to Do not use Missing or stale facts (new maintenance bulletin) RAG (C7) Better chunking/rerank Fine-tuning (facts go stale, and you cannot cite weights) Wrong output format or schema drift Structured outputs (C3) SFT if the schema is complex and the call volume is high DPO Inconsistent label policy on edge cases Few-shot with curated hard examples, prompt-cached SFT on adjudicated labels RAG Tone or completeness preferences Prompt + rubric DPO from preference pairs SFT on "good" examples alone (it misses the contrast) Correct answer is verifiable by code Prompt + validator + retry RFT with a code grader LLM-judge rewards that can be gamed Frontier quality is fine but cost/latency is not Smaller model + few-shot; model router (D5) Distillation into a small model Bigger prompt Closed label set, high volume, tabular-ish features ML.NET classifier or a "decision model" Fine-tuned small LM Any generative model, by default Data must not leave the site, or the site is offline Local SLM (Foundry Local) LoRA-tuned local SLM Cloud-only design

Exit criterion for every rung: a pre-registered metric target on a frozen test set. If prompting plus few-shot reaches 95% of the target, the remaining 5% rarely justifies a training pipeline you must then own for 18 months.

Misconceptions to unlearn: - "Fine-tuning teaches the model our latest data." It shifts behaviour. Use retrieval for knowledge. - "More epochs = better." Small datasets overfit within 2–4 epochs. - "The fine-tuned model is ours forever." The base model has a retirement date (C15, A5). GA Azure models typically retire at 18 months and partner models at 12. Plan for re-training. - "Open-weight means free to use." Licences vary (MIT, Apache-2.0, custom). Audit them.

docs.title: 2. Managed fine-tuning on Microsoft Foundry (as of Oct 2026)
docs.text:
Foundry offers three managed training signals: - SFT: (prompt, ideal response) demonstrations. - DPO: (prompt, preferred, rejected) pairs. Use it when quality depends on preferences such as tone or completeness. - RFT: prompts plus a grader that scores responses. Use it when many answers are valid and quality can be scored reliably. Microsoft says graders "should be tested against correct, incorrect, and adversarial responses", because reward hacking is the default failure.

Distillation is SFT on teacher-generated data. Interactive training (preview, approval required, [Python]) lets you write your own training loop, controlling losses, rewards, rollouts and checkpoints.

Fine-tunable models listed on Learn (page updated 2026-10-08). Treat this list as perishable:

Model Methods Notes gpt-4.1, gpt-4.1-mini, gpt-4.1-nano SFT, DPO The practical cloud student family gpt-4o SFT, DPO Older gpt-4o-mini SFT Older o4-mini RFT Reasoning RFT gpt-5 RFT Invitation only gpt-oss-20b SFT Open weights gpt-oss-120b SFT, RFT Preview Qwen3-32B SFT Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.8-27B SFT, RFT Preview; 35B-A3B is MoE Muse-Glimmer-30B (Meta) SFT, RFT Preview, Apache-2.0 Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct SFT Ministral-3B SFT Smallest listed LLM MAI-Code-1.1-Flash RFT Preview

No GPT-5.x/GPT-6 SFT is listed. You cannot fine-tune the current frontier tier. You distil from it.

Training tiers: Standard (in-region, keeps residency), Data zone (US only; verify against current documentation), Global (cheaper, no residency guarantee), Developer (lowest cost, preemptible, no SLA). Build 2026 also announced a developer tier "with no hosting fees" and "Frontier Tuning", whose scope is undescribed: verify against current documentation. For Trakia's GDPR-bound data, Global and Data zone are out. Use Standard in an EU region where the model is trainable (verify per model). Use Developer only on synthetic or fully pseudonymized data, and record that in the DPIA (C18).

Deployment: Serverless (the usual OpenAI-family path), Managed compute (preview; base model plus compatible LoRA adapters), or Fireworks on Foundry (preview; one merged adapter).

Prices were not collected for this release, so take them from the pricing page on the day you teach. RFT grader types were not verified, so check the RFT how-to before Lab 2's stretch.

docs.title: 3. PEFT, LoRA and QLoRA — enough math to make decisions
docs.text:
LoRA freezes a weight matrix W (d_out × d_in) and learns a low-rank update ΔW = B·A, where B is d_out × r and A is r × d_in, scaled by α/r. Trainable parameters per adapted matrix are r·(d_in + d_out).

Worked example: d_in = d_out = 4096 and r = 16 give 131,072 trainable parameters, against 16.8M for the full matrix (0.78%). Adapt Q, K, V and O in 32 layers and the adapter is ~16.8M parameters, about 34 MB in FP16. You can ship that over a depot's slow link. A full 8B checkpoint is ~16 GB.

Rank choice. r = 8–16 is the usual starting band for classification or format tasks. Raise r only when the validation loss plateaus high (underfitting). Adapting MLP layers as well as attention layers adds capacity, and with it the risk of forgetting.

QLoRA trains LoRA adapters on top of a base frozen in 4-bit NF4, which lets you fine-tune a 7–8B model on a single GPU. The adapter is trained in higher precision. When you later merge the adapter and re-quantize for serving, you introduce a second quantization error, so you must evaluate after the final export, not after training.

Serving adapters.

Pattern When Trade-off Merge into base, then quantize One task per edge device Simplest runtime. A new task means a new full model Hot-swap adapters on a shared base (multi-LoRA) Many tasks or tenants on one GPU (vLLM supports this; Foundry managed compute lists base + compatible LoRA adapters, preview) Small per-task artifacts. Batching across adapters is engine-specific One merged adapter on a hosted platform (Fireworks on Foundry, preview) Managed serving of an open model Vendor-specific limits

docs.title: 4. Data preparation: where most fine-tunes actually fail
docs.text:
• Format. Chat-format JSONL with the same system prompt and schema used at inference. A prompt mismatch silently kills quality.
  • Grouped splits. Trakia's work orders repeat (same truck, same DTC, same phrasing), so a random split leaks near-duplicates into test. Split by vehicle and report random-split vs grouped-split scores. The gap is your leakage estimate.
  • Dedup. Exact hash plus near-duplicates (embedding cosine > 0.95 or MinHash).
  • Label audit. Mechanic-confirmed resolutions are ground truth; teacher labels are not. Have an expert adjudicate 100 labels per class and measure the teacher–expert agreement.
  • Critical tail. StopNow (oil pressure, brakes) may be 4% of rows. Oversample it in training, never in test, and track its recall separately.
  • Quantity. Hundreds of examples move format and policy. Distilling a 15-class decision wants low thousands. Plot learning curves at 250/500/1,000/2,000.
  • PII. Scrub names and phone numbers from free-text notes. "Forget a driver" means re-training, not editing weights, so document it in the DPIA.

docs.title: 5. Evaluation before and after — the experiment design
docs.text:
Freeze one test set (grouped split, never used for prompt tuning or checkpoint selection) and one dev set (for epoch and rank choice). Every candidate gets the same matrix:

Dimension Metric Why Target task Macro-F1 (severity), accuracy (subsystem) Overall quality Safety tail Recall and precision on StopNow, with a 95% Wilson interval A miss is the expensive error Cost-weighted error Σ errors × business cost matrix (missed StopNow = 100, false StopNow = 5) Turns F1 into money Format adherence % schema-valid outputs without repair Small models break schemas General regression Pass rate on a 100-item "keep" suite (BG/EN fleet Q&A, refusals, the instruction-following checks from C5) Catastrophic forgetting Calibration Reliability of the confidence field or logprob threshold Needed for cascades (D5) Ops p50/p95 latency on target hardware, € per 1,000 calls, memory footprint The reason you are here

Use paired comparisons (the same items, models A and B) and McNemar's test for "is the student really worse?". With 600 test items, a 2-point F1 difference is often noise. See D7 for the statistics.

docs.title: 6. Overfitting and catastrophic forgetting
docs.text:
Overfitting shows as validation loss turning up while training loss falls, verbatim reproduction of training phrasings, and dev scores far above grouped-test scores. Mitigate with fewer epochs (start at 2–3), a lower learning-rate multiplier (Foundry's hyperparameter names vary by model, so verify them), more diverse data, and early stopping or checkpoint selection on dev.

Catastrophic forgetting is the loss of prior skills: no more refusals, no more Bulgarian, ignored system instructions. The keep suite detects it. Mitigate with LoRA instead of full fine-tuning, a lower rank, 10–20% general instruction data mixed in, and a narrow task. Accept forgetting deliberately only for a single-purpose component behind a router, and say so in the ADR.

docs.title: 7. Distillation done properly
docs.text:
Teacher-to-student distillation ("knowledge distillation", Hinton et al.) here means the frontier model labels a large unlabeled pool and the small model is trained on those labels.

Expert refinements: 1. Filter teacher outputs. Keep items where the teacher matches confirmed outcomes or two teacher runs agree. Teacher errors become student beliefs. 2. Labels vs rationales. A short distilled rationale can help on multi-factor cases but costs output tokens, so measure both. 3. Distil the policy, not the prompt. The point is to remove the long few-shot prefix from every call. 4. Verifiable labels → consider RFT. A code grader (parses, severity equals the confirmed outcome, subsystem consistent with the DTC family) rewards the true objective. Test it against adversaries: "always StopNow" must not score well.

docs.title: 8. Small models, memory and quantization
docs.text:
Weight memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter: FP16 = 2, INT8 = 1, INT4 ≈ 0.5 (plus ~5–10% for scales and zero-points).

KV cache per sequence ≈ 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × tokens × bytes. GQA shrinks kv_heads, so read it from the model card.

For MoE, memory follows total parameters and compute follows active parameters. A "35B-A3B" model needs ~17–18 GB at INT4 even though each token uses ~3B parameters.

Model class FP16 INT8 INT4 Depot fit (16 GB RAM, iGPU/NPU) ~3B dense 6 GB 3 GB ~1.7 GB Yes ~8B dense 16 GB 8 GB ~4.5 GB INT4 only ~27B dense 54 GB 27 GB ~15 GB No (a ternary 27B at 5.9 GB is a vendor claim; verify) 35B-A3B MoE 70 GB 35 GB ~18 GB No 120B (gpt-oss-120b) 240 GB 120 GB ~60 GB Server GPU only

Formats and methods: - GGUF is llama.cpp's container. Its quant levels (for example Q8_0, Q4_K_M) are used by LLamaSharp and Ollama. - GPTQ and AWQ are post-training weight quantization methods. - ONNX INT4 models run on ONNX Runtime GenAI, which Foundry Local wraps.

Quantization loss is not uniform. It concentrates on rare tokens and rare classes. Always re-run the safety-tail metric after quantization.

docs.title: 9. Local runtimes behind one abstraction
docs.text:
All four .NET local options plug into Microsoft.Extensions.AI IChatClient, so the application code does not change:

Runtime Model format Hardware Use when Foundry Local (GA 9 Apr 2026; C# SDK Microsoft.AI.Foundry.Local) ONNX, from a curated catalogue (GPT OSS, Qwen, Whisper, DeepSeek, Mistral, Phi) Automatic GPU/NPU/CPU EP selection; Windows ML EPs on Windows, Metal on Apple silicon; Linux x64 Managed path; OpenAI-compatible API incl. Responses; ~20 MB runtime; offline ONNX Runtime GenAI ONNX CUDA, OpenVINO, QNN, TensorRT EPs Maximum control; custom ONNX exports LLamaSharp GGUF CPU, CUDA, Metal, Vulkan Bring-your-own GGUF; quick quant comparisons Ollama GGUF (external runner) Varies Prototyping only

Foundry Local also runs on Azure Local (preview) for on-prem servers. Loading your own fine-tuned or converted model into Foundry Local (rather than a catalogue model) was not confirmed in our sources, so verify against current documentation. The lab keeps ONNX Runtime GenAI and LLamaSharp as GA-independent fallbacks.

vLLM (self-hosted serving on AKS GPU nodes) introduced three ideas: PagedAttention (KV cache managed like virtual memory), continuous batching, and multi-LoRA serving. It is the reference engine when Trakia sells the product to other fleets and needs one GPU pool serving per-tenant adapters (A-track). Throughput claims depend on the hardware, so measure them with a load test (D5).

Edge as artifact. Version an edge model in the registry with a content hash, data snapshot ID and eval report. Roll it out per depot (Varna as canary) and log local decisions to an outbox that syncs when the link returns. Low-confidence inputs go to the cloud when it is reachable, otherwise to a conservative default. For safety triage that default is "escalate to a mechanic", never "continue driving".

docs.title: Labs
docs.text: Lab repo: trakia-fleetops. All models are referenced by role in appsettings.json, for example Models:Teacher, Models:CloudStudent, Models:EdgeSlm. The fault-code dataset is generated from TrakiaOps.MaintenanceWorkOrders joined to TelematicsEvents (DTC events) with the mechanic-confirmed resolution as ground truth.

docs.title: Lab 1 — Baseline matrix and a leakage-proof eval harness (≈2.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Establish the bar every customized model must beat, and prove the test set does not leak.
  • Start state: tag d1/lab1-start. It contains FaultTriage contracts, a 1,400-row labeled export and an empty Trakia.FaultTriage.Evals xUnit project.
  • Steps:
  • Define the output contract: 
    public enum Severity { Continue, ScheduleWithin7Days, StopNow }
public sealed record FaultTriage(Severity Severity, string Subsystem, double Confidence, string? Rationale);
public sealed record FaultCase(string CaseId, string VehicleId, string Dtc, string TelematicsSummary, string MechanicNote, string Lang);
  • Build grouped splits by VehicleId (60/20/20), with dedup by normalized (Dtc, MechanicNote) hash plus embedding similarity > 0.95. Persist splits.json with the dataset snapshot hash.
  • Implement ITriageModel over IChatClient, using structured output: 
    ChatResponse<FaultTriage> r = await chat.GetResponseAsync<FaultTriage>(
    [new(ChatRole.System, TriagePrompt.V1), new(ChatRole.User, fc.ToPromptText())],
    new ChatOptions { Temperature = 0 }, ct);
  • Run four baselines on dev and test: (a) frontier model zero-shot, (b) frontier with 12 curated few-shot examples and a prompt-cache-friendly prefix, (c) the fast small cloud model with few-shot, (d) an ML.NET multiclass classifier (text featurizer over DTC + note, plus one-hot DTC family).
  • Compute the full matrix from Concepts §5 per baseline: macro-F1, StopNow recall with a Wilson 95% CI, cost-weighted error, schema validity, p50/p95 latency and € per 1,000 calls (from the usage tokens × prices in config).
  • Emit baseline-report.md and baseline.json as CI artifacts.
  • Break it: Re-run with a random row split. Record the inflation in macro-F1 for the ML.NET model and for few-shot. Explain in three sentences why near-duplicate work orders cause it.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • dotnet test --filter Category=Baseline passes.
  • The report contains all 4 baselines × 7 metrics.
  • A test asserts zero vehicle overlap between the train and test splits.
  • The random-vs-grouped gap is reported.
  • Stretch: Add a "decision model"-style baseline, logprob thresholding on a single severity token, and plot its calibration.

docs.title: Lab 2 — Distil a cloud student with Foundry SFT, then overfit it on purpose (≈3.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Train a small cloud model that removes the few-shot prefix and the frontier price, and observe overfitting and forgetting with your own eyes.
  • Start state: tag d1/lab2-start (Lab 1 solution + 6,000 unlabeled historical work orders).
  • Steps:
  • Label the unlabeled pool with the teacher at temperature 0, twice. Keep items where both runs agree and (where available) the teacher matches the confirmed resolution. Report the yield and the teacher–expert agreement on a 150-item adjudicated sample.
  • Write chat-format JSONL with the short production prompt (no few-shot). Oversample StopNow ×3 in train only. Mix in 10% general instruction items from the keep suite's training partition.
  • Upload the data and create an SFT job on the Models:CloudStudent base (for example gpt-4.1-nano or gpt-4.1-mini) in a Standard EU region. Use the Developer tier only if the pool is fully pseudonymized. Use the OpenAI client against /openai/v1/ or the Foundry project client: 
    #pragma warning disable OPENAI001
// Shape only — verify exact fine-tuning client/method names against current OpenAI .NET + Foundry docs
var files = openAi.GetOpenAIFileClient();
var trainFile = await files.UploadFileAsync("train.jsonl", FileUploadPurpose.FineTune);
var ft = openAi.GetFineTuningClient();
var job = await ft.FineTuneAsync(baseModel: cfg["Models:CloudStudent"], trainingFileId: trainFile.Value.Id,
    waitUntilCompleted: false, options: new() { ValidationFile = valFile.Value.Id /* epochs, lr multiplier: verify names */ });
  • Deploy the resulting model (serverless) and evaluate it with the Lab 1 harness on the same test split. Add it to the matrix.
  • Overfit experiment: train a second job on only 20 examples for many epochs. Plot the training vs validation loss from the job's metrics, and run the keep suite.
  • Break it: Train a variant with the long few-shot prompt in training but the short one at inference, and measure the drop. Run the keep suite in Bulgarian and record any forgetting.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The student reaches macro-F1 ≥ (frontier few-shot − 2.0) and StopNow recall ≥ 0.97 on the grouped test, or the lab report explains why not with evidence.
  • The keep-suite pass rate drops by ≤ 3 points.
  • €/1k calls ≤ 10% of the frontier few-shot cost.
  • The overfit run's loss plot and keep-suite delta are committed under reports/d1/.
  • Stretch: Write a C# grader (schema valid ∧ severity equals the confirmed outcome ∧ subsystem consistent with the DTC family). Test it against an "always StopNow" adversary and a "copy the mechanic note" adversary. Then sketch an RFT job on an RFT-capable model (verify the grader types first).

docs.title: Lab 3 — LoRA/QLoRA an open-weight edge model and measure quantization loss (≈4h) [Python]
docs.text:
• Goal: Produce a small open-weight model that can run at a depot, and measure what each compression step costs on the critical class.
  • Start state: tag d1/lab3-start. It contains the scripts/ devcontainer with pinned Python, PEFT/TRL and the ONNX tooling.
  • Steps:
  • Pick Models:EdgeSlm, a ≤ 4B-parameter open-weight instruct model whose licence permits commercial fine-tuning. Record the licence in models/LICENCES.md.
  • Run QLoRA (NF4 base, r = 16, α = 32, attention projections only, 2 epochs) on the Lab 2 distilled data. Save the adapter (~tens of MB) and log the loss curves.
  • Merge the adapter into the base. Export (a) an ONNX INT4 model for ONNX Runtime GenAI or Foundry Local (verify the current export tooling) and (b) GGUF Q8_0 and Q4_K_M for LLamaSharp.
  • Back in C#, register three IChatClients (ORT GenAI INT4, LLamaSharp Q8, LLamaSharp Q4) by keyed DI and run the Lab 1 harness on each.
  • Record the quality ladder: base SLM few-shot → LoRA FP16 → INT8/Q8 → INT4/Q4.
  • Break it: Quantize the model before merging (merge an FP16 adapter into an already-INT4 base) and compare StopNow recall. Explain the double-quantization effect.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The report shows the quality ladder with StopNow recall CIs.
  • The chosen export loses ≤ 1.5 macro-F1 points relative to LoRA FP16 and keeps StopNow recall ≥ 0.97.
  • Artifacts are hash-pinned in models/manifest.json, alongside the training-data snapshot hash.
  • Stretch: Serve two adapters (triage + Bulgarian incident summary) on one base with vLLM and compare memory and latency against two merged models.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Deploy to the depot edge with Foundry Local and an offline-first fallback chain (≈3.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Run triage at the Varna depot with no cloud dependency, and degrade safely.
  • Start state: tag d1/lab4-start. It contains the Trakia.Depot.Edge .NET 10 Worker Service and an Aspire AppHost that simulates depot and cloud.
  • Steps:
  • Start Foundry Local from the C# SDK and wrap it as IChatClient: 
    // Shape only — verify exact Microsoft.AI.Foundry.Local API (manager, model load, endpoint) against current docs
var manager = await FoundryLocalManager.StartModelAsync(aliasOrModelId: cfg["Models:EdgeSlmAlias"]);
IChatClient edge = new OpenAIClient(new ApiKeyCredential(manager.ApiKey),
        new OpenAIClientOptions { Endpoint = manager.Endpoint })
    .GetChatClient(manager.ModelId).AsIChatClient();
    If your fine-tuned export cannot be loaded into Foundry Local, register the Lab 3 ORT GenAI client under the same key. The application code must not change.
  • Build the pipeline with ChatClientBuilder: OTel → a schema-validation middleware → a ConfidenceGate middleware → the inner client.
  • Implement FallbackTriageModel:
    • edge first;
    • if the confidence is < τ, the output is schema-invalid, or the DTC family was not in the training distribution, call the cloud student when connectivity is up;
    • if the cloud is down, return Severity.StopNow with Subsystem = "escalate-to-mechanic" and raise a depot alert. Tune τ on dev to keep StopNow recall ≥ 0.98 end to end.
  • Write every decision to a local SQLite outbox. A background service syncs the outbox to App Insights with idempotent upserts.
  • Measure p50/p95 latency on CPU-only and (if present) GPU/NPU, using the course's reference depot spec (16 GB RAM).
  • Break it:
  • Disconnect the network mid-run (toxiproxy in the AppHost). Verify there is no lost decision and no unsafe default.
  • Then disable the GPU/NPU execution provider and check whether the p95 budget still holds on CPU. Record the result honestly.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The integration test EdgeOfflineTests passes: 200 cases with the network down give 0 exceptions, 100% are persisted, and every low-confidence case is escalated.
  • p95 < 400 ms on the reference spec, or a documented exception.
  • Swapping Models:Provider from FoundryLocal to Ollama in config passes the same tests with no code change.
  • Stretch: Canary roll-out. Ship model v2 to Varna only, compare decision distributions against Plovdiv for drift, and automate rollback on a StopNow-rate anomaly.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Decision report and ADR (≈1.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Turn the measurements into a decision another engineer can reproduce and challenge.
  • Start state: your Lab 1–4 artifacts.
  • Steps:
  • Build one table covering frontier zero-shot, frontier few-shot, ML.NET, cloud student, edge SLM base, edge LoRA INT4 and edge + cloud fallback. Columns: macro-F1, StopNow recall (CI), cost-weighted error, € per 1,000 calls, p95, data residency and an operational burden score.
  • Write docs/adr/ADR-0D1-fault-triage-model.md. It records the chosen architecture, the rejected options with evidence, the retraining triggers (base model deprecation notice, drift on the DTC mix, new truck models) and the owner.
  • Add the retirement date of every base model used to the model registry.
  • Break it: Ask a peer to reproduce one row from your manifest alone. Fix whatever they could not reproduce.
  • Acceptance criteria: The ADR links every number to a committed artifact, and a CI job re-runs the test-set evaluation for the chosen model nightly.
  • Stretch: Add a DPO plan. Specify how thumbs-down feedback from mechanics (C15 feedback events) becomes preference pairs, and what minimum volume would justify a run.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text:
"Which rung?" (25 min, repeat 4×). The instructor hands you a failure cluster from a trace sample, with counts. Variations: 1. Answers cite a superseded maintenance bulletin. 2. Severity is correct but the JSON breaks on Bulgarian notes. 3. Mechanics prefer terser rationales. 4. Classification is correct but costs €0.004 per call at 40k calls/day.

In 25 minutes, write a one-paragraph decision. Name the rung and why the lower rungs do not suffice, the metric and target, the data you need (with volume), the expected cost (training + hosting + inference/month), and the trigger that would make you revisit the decision. The instructor reveals the "expert answer", including the cases where the answer is "don't customize".

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text: The fault-code triage capability now runs on a distilled, LoRA-tuned small model at the depots via Foundry Local (or the ORT GenAI fallback). It sits behind the same IChatClient contract, with a confidence-gated cloud fallback and a safe offline default. The cloud student serves the central Fleet Assistant (C9) as a cheap first tier, ready for the cascade in D5. The model registry records the dataset snapshot, eval report, licence and base-model retirement date for every model.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text:
• A /finetune-experiment skill (Claude Code and Copilot custom agent) scaffolds the dataset card, grouped splits, the eval matrix and an ADR stub from a template. It refuses to submit a training job unless baseline.json exists and the success criterion is filled in.
  • A pre-commit hook blocks commits of JSONL training files that fail the PII scanner or lack a dataset snapshot hash.
  • CI gains a nightly model-eval workflow for each registered model. It opens an issue when a metric drifts or a base model's retirement is under 120 days away (Models API lifecycle status).
  • The coding agent may write data-prep code and eval harnesses. Humans own the label adjudication and the success criterion, and this is recorded in AGENTS.md.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Ladder decision Fine-tunes by default Picks a plausible rung Justifies the rung with error analysis and a cost estimate Pre-registers a target; shows when not to customize; plans retraining against base-model retirement Data & leakage Random split, no dedup Dedup only Grouped split, PII scrub, label audit Quantifies leakage (random vs grouped gap) and teacher–expert agreement; dataset card reproducible from a hash Evaluation Single accuracy number Macro-F1 on held-out data Full matrix incl. safety tail and keep suite Paired significance tests, CIs, cost-weighted error; post-export (quantized) re-eval Edge engineering Runs a local model in a demo IChatClient swap works Fallback chain + outbox Offline-safe defaults proven by tests; per-depot canary with rollback; honest CPU-only numbers Communication Screenshots Report with numbers ADR with rejected options ADR another engineer reproduces from manifests; clear retraining triggers and owner

Auto-checked: - the CI test categories Baseline, Student, Edge, EdgeOffline; - the zero-overlap split assertion; - the threshold gates (macro-F1 delta, StopNow recall ≥ 0.97, p95); - the presence and schema of models/manifest.json; - the nightly model-eval workflow status.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Training with one system prompt and serving with another.
  • Random splits on repetitive operational data.
  • Trusting teacher labels as ground truth.
  • Evaluating the LoRA checkpoint instead of the shipped, quantized artifact.
  • Oversampling the rare class in test.
  • Ignoring the base model's lifecycle. A fine-tune on a retired base returns 410 Gone too.
  • Global or Data zone training tiers for EU personal data.
  • Measuring on a laptop instead of the depot reference spec (CPU-only included).
  • An unsafe fallback ("when in doubt, continue driving").
  • Skipping the ML.NET baseline, which is often within a point of the LLM at a fraction of the cost.
