docs.title: D7 — Agent reliability engineering
docs.text: Level: Expert (AI Solution Developer track) · Duration: 18h (theory 25% / labs 75%) · Prerequisites: Core C0–C19 and Gate G3; especially C5/C14 (evals, calibrated judges), C15 (tracing, versioning), C17 (APIM, deployment); D2 (durable agents) and D5 (CPST) recommended · Volatility: Medium (methods are stable; Foundry evaluator status, benchmark leaderboards and tooling change quarterly)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
A proficient practitioner has an eval suite, an LLM judge and a CI gate. An expert treats agent reliability statistically and operationally: - measures whether the agent succeeds every time (pass^k), not whether it can succeed (pass@1); - tells a real regression from noise with the right test and sample size; - covers the long tail with simulated users and environments; - injects faults into tools and models to prove graceful degradation; - runs agent behaviour under SLOs with error budgets; - writes postmortems whose output is new evals; - reads every benchmark claim, including vendors' and Microsoft's own, with a critic's eye.

The τ-bench authors introduced pass^k precisely because agents that look strong at pass@1 collapse when asked to succeed consistently. If one trial succeeds with p = 0.9 and trials are independent, pass^4 ≈ 0.66 and pass^8 ≈ 0.43.

Trakia now runs the Fleet Assistant, the Fleet Analyst, the incident workflow, the durable planner, the voice assistant and two customer pilots. Last month three things happened: - A provider-side model update shifted the Fleet Assistant's tool-calling behaviour, and maintenance bookings started missing the depot parameter. The cached CI evals stayed green. - A dispatcher "flaky test" was quarantined for weeks. It turned out to be a real 12% failure mode on Bulgarian plates. - A conference talk claimed a memory feature gave "+14% on τ-bench", and someone proposed adopting it immediately. Microsoft's own two posts disagree on the size of that gain (≈5% vs 7–14%).

Reliability engineering is the discipline that would have caught all three.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Build a τ-bench-style simulation harness (LLM user simulator, policy document, tool backends over a database snapshot, end-state graders) for a Trakia agent, and audit simulator-induced false failures.
  2. Curate a versioned scenario library with an explicit taxonomy and coverage matrix, fed by production failures and synthetic tuples.
  3. Quantify reliability with pass@1, pass^k and per-scenario success rates with confidence intervals, and distinguish flaky scenarios from hard ones and regressions from noise (paired tests, sample-size planning).
  4. Design and run chaos experiments for tools and models (errors, latency, malformed results, 429s, model swap, retirement 410 Gone, injection) with steady-state hypotheses and expected behaviours.
  5. Define agent SLIs/SLOs (task success, safety violations, escalations, latency, CPST) with error budgets and multi-window burn-rate alerts, including measurement error from judges.
  6. Operate continuous evaluation in production (sampling, online judges, canary comparisons, drift detection), and feed it back into offline suites.
  7. Lead a blameless postmortem for an AI failure that produces concrete new scenarios, checks and guardrails.
  8. Critique public benchmark and vendor claims (SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench, GAIA, τ-bench, OSWorld): saturation, harness effects, contamination, variance, cost.

docs.title: 1. Reliability is not accuracy
docs.text:
Metric Definition Answers pass@1 Success rate of a single attempt (averaged over scenarios) "How good is it typically?" pass@k ≥ 1 success in k attempts "Can it ever do this?" (useful with a verifier and retries) pass^k All k attempts succeed "Will it do this every time a user asks?" Per-scenario success distribution Success rate per scenario across N trials "Which scenarios are reliable, flaky or broken?"

Users experience per-attempt behaviour, repeatedly. A dispatcher who asks 30 questions a day experiences pass^30 on a scenario family, not pass@1. Report pass^k alongside pass@1 for agentic tasks with side effects. Track the share of scenarios with success ≥ 0.95 (the "reliable set"); it is more actionable than the mean.

Non-determinism is structural. Temperature 0 is not deterministic in production serving, because inference kernels are not batch-invariant. Your tests must therefore be statistical. Use MEAI.Evaluation response caching to make PR-time CI repeatable for unchanged prompts. Never mistake that for reliability, and always run an uncached suite nightly against live endpoints.

docs.title: 2. Simulation-based testing (τ-bench style)
docs.text:
τ-bench evaluates tool-agent-user interaction with four parts: - an LLM-simulated user that has a goal and private information; - a domain policy document; - tools over a database; - a check of the database end state against the goal.

τ²-bench adds dual-control environments in which the user also acts on the world. The design lesson: grade outcomes and policy adherence, not the exact turn-by-turn path. Stateful agents can reach the right end state many ways.

TrakiaSim generalises the C14 Lab 3 dispatcher simulator (one persona family, 30 scenarios, pass^4) into a reusable, statistically sound harness. Do not rebuild C14's simulator; extend it: - Environment: a containerized SQL Server snapshot of TrakiaOps (reset per episode), the mock ticketing, scheduling and parts APIs, and the real Trakia MCP server. - Simulated users: - a dispatcher (terse, Bulgarian/English code-switching); - a customer-service agent (relays a customer's angry email); - a driver (voice transcripts from D3); - an adversarial user (pressure to bypass approval).

Each has a goal, known facts, hidden facts revealed only if asked, and a termination rule. - Policy: excerpts of the fleet policy handbook, for example "maintenance bookings require depot capacity check; urgent DTCs override routing". - Graders: - (a) end-state diff (expected rows created or updated, nothing else changed); - (b) policy-violation checks in code (booking without a capacity check, notification before approval); - (c) a calibrated judge for conversational requirements (asked for missing info, confirmed before acting, language matched).

Simulator fidelity is a threat to validity: - simulated users are often too cooperative, too verbose, or leak hidden facts early; - they also make mistakes that cause false failures.

Mitigations: - calibrate personas against 30+ real transcripts; - run the simulator at low temperature with a different model family from the agent's (reduces correlated blind spots); - audit every failure cluster and label it "agent fault", "simulator fault" or "scenario bug"; - report the agent's pass rate only over valid episodes, and track the simulator fault rate as a metric.

docs.title: 3. Scenario libraries
docs.text:
A scenario is data: {id, version, persona, goal, hidden_facts, initial_db_fixture, policy_refs, expected_end_state, checks[], tags[]}.

  • Taxonomy dimensions:
  • intent family;
  • complexity (number of tools and turns);
  • language (BG/EN/mixed);
  • data condition (missing, stale, conflicting);
  • permission context (role);
  • adversarial type (injection, social pressure);
  • modality (text/voice).

Maintain a coverage matrix and target the cells that production traffic and risk say matter. Do not aim for uniform coverage. - Sources: 1. production failures from error analysis and postmortems (highest value); 2. synthetic tuples: define the dimensions, hand-write about 20 tuples, generate more, then turn each tuple into a scenario in a separate step and review it by hand (Hamel & Shankar); 3. policy-derived edge cases; 4. red-team findings (C14/C16).

Synthetic data cannot tell you how frequent a failure is. Use production sampling for that. - Sets: - smoke (20, every PR, cached); - regression (150–300, every PR touching prompts, tools or models, multiple trials, nightly uncached); - exploratory/long-tail (weekly); - holdout (never used for tuning; quarterly, to detect overfitting to the suite). - Versioning: scenarios evolve with policy. Pin each suite version in the eval report and keep the old versions for trend comparability.

docs.title: 4. Statistics for regression gates and flakiness
docs.text:
• Confidence intervals. 45/50 successes is 90%, with a Wilson 95% CI of ≈ 79–96%. A 50-scenario suite cannot distinguish 88% from 92%. Report intervals, always.
  • Sample size. To detect a drop from 90% to 85% with an unpaired two-proportion test (α = 0.05 two-sided, power 0.8), you need ≈ 690 episodes per arm. Paired designs (the same scenarios under both versions) are far more efficient. Use McNemar's test on discordant pairs, and with multiple trials per scenario, a paired test on per-scenario success rates (or a permutation test).
  • Pre-register the primary metric. Gate on 1–2 primary metrics (for example, task success on the regression set, and safety violations = 0 on the safety set). Monitor the others. With 20 metrics at α = 0.05, one "regression" per run is expected by chance. Correct with Holm if you must gate on many.
  • Flaky vs hard vs regressed. Run each scenario N = 5–10 times:
  • success near 0 → broken/hard: fix the agent or the scenario;
  • near 1 → reliable;
  • in between → flaky: a real reliability defect or a scenario/simulator defect.

Never auto-quarantine flaky agent scenarios. Quarantine is legitimate only after an audit attributes the variance to the simulator or the environment, and the scenario is fixed within an SLA. - Variance decomposition. Separate between-scenario variance (difficulty) from within-scenario variance (stochasticity). A change that lowers within-scenario variance at equal mean is a reliability improvement worth shipping. - Cost. Trials multiply cost (scenarios × trials × tokens). Use cached PR runs, a smaller smoke set, nightly full runs and budget caps (D5).

docs.title: 5. Chaos engineering for agents
docs.text:
Start from a steady-state hypothesis ("≥ 95% of booking scenarios succeed or escalate correctly"). Inject one fault class at a time, observe, and widen the blast radius gradually.

Fault Injection point Expected agent behaviour Tool 5xx / timeout Tool wrapper, toxiproxy Code retries with backoff (not the model); after N failures, an actionable error message to the model; graceful partial answer or escalation Tool returns malformed or partial data Tool wrapper Schema validation catches it; the model is told what is wrong; no fabricated fill-in Slow tool (P99 × 10) Latency injection Timeout budget respected; user informed (D4); no duplicate side effects on retry (D2 idempotency) 429 with Retry-After APIM fault policy / mock backend Honour Retry-After; spill to the secondary pool (D5); no retry storm Model swap (new version, router change, fallback model) Config via IChatClient registration Eval deltas within tolerance; tool-call argument accuracy unchanged; if not, the gate blocks the promotion Model retired → 410 Gone Mock backend Fail over to the configured successor; alert; no silent outage. GA models are deprecated at 12 months and retired at 18; partner models get 12 months (Grok sometimes 6); notice is ≥ 60 days; dates cannot be extended Context pressure (huge tool result, long session) Tool wrapper Truncation/pagination or compaction kicks in; no lost instructions Stale or conflicting data DB fixture The agent surfaces the conflict, prefers the authoritative source, cites the version Injected instructions in tool results Tool wrapper No consequential action (C16 patterns); a violation counts as a safety SLI breach

In .NET, faults are injected as middleware, so the same agent code is tested:

public sealed class ChaosChatClient(IChatClient inner, ChaosPolicy policy) : DelegatingChatClient(inner)
{
    public override async Task<ChatResponse> GetResponseAsync(IEnumerable<ChatMessage> messages,
        ChatOptions? options = null, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        if (policy.ShouldFail("model.429")) throw new HttpRequestException("429", null, HttpStatusCode.TooManyRequests);
        if (policy.ShouldFail("model.410")) throw new HttpRequestException("410 Gone", null, HttpStatusCode.Gone);
        await policy.MaybeDelayAsync("model.latency", ct);
        return await base.GetResponseAsync(messages, options, ct);
    }
}
// Tools: wrap each AIFunction with ChaosToolDecorator (errors, latency, malformed JSON, injected text) — same ChaosPolicy, seeded per episode.

Run chaos in TrakiaSim (the simulator plus faults), not only in unit tests. Behaviour under faults is a property of the whole loop.

docs.title: 6. Benchmark literacy
docs.text:
Benchmark Measures Read with care because SWE-bench / Verified (500 human-validated tasks) Resolving real GitHub issues, verified by tests Saturating (Vals AI archived its coverage citing saturation); the harness/scaffold matters as much as the model; contamination risk Terminal-Bench Agent tasks in real terminals Newer, differentiating in 2026; harness-dependent GAIA General assistant tasks (reasoning, browsing, tools); humans ≈ 92% at release Web drift changes answers; tool set matters τ-bench / τ²-bench Tool-agent-user interaction with policies; pass^k Simulator fidelity; domain is retail/airline/telecom, not yours OSWorld Real OS tasks for computer-use agents Environment setup variance; pixel vs accessibility approaches

A checklist for any claim, including vendor and Microsoft posts: 1. Who ran it (vendor-run or independent)? 2. Which harness/scaffold, which settings (effort, tools, retries, best-of-n)? 3. pass@1 or best-of-k? Is variance reported? 4. Is cost per task reported? 5. Is there a contamination analysis? 6. Is the gain relative or absolute, against which baseline? 7. Does the task distribution resemble ours?

Course examples: - Anthropic's multi-agent system beat single-agent Opus by 90.2% on an internal eval: not reproducible by you, but internally consistent with token-usage findings. - Microsoft's procedural memory: "≈5% on STATE-Bench and τ-bench" in one post vs "+7–14% absolute on τ-bench" in another. - Mem0's vendor-authored LOCOMO gains are publicly disputed by Letta.

The expert response: "promising; run it on TrakiaSim with pass^k before adopting".

docs.title: 7. SLOs for agents
docs.text:
SLI Measurement Example SLO (Fleet Assistant) Task success Online sampled judges (calibrated, TPR/TNR known) + outcome signals (no human override, no rollback) ≥ 92% over 28 days Safety violations Policy-check failures, guardrail-confirmed unsafe actions 0 critical; ≤ 0.1% minor Escalation rate Agent → human handoffs 5–15% (too low can mean overconfidence) Latency P95 E2E / TTFT per task type P95 ≤ 6 s (analyst), ≤ 2.5 s (assistant) Availability Non-error responses / requests ≥ 99.5% Cost CPST (D5) ≤ €0.04 per successful assistant task
  • Error budgets and multi-window burn-rate alerts (for example, 1h and 6h windows at 14× and 6× burn) apply as in classic SRE, with one twist.
  • Judge-based SLIs carry measurement error. A judge with TPR 0.92 and TNR 0.95 biases the observed success rate. Correct for it (Rogan–Gladen style: true ≈ (observed + TNR − 1)/(TPR + TNR − 1)) or report the bounds.
  • Sample enough traffic for the alert windows. Low-traffic tenants need longer windows.
  • Separate behavioural SLOs (success, safety) from infrastructure SLOs (availability, latency). A behavioural burn should page the AI owner, not the platform on-call.

docs.title: 8. Continuous evaluation in production
docs.text:
• Sampling: random (unbiased SLI estimation) plus targeted (thumbs-down, retries, long traces, unusual tool sequences, new intents). Keep the two pools separate, because targeted samples bias rates.
  • Online judges: small, calibrated, cost-capped. Foundry continuous evaluation samples live agent responses, scores quality and risk dimensions, shows results on the agent's Monitor tab and supports alerts. It requires App Insights and the project managed identity with the Foundry User role. Some agent evaluators are still preview, and per a practitioner source, evaluations, monitoring and tracing reached GA in March 2026.
  • Canary and shadow: route 5–10% through APIM weighted backends to the new model or prompt version, then compare SLIs with a paired-by-intent analysis before promotion. Shadow mode (run the new version without showing the result) for side-effect-free tasks.
  • Drift:
  • input drift: intent mix, language mix, token lengths;
  • output drift: length, tool-usage patterns, refusal rate;
  • judge pass-rate drift;
  • the provider changing under you, detected by the nightly uncached golden run.
  • The loop: online failures → error analysis queue → new scenarios in TrakiaSim → regression set. A failure seen twice in production without a scenario is a process defect.

docs.title: 9. Postmortems for AI failures
docs.text:
Use the classic blameless format plus AI-specific sections: - Versions at incident time: model and deployment version, router version, prompt/agent definition hash, tool contract versions, index alias/corpus version, guardrail config, cache state. - Failure class: provider drift, prompt change, retrieval/index, tool contract change, injection/abuse, runaway cost, unsafe action, regulated-value hallucination, simulator/eval blind spot. - "Why didn't our evals catch it?" This section is mandatory. Typical answers: no scenario covered it, the judge was miscalibrated, the cached CI masked drift, flaky-quarantined, SLI not sampled. - Outputs: ≥ 1 new scenario, ≥ 1 new check or judge, a guardrail or design change, SLO or alert tuning, and an owner and date for each. - Regulatory hooks: personal-data leaks trigger GDPR breach assessment (72-hour notification duty). For high-risk systems, AI Act serious-incident duties apply once the Annex III obligations take effect (2 Dec 2027 after the Digital Omnibus). Know which applies to which Trakia component (C18).

Misconceptions to unlearn: - "Green CI = reliable." Cached, single-trial, small-N suites prove little. - "Flaky tests are noise." In agents, flakiness is the reliability defect. - "A leaderboard win transfers to our domain." - "The judge's score is the truth." It is a measurement instrument with error rates.

docs.title: Labs
docs.text: Lab repo: trakia-fleetops, folder reliability/ (TrakiaSim .NET project, scenarios/ YAML library, chaos/ policies, slo/ Bicep for alerts and workbooks).

docs.title: Lab 1 — TrakiaSim: a τ-bench-style harness for the Fleet Assistant (≈5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Measure the Fleet Assistant's reliability on realistic multi-turn tasks with end-state grading and pass^k.
  • Start state: tag d7/lab1-start (your C14 Lab 3 dispatcher simulator and scenarios, plus the scenario schema, the SQL Server snapshot container with a reset script, and the mock APIs). New relative to C14: per-episode DB reset and end-state diff, four persona families incl. adversarial, simulator-fault attribution, CIs and the reliable-set share.
  • Steps:
  • Implement UserSimulator, a separate IChatClient (a different model family from the agent's) with a persona prompt containing the goal, known facts and hidden facts, the rule "reveal hidden facts only when asked", and a ###STOP### termination token.
  • Implement Episode.RunAsync: reset the DB, then loop between simulator and agent until stop, max turns or budget. Record the trace and compute the end-state diff: 
    var before = await Db.SnapshotAsync(scenario.Fixture);
var transcript = await Episode.RunAsync(agent, simulator, scenario, budget, ct);
var diff = await Db.DiffAsync(before);
var verdict = Graders.EndState(diff, scenario.ExpectedEndState)
            & Graders.Policy(transcript.ToolCalls, scenario.PolicyRefs)       // code checks
            & await Judges.Conversation(transcript, scenario.ConversationChecks); // calibrated judges
  • Author 40 scenarios across 4 personas and 8 intents, including Bulgarian and code-switched dispatcher scenarios and 6 adversarial "skip approval" scenarios.
  • Run 4 trials per scenario. Report pass@1, pass^4, the reliable-set share (≥ 0.95 success) and the per-intent breakdown, all with Wilson CIs.
  • Audit every failing episode and label it agent fault, simulator fault or scenario bug. Fix the simulator and scenario bugs, and report the simulator fault rate.
  • Break it: Make the simulator "helpful", so it volunteers hidden facts in the first message. Observe the inflated pass rate on information-gathering scenarios, then restore it and add a simulator-fidelity check (hidden facts may not appear before the agent asks).
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • TrakiaSim runs in CI on the 40-scenario suite (nightly, uncached, budget-capped).
  • The report contains pass@1, pass^4, CIs and failure attribution.
  • The simulator fault rate is ≤ 5% after fixes.
  • The 6 adversarial scenarios have 0 approval bypasses.
  • Stretch: Add a τ²-style dual-control scenario in which the driver must perform a step (confirm the odometer reading) that the agent cannot do itself.

docs.title: Lab 2 — Scenario library, flakiness and a statistically sound regression gate (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Turn the suite into a library with coverage, and a gate that catches real regressions without crying wolf.
  • Start state: tag d7/lab2-start.
  • Steps:
  • Define the taxonomy (intent, complexity, language, data condition, role, adversarial, modality) and generate a coverage matrix report. Add 30 scenarios from last month's production failure clusters (C14 error-analysis exports) and 20 from synthetic tuples, reviewed by hand.
  • Run 8 trials per scenario on the current version. Classify each scenario as reliable, flaky or broken, and investigate the top 5 flaky ones.
  • Make a prompt change (the Fleet Assistant v3.2, "more concise confirmations"). Compare it with v3.1 on the same scenarios and trials: a paired per-scenario analysis plus McNemar on first-trial outcomes, with primary metrics pre-registered in gate.yaml.
  • Implement the gate:
    • fail if the paired lower 95% bound of the success delta is < −2 points on the primary set;
    • fail on any safety-set violation;
    • warn (not fail) on secondary metrics, with a Holm correction.
  • Write a sample-size note: how many scenarios × trials are needed to detect a 3-point drop on this suite.
  • Break it: Gate on a single cached trial of 50 scenarios, re-run the identical version 10 times uncached, and count the false alarms. Compare with your gate.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • gate.yaml and the gate implementation are committed.
  • The false-alarm rate is ≤ 1 in 10 identical-version runs.
  • The seeded real regression (the instructor provides a v3.2b that drops the depot parameter in 10% of bookings) is caught.
  • The flaky-scenario investigation finds at least one real agent defect, or documents why none exists.
  • Stretch: Add sequential testing, stopping early when the evidence is conclusive, to cut trial costs. Report the savings.

docs.title: Lab 3 — Chaos for tools and models (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Prove graceful degradation under realistic faults, including a model swap and a retirement.
  • Start state: tag d7/lab3-start (ChaosChatClient, ChaosToolDecorator and the APIM fault policy fragments, all disabled).
  • Steps:
  • Write steady-state hypotheses for 3 intents (booking, analyst query, incident triage).
  • Run the experiments in TrakiaSim, one fault class at a time, at 5%, 20% and 50% intensity:
    • tool 5xx;
    • tool latency ×10;
    • malformed JSON;
    • 429 with Retry-After at the gateway;
    • injected instructions in tool output;
    • a stale fixture.
  • Model-swap drill: point Models:Assistant at a different version or model through config, run the regression set (paired), and decide go/no-go with the Lab 2 gate.
  • Retirement drill: the mock backend returns 410 Gone for the primary deployment. Verify failover to the configured successor and the alert, and write the runbook step.
  • Fix at least two weaknesses found. Typical ones: the model was retrying tools itself (move the retries into code); fabricated values after a malformed result (strengthen validation and the error message).
  • Break it: Remove idempotency keys from the booking tool (D2) and rerun the latency fault. Count the duplicate bookings, then restore the keys.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • ChaosSuite passes: each steady-state hypothesis holds at 20% intensity.
  • There are 0 duplicate side effects.
  • There are 0 consequential actions from injected tool text.
  • The 410 drill fails over within the configured time and raises the alert.
  • The model-swap decision is documented with paired evidence.
  • Stretch: Run a gateway-level chaos experiment in a staging environment with Azure Chaos Studio (network latency to the Foundry endpoint) while the load test from D5 runs.

docs.title: Lab 4 — SLOs, continuous evaluation and an AI incident postmortem (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Operate the agents against behavioural SLOs, detect a live incident, and learn from it.
  • Start state: tag d7/lab4-start (staging environment with synthetic traffic generators).
  • Steps:
  • Define the SLIs and SLOs in slo/slo.yaml for the Fleet Assistant and the Fleet Analyst. Implement them as KQL over traces and judge events, and deploy multi-window burn-rate alerts via Bicep.
  • Enable online evaluation. Either use Foundry continuous evaluation on the hosted agent, or a .NET sampler that scores a 5% random sample plus all targeted samples with calibrated judges. Apply the judge-error correction to the reported success SLI.
  • Run a canary: 10% of traffic to the assistant prompt v3.2 via APIM weighted backends, and compare SLIs per intent.
  • Incident: the instructor flips a hidden change (the provider deployment or the index alias switches to a version that drops a policy chapter). Detect it from the burn-rate alert, triage it with traces (optionally with Azure SRE Agent in Reader mode), and mitigate it (roll back the alias or route).
  • Write the postmortem with the AI-specific sections (versions, failure class, "why evals didn't catch it"). Add the new scenarios and checks to TrakiaSim and prove they fail on the broken version and pass on the fixed one.
  • Break it: Silence the uncached nightly run and repeat the incident. How long until detection? Quantify the value of the nightly run in hours of exposure.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • SLO alerts are deployed as code.
  • The incident is detected within the target window (≤ 1h at the staging traffic level).
  • The postmortem is merged with ≥ 2 new scenarios and ≥ 1 new check, all red on the broken version and green on the fixed one.
  • The canary analysis report is attached.
  • Stretch: An error-budget policy. Write the rule for freezing prompt and model changes when the budget is exhausted, and automate it as a CI check reading the SLO status.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text:
"Signal or noise?" (25 min, repeat 4×). You get two eval reports (version A vs B) with per-scenario, per-trial outcomes: - Variant 1: 50 scenarios × 1 trial, −4 points. - Variant 2: 200 × 5, −1.5 points, concentrated in Bulgarian scenarios. - Variant 3: +3 points on pass@1 but lower pass^4. - Variant 4: a vendor blog claiming +12% on τ-bench.

For each, decide ship/hold/investigate and justify it with the right statistic: a CI, a paired test, a pass^k comparison, or the benchmark checklist. The instructor reveals the ground truth (simulated with known effects).

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text: Fleet Ops Copilot is now operated as a reliable service: - TrakiaSim covers the core agents with pass^k reporting. - A versioned scenario library has a coverage matrix fed by production failures. - A statistical regression gate with pre-registered primary metrics. - A chaos suite covers tool, gateway and model faults, with retirement and model-swap drills. - Behavioural SLOs with burn-rate alerts. - Continuous evaluation with judge-error correction, and a canary process. - A postmortem template whose outputs land as tests.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text:
• Coding agents must run the smoke set (cached) and attach the TrakiaSim delta for any PR touching prompts, tools or agent definitions. A Stop hook or Copilot custom-agent rule enforces it.
  • A regression triage agent (headless, D6 tooling) runs on every nightly failure. It clusters failing episodes, labels likely simulator faults vs agent faults for human confirmation, and opens issues with traces attached. It may not quarantine scenarios.
  • Postmortem action items are created as issues tagged eval-gap. The cloud agent drafts the scenario YAML and the check, and humans review the expected end states.
  • The error-budget policy is enforced in CI: prompt and model changes are blocked while the budget is exhausted, unless the PR is labelled as a reliability fix.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Simulation & scenarios Single-turn Q&A evals Multi-turn scripted tests Simulator + end-state grading + library Calibrated simulator with fault attribution; coverage matrix driven by risk and production failures; holdout set Statistics Point estimates Averages over trials CIs and pass^k Paired tests, pre-registered gates, sample-size planning, judge-error correction, measured false-alarm rate Chaos None Unit tests for tool errors Fault injection in the loop Hypothesis-driven experiments incl. model swap and retirement; fixes verified; no duplicate side effects Operations Dashboards SLIs defined SLOs + alerts + online evals Error budgets with policy, canary analysis, drift detection, incident detected and mitigated within target Learning from failure Fixes the bug Writes an incident note Blameless postmortem "Why evals missed it" answered; new scenarios/checks proven red→green; benchmark claims critiqued with the checklist

Auto-checked: the nightly TrakiaSim run, the simulator fault-rate threshold, the gate false-alarm test (10 identical runs), detection of the seeded regression, ChaosSuite, the 410 drill, SLO alert deployment, postmortem scenarios red→green on the broken and fixed versions, and the error-budget CI check.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Gating on cached, single-trial, small-N suites and calling it reliability.
  • Reporting only pass@1 for agents with side effects.
  • Auto-quarantining flaky scenarios, which hides the real reliability defect.
  • Trusting simulators without auditing simulator-caused failures.
  • Grading exact tool-call sequences instead of end state plus policy checks, and so failing valid alternative paths.
  • Retrying tools via the model instead of in code. Retrying side effects without idempotency.
  • Treating judge scores as ground truth in SLIs.
  • Paging platform on-call for behavioural SLO burns, or not paging anyone at all.
  • Adopting features on vendor benchmark deltas without running them on your own simulator.
  • Postmortems without new tests.

docs.title: A1 — AI strategy, use-case discovery & business case
docs.text: Level: Expert — AI Solution Architect track · Duration: 16h (theory 30% / labs 70%) · Prerequisites: Core C0–C19 and Gate G3 passed (you have a working, traced, evaluated Fleet Ops Copilot) · Volatility: Med (methods are stable; prices, SKUs, licensing and certification blueprints change quarterly)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
What separates an expert architect from a proficient one here: a proficient architect can estimate what an AI feature costs to run. An expert can show, with numbers they can defend, which problems deserve AI at all, which should be bought instead of built, and what evidence must exist before a pilot is allowed to become a product. The expert treats the business case as a falsifiable hypothesis that evals and telemetry will confirm or kill. The proficient architect treats it as a slide that unlocks budget.

Trakia Freight's board has decided, after a good demo, to (a) roll Fleet Ops Copilot out to all 600 drivers, ~45 dispatchers, ~35 mechanics and the office functions across Plovdiv, Sofia and Varna, and (b) sell it as multi-tenant SaaS to other fleets. The usual failure pattern follows:

  • Every department submits "AI ideas" and the team builds the loudest one.
  • Time savings are counted as cash.
  • Token costs are estimated from one happy-path prompt, although a multi-agent workflow burns roughly 15× the tokens of a chat turn.
  • Nobody budgets for eval labelling, red-teaming or the model migrations that 12–18-month lifecycles force.
  • The HR policy bot is custom-built when an M365 Copilot licence would have done.
  • Driver-behaviour scoring, an EU AI Act Annex III employment use case, slips in as "just analytics".

Experts run discovery as a structured, evidence-producing process:

  • They score use cases on value, feasibility and risk, and kill most of them early and cheaply.
  • They model TCO across five cost families: tokens, infrastructure, people, evals and ops.
  • They apply the Cloud Adoption Framework (CAF) rule of "least operational responsibility".
  • They write pilot-to-production criteria before the pilot starts.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
By the end of this module you can:

  1. Facilitate a use-case discovery workshop, using persona interviews, a process walk and a pain/value inventory, and produce a backlog of at least 8 use-case canvases with explicit value hypotheses.
  2. Score and rank use cases on value, feasibility and risk with a weighted, documented rubric. Defend at least two "kill" decisions and one "not an LLM problem" decision.
  3. Assess AI readiness across six dimensions (data, platform, skills, governance, process, culture) and quantify data readiness with queries against the real estate (TrakiaOps, document corpus).
  4. Build a ROI/TCO model as code plus a spreadsheet view, covering tokens, infrastructure, people, evals and ops. Calibrate cost per task from production traces, not prompt guesses.
  5. Run sensitivity and Monte Carlo analysis, and identify the three assumptions that drive the business case.
  6. Choose and justify build vs buy vs extend per use case (M365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, Foundry agents, custom MAF), applying the CAF "least operational responsibility" rule, and record the choice as an ADR.
  7. Define measurable pilot-to-production gates covering eval thresholds, adoption, cost per task, SLOs, security and compliance, plus success metrics with leading, lagging and guardrail indicators.
  8. Map your deliverables to the AB-100 "Plan AI-powered business solutions" skill area.

docs.title: 1. Strategy is a portfolio, not a project
docs.text:
An AI strategy for a mid-size company is a portfolio of bets with different risk/return profiles, governed by one platform and one set of controls. For Trakia it has three horizons:

  • H1 — productivity inside existing workflows (low risk, mostly buy/extend): HR and policy Q&A, email drafting for customer service, meeting summaries.
  • H2 — process redesign with agents (medium risk, build on the platform): incident triage → diagnostics → maintenance booking (C12), the Fleet Analyst over telematics (C10).
  • H3 — new revenue (high risk, build): Fleet Ops Copilot as SaaS for other fleets.

H1 funds credibility, H2 funds the platform, and H3 needs the platform to exist. A common mistake is to start H3 (SaaS) before H2 has proven unit economics and operational maturity internally. Trakia's internal rollout is the cheapest place to learn what a tenant costs.

The CAF AI adoption scenario structures the journey as AI planning → AI ready → govern, secure, manage. Its build-vs-buy heuristic is explicit: prefer the option "with the least operational responsibility". That means SaaS such as M365 Copilot and Copilot Studio first, then PaaS (Foundry, Fabric, Azure ML, Container Apps). IaaS "shouldn't be the default". CAF folds skilling into workforce enablement and has no separate agent-adoption guidance, so you supply that yourself (A7).

docs.title: 2. Use-case discovery: how experts run it
docs.text:
Discovery fails when it starts from "where can we use AI?". It succeeds when it starts from work: who does what, how often, how long it takes, what it costs when it goes wrong, and what data exists at that moment. The expert sequence:

  1. Frame: the business goals for the year (Trakia: cut unplanned downtime, cut SLA penalties, grow revenue without growing headcount 1:1) and the constraints (GDPR, EU AI Act, Bulgarian-language users, works council).
  2. Persona interviews (30 min each, 6–8 personas): use "tell me about the last time…" questions, never "would AI help you?".
  3. Process walk: map the incident flow from fault code to repaired truck. Mark waiting time, handoffs, rework and lookups.
  4. Pain/value inventory: one sticky per pain with frequency × time × cost-of-error.
  5. Use-case canvas per candidate, with these fields:
  6. actor and trigger;
  7. task;
  8. current KPI baseline;
  9. value hypothesis ("We believe X will reduce Y from A to B, measured by M");
  10. data needed and where it lives;
  11. action level (inform / recommend / act with approval / act autonomously);
  12. failure cost;
  13. regulatory flags;
  14. "is an LLM the right tool?" check.
  15. Score, then cut: most candidates should die at this step.

"Is it an LLM problem?" check. Apply it ruthlessly, because many of Trakia's ideas are not LLM problems:

  • Predicting component failure from telematics is tabular prediction → ML.NET/AutoML.
  • Reading scanned delivery notes is fixed-layout extraction with per-field confidence → Content Understanding or Document Intelligence.
  • Classifying 50k engine fault codes per day is high-volume deterministic classification → a fine-tuned small model (D1) or a typed decision model.
  • Answering "which clause of the customer SLA applies to this late delivery?" needs language understanding over documents → an LLM with RAG.

The architect's value is often in redirecting a use case to the cheaper, more explainable technique.

docs.title: 3. Scoring: value × feasibility × risk
docs.text:
Use a weighted rubric with anchored levels (1–5). Anchors make scores comparable between assessors.

Dimension Sub-criteria (weight) Anchor examples Value (40%) Hard € impact (50%), strategic fit (20%), frequency × reach (20%), time-to-value (10%) 5 = > €200k/yr hard benefit or enables revenue; 1 = < €10k/yr, soft only Feasibility (35%) Data readiness (35%), eval-ability (25%; can we define pass/fail?), integration effort (20%), skills (20%) 5 = data clean and accessible, golden set exists; 1 = data on paper, no ground truth Risk (25%, scored inverted) Regulatory class (35%), failure cost and reversibility (30%), security exposure / lethal trifecta (20%), change/people impact (15%) 5 = minimal-risk, read-only, reversible; 1 = Annex III high-risk, autonomous actions on people

Two decision rules sit on top of the weighted score:

  • Hard gates override the score. A prohibited practice (Art. 5) is killed regardless of value. An Annex III use case cannot enter a pilot without a governance-board decision (A6). A use case with eval-ability 1 cannot enter a pilot until someone can say what "correct" means.
  • Plot, don't just rank. A value-vs-feasibility bubble chart, with bubble size = risk, shows the "quick wins", the "strategic bets" that need a spike first, and the "money pits".

Misconception to unlearn: "high value + high feasibility = do it now". For an agent that acts (books maintenance, emails a customer), feasibility must include whether you can build the HITL step and the evals for that action. "We can call the API" is not enough.

docs.title: 4. AI readiness assessment
docs.text:
Microsoft and others publish AI readiness instruments (verify the current Microsoft instrument before teaching). This course uses a six-dimension, evidence-based assessment. The rule is that every score must cite an artefact or a query result, never an opinion.

Dimension Evidence you collect at Trakia Data % of incident reports with a valid vehicle ID; document freshness (share of policies reviewed < 12 months ago); ACL coverage (share of documents with role metadata); BG/EN split; corpus size in tokens Platform Landing zone exists? Private networking? APIM? Observability (C15)? IaC coverage? Skills Who can run error analysis, write evals, operate agents? Named people, not roles Governance AI policy, inventory, DPIA practice, risk classification process (A6) Process Can the target process absorb a recommendation? Who acts on it, and in which system? Culture / change Works council stance, driver trust, manager sponsorship

Corpus size is a design input, not trivia. Anthropic's rule of thumb is that knowledge bases under ~200k tokens can skip RAG and go into a cached prompt. A department-specific use case (e.g., the 40-page depot safety handbook) may need no retrieval pipeline at all.

docs.title: 5. ROI and TCO: the five cost families
docs.text:
The TCO of an AI product has five families. Most business cases model only the first.

  1. Tokens.
  2. Formula: cost per task = Σ over model calls of (uncached input × p_in + cached input × p_cached + (output + reasoning tokens) × p_out). Reasoning tokens are billed and share the context budget.
  3. Per-token price ≠ per-task cost. A model with a cheaper per-token price can cost more per task because it uses more tokens.
  4. Multi-agent multiplier: multi-agent systems use ~15× the tokens of chat (Anthropic's research system). Calibrate from your C15 traces, never from a single prompt.
  5. Infrastructure.
  6. Fixed baseline: AI Search tier, Cosmos DB, App Gateway + WAF, Azure Firewall, DDoS Protection, APIM tier, private endpoints, Log Analytics ingestion. The baseline Foundry chat reference architecture names Cosmos DB, AI Search and DDoS Protection as the largest cost lines.
  7. Variable: compute for hosted agents and Container Apps, Redis for the semantic cache, storage, egress.
  8. People.
  9. Platform team, product team share, an SME "benevolent dictator" for quality labels, a governance role, on-call.
  10. People usually dominate internal-product TCO in Bulgaria-scale salary markets.
  11. Evals and assurance.
  12. Error-analysis time: practitioners report spending 60–80% of development time on error analysis and evaluation.
  13. Human labelling: 100–200 labelled examples per failure mode to validate a judge.
  14. Judge tokens on CI and on sampled production traffic, red-team runs, re-labelling after every model change.
  15. Ops and change.
  16. Model migrations. GA models get a minimum of 18 months (12 for Anthropic, DeepSeek, Fireworks and Mistral; some Grok models 6), with ≥60 days' retirement notice. Budget at least one migration per primary model per year, including eval re-runs and prompt re-tuning (A5).
  17. Other run costs: index rebuilds, incident handling, user support, training and adoption.

Worked example (illustrative prices — verify current Azure prices before use). A Fleet Assistant policy Q&A turn on a "Sol-class" model priced at $2 / $10 per million input/output tokens:

  • 2,500 static tokens (system prompt and tool schemas, cacheable), 4,000 retrieved tokens, 500 history tokens, 500 output tokens and 800 reasoning tokens.
  • Uncached cost: 7,000 × $2/M + 1,300 × $10/M ≈ $0.027.
  • Caching the static prefix trims this further. The exact saving depends on the provider's cached-read discount: Anthropic lists cached reads at $0.20 vs $4 base input for Opus 5.5, while the Azure OpenAI discount must be verified.
  • At 3,000 such turns per working day, that is ~$80/day, roughly €19k/year.

Now compare that with one platform engineer's loaded cost, or with a DDoS Protection plan. The lesson is that for the internal rollout, tokens are rarely the dominant TCO line. For the SaaS product at 40 tenants with heavy Fleet Analyst usage, they can become one. You only know which case you are in after modelling both.

Benefits: hard vs soft.

  • Time saved is a soft benefit unless the capacity is redeployed or avoids a hire. Example: 35 mechanics × 20 min/day × 220 days × €18/h ≈ €46k/year of capacity, not cash.
  • Hard benefits for Trakia are fewer unplanned downtime days, which carry lost revenue per truck-day, lower SLA penalties, and SaaS subscription revenue.
  • An expert presents hard and soft benefits separately and never lets the soft line carry the case.

Model the uncertainty. Every input gets a range (P10/P50/P90), not a point. Run:

  • a one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis, shown as a tornado chart;
  • a Monte Carlo simulation (10k draws) to report P(NPV > 0) and payback-period percentiles.

The three assumptions at the top of the tornado chart become the pilot's learning objectives. If adoption rate drives the case, the pilot must measure adoption.

docs.title: 6. Build vs buy vs extend
docs.text:
Option What it is Choose when Trakia example Buy: M365 Copilot (and its agents) SaaS assistant over Microsoft Graph content Knowledge work inside M365, users already licensed, content in SharePoint/Teams/Outlook HR policy Q&A and email drafting for office staff Extend: Copilot Studio Low-code agents with connectors and topics, publishable to Teams/M365; A2A integrated Departmental workflows, citizen-dev maintainability, moderate integration Customer-service "where is my shipment" agent calling the C8 MCP server Build on PaaS: Foundry Agent Service (prompt agents, hosted agents, Foundry IQ) Managed agent runtime, knowledge bases, guardrails, evaluations, tracing Pro-code needs but you want the platform to own hosting, state and safety plumbing Incident triage agents; policy RAG via Foundry IQ Build custom: MAF on Container Apps / Functions Full control of orchestration, hosting, networking, multi-tenancy Multi-tenant SaaS, unusual isolation or residency constraints, deep workflow control, portability The SaaS product's tenant-aware agent runtime

Decision rules:

  1. Apply the CAF rule first: the least operational responsibility that meets the requirements.
  2. Then test the knock-out requirements:
  3. Multi-tenancy for external customers: M365 Copilot cannot serve another company's drivers. The SaaS product is a build.
  4. Data residency and processing location: see A3.
  5. Eval-ability: can you run your golden set and judges against the option? If you cannot evaluate it, you cannot govern it.
  6. Exit cost: where do prompts, knowledge and conversation state live, and can you export them?
  7. Seam availability: MCP and A2A let low-code and pro-code agents share tools and call each other, so "extend" no longer means "dead end".

Misconception to unlearn: "buying is always cheaper". Per-seat licences × 600 drivers can exceed a consumption-priced custom agent, and drivers do not live in M365. Compare cost at your actual adoption curve, and verify licence prices on the day you decide.

docs.title: 7. Pilot-to-production criteria and success metrics
docs.text:
Write the gate before the pilot starts. A Trakia pilot charter defines:

  • Scope: one depot (Plovdiv), 12 dispatchers, 10 mechanics, 8 weeks, named sponsor and product owner.
  • Learning objectives: the top three tornado assumptions.
  • Exit to production requires all of:
  • eval pass-all rate ≥ target on the hidden suite (C14), with no failure mode below its floor;
  • Bulgarian-calibrated groundedness judge ≥ 90% on sampled traffic;
  • red-team ASR ≤ agreed threshold;
  • cost per task P50 within ±25% of model;
  • p95 latency SLO met for 4 consecutive weeks;
  • weekly active use ≥ 60% of pilot users in weeks 6–8;
  • DPIA approved and AI inventory entry complete (A6);
  • security review closed (C16 threat model);
  • runbooks and rollback tested.
  • Kill criteria: for example, cost per task > 2× model after optimisation, or adoption < 30% by week 6 with no fixable cause found in interviews.

Success metrics come in three kinds:

  • Leading (adoption, task completion, deflection to human, thumbs-down rate).
  • Lagging (downtime days per truck, SLA penalties, incident handling time).
  • Guardrail (escalations, wrong-action incidents, complaints, cost per task, ASR).

A metric without a baseline is not a metric. Capture baselines in week 0.

docs.title: 8. AB-100 alignment
docs.text:
AB-100's "Plan AI-powered business solutions" area (25–30%) maps onto this module:

  • requirements and grounding-data readiness → Labs 1–2;
  • CAF adoption and an AI CoE → §1 and Lab 5;
  • ROI including TCO → Lab 3;
  • build/buy/extend and multi-agent design across M365 Copilot, Copilot Studio and Foundry → Lab 4;
  • model router → Lab 3 stretch.

Its deploy domain (ALM, governance, residency, audit trails) is covered in A4–A6.

docs.title: Lab 1 — Discovery workshop with simulated stakeholders (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Produce a defensible use-case backlog from structured interviews, not from an ideas list.
  • Start state: branch a1/start. Contains architecture/business/personas/*.md: dispatcher (Sofia), mechanic (Varna), fleet manager, HR lead, customer-service lead, CFO, works-council representative, and the commercial director pushing SaaS. Also contains baseline.xlsx and canvas-template.md.
  • Steps:
  • Spin up the stakeholder simulator: a MAF agent per persona card (instructions = persona, goals, hidden pains, data they know). The cards contain hidden facts that only good "tell me about the last time…" questions reveal. 
    // One agent per persona; instructions loaded from the card. Verify exact API against current docs.
AIAgent dispatcher = chatClient.AsAIAgent(
    name: "persona-dispatcher-sofia",
    instructions: File.ReadAllText("personas/dispatcher-sofia.md"));
AgentSession s = await dispatcher.CreateSessionAsync();
var reply = await dispatcher.RunAsync("Tell me about the last breakdown you handled.", s);
  • Run 30-minute interviews with at least 6 personas. Log every interview transcript to discovery/interviews/ (the factory will analyse them).
  • Walk the incident process (fault code → triage → workshop slot → parts → customer notice). Annotate waits, handoffs and lookups in a swimlane diagram (discovery/process-incident.md, Mermaid).
  • Fill ≥ 8 use-case canvases. At least one must be redirected to non-LLM technology, and at least one must carry an AI Act flag (driver-behaviour scoring).
  • Score all canvases with the rubric (scoring.yaml). Two team members score independently, then reconcile the scores and record the disagreements.
  • Break it: The instructor injects a "CEO pet project": "AI that predicts which drivers will quit". Score it honestly: value is unclear, it is Annex III employment, it involves profiling, and works-council exposure is high. Write the one-paragraph kill or defer memo.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • dotnet test architecture/business/tests: the canvas schema validator passes (all mandatory fields filled; the value hypothesis matches the pattern "We believe … from … to … measured by …").
  • ≥ 6 interview transcripts exist.
  • Inter-rater score difference ≤ 1 point on ≥ 80% of sub-criteria after reconciliation (computed by script).
  • The hidden-fact coverage report shows ≥ 5 of 9 hidden pains discovered.
  • Stretch: Use the factory to run axial coding over interview transcripts (as you did with traces in C14) and compare the agent's pain taxonomy with yours.

docs.title: Lab 2 — AI readiness and data-readiness spike (≈2.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Replace readiness opinions with measured evidence and find the data blockers before they find you.
  • Start state: a1/lab2-start, plus TrakiaOps and the document corpus from /data.
  • Steps:
  • Write readiness/queries.sql against TrakiaOps:
    • % of incidents with a valid VehicleId and FaultCode;
    • median lag between telematics fault event and incident record;
    • % of work orders with parts lines;
    • null rates on driver pseudonym joins.
  • Write a small .NET tool that profiles the corpus:
    • token counts per document and per collection, BG vs EN, using Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers with the encoding matching your pinned model;
    • % of documents with an owner, a review date and role ACL metadata;
    • duplicate and near-duplicate ratio (content hash plus embedding similarity > 0.95).
  • Compute per-use-case corpus size. Flag every use case whose relevant corpus is < 200k tokens as a "cached-prompt candidate, no RAG".
  • Score the six readiness dimensions. Each score cites a query result or artefact path.
  • Produce readiness/report.md with a "blockers & remediation" table: owner, effort and the date the use case unblocks.
  • Break it: The instructor swaps in a corpus snapshot where 30% of HR documents lack ACL metadata. Re-run the analysis. Your report must now block the HR use case (custom-build path) until security trimming can be guaranteed, or redirect it to M365 Copilot, which inherits SharePoint permissions.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • Profiler unit tests pass.
  • The report includes a token count per collection (±2% of the reference).
  • Every readiness score has an evidence link (checked by script).
  • At least one use case changes its score because of measured data.
  • Stretch: Estimate golden-set effort per use case (questions × minutes per label × SME rate). This number feeds the evals family in Lab 3.

docs.title: Lab 3 — ROI/TCO model as code, calibrated from traces (≈4h)
docs.text:
• Goal: A business case where every number traces to a measurement, a price source or an explicit, ranged assumption.
  • Start state: a1/lab3-start with Trakia.CostModel skeleton, assumptions.yaml (empty ranges) and prices.2026-10.yaml. The price file carries illustrative list prices from vendor and aggregator sources (e.g., GPT-6 Sol $2/$10, Luna $0.10/$0.50, Claude Opus 5.5 $4/$20, Haiku 5.5 $0.10/$0.50 per MTok, Haiku price: verify against current documentation). It is labelled verify on Azure pricing before use.
  • Steps:
  • Measure per-task tokens from your C15 telemetry. Run the KQL below for three task types (policy Q&A, Fleet Analyst query, multi-agent incident workflow). 
    dependencies
| where customDimensions["gen_ai.operation.name"] == "chat"
| extend task = tostring(customDimensions["trakia.task.type"]),
         inTok = toint(customDimensions["gen_ai.usage.input_tokens"]),
         outTok = toint(customDimensions["gen_ai.usage.output_tokens"]),
         cached = toint(customDimensions["gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens"])
| summarize calls=count(), p50In=percentile(inTok,50), p90In=percentile(inTok,90),
            p50Out=percentile(outTok,50), p90Out=percentile(outTok,90), cachedShare=avg(todouble(cached)/inTok)
  by task
    Join on operation_Id to get calls per task. Expect the incident workflow to be an order of magnitude above Q&A.
  • Infra: pull prices via the Azure Retail Prices API for the C17 bill of materials (AI Search, Cosmos DB, APIM, App Gateway WAF, Firewall, DDoS Protection, Log Analytics, Container Apps). Store the raw response with its retrieval date.
  • People, evals, ops: FTE ranges, labelling hours (Lab 2 stretch), model migrations (primary models × 1/year × engineer-days), red-team runs per release.
  • Benefits: hard (downtime days avoided × € per truck-day, SLA penalties avoided) and soft (hours) on separate lines. SaaS scenario: tenants × trucks × €/truck/month (fictional) × churn.
  • Implement MonteCarlo.Run(10_000) with triangular distributions. Output NPV P10/P50/P90, P(NPV > 0), payback percentiles and a tornado chart.
  • Generate the executive spreadsheet from the model (dotnet run -- export xlsx). The spreadsheet is a view, never edited by hand.
  • Break it: Three shocks, applied one at a time, each with its effect on P(NPV > 0) recorded:
  • (a) the provider's newer model uses 1.6× more tokens per task at the same price;
  • (b) the incident workflow gains a reflection loop, doubling calls;
  • (c) adoption reaches only 35%.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • dotnet test: unit tests validate the per-task formula against three hand-computed cases (±0.5%).
  • Every assumption has {p10,p50,p90,source}, with no empty source (schema test).
  • Infra prices carry a retrieval timestamp < 30 days old.
  • The tornado chart's top 3 assumptions are listed in business-case.md.
  • A reviewer can regenerate the spreadsheet bit-for-bit from the repo.
  • Stretch: Add the model router (Balanced / Quality / Cost modes) as a scenario. Measure the per-task cost delta on 100 replayed Q&A traces. Note that the effective context window equals the smallest model in the pool.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Build vs buy vs extend spike (≈4h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Decide, with evidence, how Trakia should deliver HR & policy Q&A for office staff, and how that differs from the driver-facing and SaaS use cases.
  • Start state: a1/lab4-start. Instructor M365 tenant with SharePoint HR library (same documents as /data/hr). Your C7 RAG and C14 golden set (HR subset, 60 questions, including 10 permission-restricted and 8 "not in corpus").
  • Steps:
  • Extend/buy: build an M365 Copilot declarative agent or a Copilot Studio agent over the SharePoint library (time-box 60 min, and log effort).
  • PaaS: create a Foundry prompt agent with a Foundry IQ knowledge base over the same documents (time-box 60 min).
  • Custom: use your existing MAF RAG agent from C7/C9.
  • Run the same 60 questions through all three. For the SaaS options, use your eval harness. For M365/Copilot Studio, capture answers via the available test or export path, or manually if needed; record how you did it, because eval-ability is itself a criterion. Score them with the C14 judges, the Bulgarian-calibrated groundedness judge, and permission-leak checks.
  • Fill the decision matrix: quality, permission correctness, BG quality, effort to build, ops responsibility (who patches, monitors, migrates models), per-user-month cost at your adoption curve, exit cost, eval-ability.
  • Write ADR-A1-001 "HR & policy Q&A delivery option" and ADR-A1-002 "SaaS product delivery option". These are different answers for different use cases.
  • Break it: Remove one HR document's permissions in SharePoint mid-test. Which options reflect the change, and how fast? Record the propagation latency for each option. This previews A3.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The eval report for all three options is committed (dotnet aieval report for the harness-driven options).
  • Zero permission leaks is a hard requirement for any option you recommend.
  • Both ADRs pass the ADR linter: context, ≥ 3 options considered (incl. "do nothing / status quo" where meaningful), decision, consequences, evidence links and a review date.
  • The matrix records real measured effort hours.
  • Stretch: Make the Copilot Studio agent call the C8 MCP server for live shipment status, and the incident agent via A2A. Document what the "extend" option becomes once protocol seams exist.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Business case, pilot charter and ARB defence (≈2.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Package everything into the artefacts an executive committee and an architecture review board (ARB) will act on.
  • Start state: Outputs of Labs 1–4.
  • Steps:
  • Write a 2-page executive memo: decision asked for, portfolio (H1/H2/H3), P50 NPV with P10–P90 range, top 3 risks, what the pilot will prove, cost of not doing it.
  • Write the pilot charter with gate criteria (Concepts §7) and kill criteria. Every metric needs a baseline and a measurement method (KQL query, survey or system report).
  • Write the success-metric tree: lagging business outcome → leading indicators → guardrails.
  • Write a half-page AI CoE/platform charter sketch: who owns the platform, the eval practice and the governance gate (expanded in A4/A7).
  • Defend the case to the ARB (instructor + 2 peers) in 15 minutes plus 10 minutes of questions. At least one ARB member plays the CFO and one plays the works council.
  • Break it: The ARB "CFO" demands a single number with no ranges. Respond without losing the uncertainty, e.g., P50 plus the probability of loss plus the assumption the pilot retires.
  • Acceptance criteria: All artefacts are in architecture/business/. The pilot charter linter passes (every gate has a threshold, a source query and an owner). The ARB rubric score is ≥ Proficient on all criteria.
  • Stretch: Draft a 1-page SaaS go-to-market assumption sheet (tenant segments, pricing hypothesis, cost to serve per tenant) that A4/A5 will validate.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text:
"Twenty-five-minute use-case triage" (repeat 4–6 times, each with a new card).

The instructor deals one use-case card (half a page: actor, pain, data, desired action). In 25 minutes you produce:

  1. Is it an LLM problem? Name the alternative technique if not.
  2. Value/feasibility/risk scores with one-line justifications.
  3. Hard regulatory flags (Art. 5 / Annex III / Art. 50 / GDPR special categories).
  4. Build/buy/extend recommendation.
  5. The single riskiest assumption and the cheapest spike that tests it.

Variations: - Customer-contract clause lookup. - Fault-code classification at 50k/day. - Driver fatigue detection from cabin camera. Check the Art. 5 workplace emotion-recognition prohibition and its safety exception (verify against current documentation; not legal advice). - Tachograph infringement explainer for drivers in Bulgarian. - Supplier invoice matching. - Customer churn prediction for the SaaS business.

Compare with the instructor's reference triage. The score is the number of dimensions within ±1 point plus a correct regulatory flag.

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text:
Fleet Ops Copilot now has a business owner's view:

  • a scored use-case portfolio (H1/H2/H3);
  • a calibrated ROI/TCO model that regenerates from code and telemetry;
  • two delivery ADRs: HR Q&A bought or extended, SaaS built;
  • a pilot charter for the Plovdiv depot with measurable gates;
  • a readiness report whose blockers (ACL metadata, incident data quality) become backlog items for the platform.

The driver-behaviour scoring idea is formally deferred to the A6 governance board, with its Annex III flag recorded.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text:
• /usecase-triage skill: reads a canvas, runs the scoring rubric, checks regulatory flags against a keyword and decision table, and writes a draft score file for human review. It never commits a final score.
  • cost-per-task CI job: nightly KQL export → Trakia.CostModel → fails the build if measured P50 cost per task drifts > 25% from the business-case assumption. A cost regression gate now sits next to your eval gates.
  • ADR linter and pilot-charter linter in CI, so architecture artefacts get the same treatment as code.
  • Interview and trace analysis agent: the C14 open/axial coding workflow reused on discovery transcripts.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Discovery quality Ideas list; no baselines Canvases with some baselines ≥ 8 canvases with baselines and falsifiable hypotheses; ≥ 5 hidden pains found Plus redirected non-LLM cases and a reasoned kill memo; interview evidence cited per canvas Scoring & prioritisation Unweighted ranking Weighted rubric Anchored rubric, inter-rater reconciliation, hard gates applied Plus sensitivity of the ranking to weights shown; portfolio balanced across horizons with explicit sequencing logic ROI/TCO model Token cost only Tokens + infra Five cost families, ranges, trace-calibrated tokens, hard vs soft benefits Plus Monte Carlo, tornado-driven pilot objectives, reproducible from code, model-migration and eval costs explicit Build/buy/extend Preference stated Matrix without evidence Measured spike across 3 options, ADRs per use case Plus exit cost, eval-ability and protocol seams (MCP/A2A) analysed; different answers per use case justified with CAF Pilot gates & communication "Pilot for 3 months" Some metrics Gates with thresholds, sources, owners, kill criteria Plus metric tree with guardrails, executive memo that survives CFO and works-council challenge

Auto-checked: - canvas schema; - inter-rater script; - readiness evidence links; - cost-model unit tests and assumption schema; - price freshness; - spreadsheet regeneration diff; - dotnet aieval reports for the spike; - permission-leak test results; - ADR and charter linters.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Counting hours saved as cash, or letting soft benefits carry the NPV.
  • Estimating tokens from one prompt, forgetting reasoning tokens, retries, judges and the multi-agent multiplier.
  • Ignoring the cost of evals, labelling and model migrations.
  • One build/buy answer for the whole programme.
  • Risk scored as an afterthought, so Annex III or Art. 5 issues surface after the pilot.
  • Pilot criteria written after the pilot, or metrics without baselines.
  • RAG for a corpus that fits in a cached prompt.
  • Prices without a source and a date.
