docs.title: A2 — Azure AI reference architectures & Well-Architected for AI
docs.text: Level: Expert — AI Solution Architect track · Duration: 20h (theory 30% / labs 70%) · Prerequisites: A1; C16 (threat model), C17 (deployed Fleet Ops Copilot with APIM, private networking, Bicep) · Volatility: High (Foundry Agent Service features, AI Landing Zones and Entra Agent ID move quarterly; WAF principles are stable)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
What separates an expert architect from a proficient one here: a proficient architect can deploy a reference architecture. An expert knows why each component is there, which guarantees it does not give, and where it has to be bent for this workload. They can show a review board the gaps between "the reference architecture" and "our production system", with evidence. For Foundry today those gaps are no built-in DR, no native load balancing, no per-user conversation authorization, and single-region standard deployments.

Trakia's C17 deployment works, but it grew one decision at a time. Customer fleets will now send security questionnaires: how is our data isolated, where are prompts processed, which identities do agents run as, what happens when a region fails? "App Service → OpenAI" answers none of that. Architects who never internalised the baseline Foundry chat architecture miss its warning that Agent Service does not enforce per-user conversation ownership (a BOLA hole in a multi-tenant product). They assume Foundry has DR, leave public data planes open "for the portal", and reach for multi-agent designs that Microsoft's own guidance says are often unnecessary.

Experts use the Well-Architected Framework (WAF) AI guidance and the reference architectures as a checklist of decisions, not a template to clone. They:

  • model AI-specific elements (models, agents, tools, knowledge, guardrails, trust boundaries) in C4;
  • land workloads in a governed landing zone;
  • pick orchestration patterns from spike evidence;
  • can restate the design in AWS or Google terms.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Assess an existing AI workload against the WAF AI workload guidance (10 design areas, pillar-mapped principles), using the Assessment Review Tool. Produce a prioritised findings register.
  2. Explain and adapt the baseline Microsoft Foundry chat reference architecture, component by component, including its documented limitations, and justify each deviation for Trakia.
  3. Deploy an AI application landing zone from Azure/AI-Landing-Zones (preview, Bicep, AVM). Validate it with policy and rule-based IaC checks.
  4. Design hub-spoke private networking for Foundry, AI Search, Cosmos DB and APIM, with private DNS and egress allow-listing, and diagnose private-endpoint and egress failures.
  5. Design the identity architecture: managed identities per component, keyless auth, Entra Agent ID for agents, persona RBAC, OBO for user-context tool calls. Close the BOLA gap in code.
  6. Select an orchestration pattern (single prompt → single agent → workflow → multi-agent) from spike evidence measured with your C14 evals, and record the decision.
  7. Model the system in C4 with an AI profile (models, agents, tools, knowledge, guardrails, trust boundaries, untrusted-content flows), validated as code.
  8. Map the design onto AWS and Google equivalents and identify the portability seams.

docs.title: 1. Well-Architected Framework for AI workloads
docs.text:
WAF's AI workload guidance (updated May 2026; verify against current documentation) organises the problem into 10 design areas:

  1. application design;
  2. application platform;
  3. training data design;
  4. grounding data design;
  5. data platform;
  6. MLOps/GenAIOps;
  7. workload operations;
  8. testing and evaluation;
  9. workload personas;
  10. responsible AI.

Design principles are mapped to the five pillars (reliability, security, cost optimisation, operational excellence, performance efficiency). An Assessment Review Tool turns this into a production-readiness questionnaire. In this track the tool is your review instrument. Every architecture package you submit from now on includes a WAF AI assessment with findings, severity and an owner.

What is different about AI workloads under WAF:

  • Nondeterminism means testing becomes evaluation. Regression suites, statistical pass rates and LLM judges validated against humans (C14) replace exact-match tests.
  • Data is part of the runtime. Grounding data has freshness, permission and residency properties that act as availability and security properties.
  • Dependencies have expiry dates. Model lifecycle policies force planned change (A5).
  • Cost has a new variable axis. Tokens scale with behaviour, not just traffic. Prompts, tool loops, reasoning effort and agent count all move the bill.
  • "Workload personas" is its own design area. Who is the user, who is the operator, who is the data owner, and which actions can each take?

docs.title: 2. The baseline Microsoft Foundry chat reference architecture
docs.text:
This is the most important reference for the track (Architecture Center, updated Aug 2026, verify against current documentation; implementation Azure-Samples/microsoft-foundry-baseline; a landing-zone variant baseline-microsoft-foundry-landing-zone exists). Learn it component by component.

Topology.

  • Agent runtime:
  • A Foundry Agent Service prompt agent in standard setup with BYO VNet.
  • Standard setup means agent state lives in customer-owned Cosmos DB (conversations and agent definitions; enterprise_memory), Storage and AI Search, all dedicated to Agent Service.
  • Front end:
  • A zone-redundant App Service hosts the chat UI.
  • Ingress and egress:
  • Application Gateway with WAF is the only ingress. WAF exclusions are needed for the chat body, otherwise prompts trip OWASP rules.
  • Azure Firewall handles egress with FQDN allow-lists. Agent traffic leaves via a delegated agent subnet and a UDR.
  • Private access:
  • Private endpoints everywhere, with public data planes blocked.
  • Portal access goes through Bastion + jump box.

Identity. - Separate system-assigned managed identities per component. - Entra ID connections. - RBAC mapped to personas. - Project-level connections only. - One Foundry resource per production workload.

Security warning to memorise. Agent Service does not enforce per-user conversation authorization. If your API accepts a conversation or thread ID from the client and passes it to the agent, any authenticated user who obtains another user's ID can read or continue that conversation. This is classic Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA). The application must store ownership (user, tenant → conversation ID) and check it on every call. In SaaS, the check is user and tenant.

Reliability, as documented. - Standard model deployments are single-region. Use Data Zone provisioned with spillover, or Global deployments. - Foundry has no native load balancing or circuit breaking, so APIM is the suggested option. - Agent Service has no built-in DR. Recovery is by reconstruction: agents-as-code, backups and delete locks. - Multi-region is out of scope of the baseline. You design it in A5.

Cost, as documented. - The largest costs are Cosmos DB, AI Search and DDoS Protection. - Agents may call tools unnecessarily, so limit tools. - Use the cheapest model that meets requirements. - Use PAYG for variable load and PTU for a stable baseline.

Operations. - Agents as code via CI/CD. - Immutable agent versions. - Regression suites, because behaviour is nondeterministic. - MAF (C#/Python) for runtime. - Azure Policy to disable local auth and require private endpoints.

The expert move is the gap analysis. For Trakia the gaps are:

  1. SaaS needs tenant isolation, which the baseline does not cover.
  2. The C12 workflow needs a code-first runtime, so you deviate to a hosted agent or self-hosted MAF.
  3. Bulgarian users need a Bulgarian-calibrated groundedness judge, because Content Safety groundedness detection is English-only.
  4. EU residency needs Data Zone EU deployments.
  5. Customer-facing availability needs multi-region (A5).
  6. APIM moves from "optional" to mandatory as the AI gateway (A4).

docs.title: 3. AI Landing Zones
docs.text:
The CAF "AI ready" phase places AI workloads into an Azure landing zone. Azure/AI-Landing-Zones (GitHub, preview, MIT) is an application landing zone for AI apps and agents in two parts:

  • the AI Foundry Landing Zone;
  • the AI Gateway Landing Zone (APIM).

Both are implemented in Bicep and Terraform on Azure Verified Modules (AVM), with a legacy Bicep branch.

Keep the platform/application split clear: - The platform landing zone (connectivity hub, identity, management, policy, owned by the platform team) provides hub networking, DNS, firewall and central logging. - The application landing zone (owned by the workload team, under platform guardrails) holds Foundry, Search, Cosmos, APIM instances and app compute.

For Trakia's SaaS, decide whether APIM is a shared AI gateway (platform-owned, many workloads) or a workload gateway (tenant-aware, product-owned). Most products end up with both: a central gateway for model access and quota, and a product gateway for tenant APIs. Record the choice in an ADR.

Preview means: - pin a commit SHA; - read the changelog before upgrading; - expect breaking changes; - keep your own deviations as overlays, never as edits to the upstream module.

docs.title: 4. Networking decisions
docs.text:
• Hub-spoke. The hub holds Firewall, Bastion and the DNS resolver. Spokes hold the AI app landing zones. Private DNS zones for each private-link service are linked to the hub. Verify the exact zone names for Foundry/AI Services, AI Search, Cosmos DB, Storage and Key Vault against current docs, because Foundry endpoints use several hostnames.
  • Public network access disabled on Foundry, Search, Cosmos, Storage and Key Vault, enforced by Azure Policy (A6).
  • Egress allow-listing. List the FQDNs your agents and tools must reach (supplier API, telematics provider, Microsoft endpoints). Hosted agents' network egress controls are preview. For self-hosted agents in Container Apps, egress goes through the Firewall via UDR.
  • Service-to-search traffic. AI Search indexers reaching private data sources need shared private links. Budget for them and test them, because they are a classic silent failure.
  • Developer access. A jump box or Bastion, or a dev environment in a peered VNet. "Temporarily enabling public access" is how data planes stay open forever.

docs.title: 5. Identity architecture
docs.text:
• Workloads use managed identities, keyless auth to Foundry, Search, Cosmos and Storage, and local auth disabled. Each component gets its own identity so that blast radius and audit trails stay separable.
  • Agents as principals. Microsoft Entra Agent ID is GA.
  • Agents get their own identities, created from agent identity blueprints (design guidance is available; the blueprint and identity creation wizard is preview).
  • Conditional Access templates for agents can block high-risk agent identities, autonomous agent access and on-behalf-of agent access.
  • Sponsor lifecycle governance gives each agent an accountable human.
  • Registry convergence under Microsoft Agent 365.
  • Federation patterns for AWS and GCP, and integrations with Bedrock and n8n.
  • Per-feature GA/preview status is ambiguous on the what's-new page, so verify against current documentation.
  • User context.
  • Tools that act as the user, such as reading the user's calendar or SharePoint, use OBO.
  • Tools that act as the system, such as creating a work order, use the agent identity with least privilege. The approval is recorded under the user.
  • Never let the model choose which identity to use.
  • Personas → RBAC. Map Trakia roles (dispatcher, mechanic, fleet manager, HR, auditor; in SaaS also tenant admin and Trakia operator) to data-plane roles and app roles. Auditors get read access to traces and evidence, not to agent configuration.

docs.title: 6. Orchestration pattern selection
docs.text:
The Architecture Center's ladder:

  1. Direct model call.
  2. Single agent with tools. Often the right enterprise default, with iteration limits.
  3. Multi-agent. Only for cross-domain problems, security boundaries or parallel specialisation.

The patterns are sequential, concurrent, group chat (≤ 3 agents), handoff and Magentic. The listed pitfalls are over-engineering and adding agents without real specialisation.

The evidence is nuanced:

  • For multi-agent: Anthropic's lead-plus-subagents research system beat a single agent by 90.2% on its internal eval, at ~15× chat tokens. The task was read-heavy and parallel.
  • Against: Cognition shows that parallel agents with partial context make conflicting decisions on write-heavy, coupled tasks.

Decision rule: - Use a deterministic workflow when the process is known (Trakia's incident flow mostly is). - Use a single agent for open-ended assistance. - Use multi-agent when there is a real boundary. Example: the Fleet Analyst holds SQL read access that the customer-notification agent must never have.

A security boundary is often the best reason for a second agent, and "it's more modular" is the worst.

docs.title: 7. C4 modelling for AI systems: the course profile
docs.text:
No authoritative standard exists for C4 extensions for AI, so this is a course-designer convention. Use it consistently and say so in reviews. Model with Structurizr DSL (diagrams as code) and use these element tags with mandatory properties:

Tag Mandatory properties Model Deployment model role, provider, version, deployment type (Global / Data Zone / Regional Standard, PTU, Batch), region(s), auto-upgrade policy, retirement date Agent kind (prompt / hosted / self-hosted MAF / Copilot Studio), identity (Agent ID), autonomy level (inform / recommend / act-with-approval / act), tools, max iterations and token budget, HITL points, owner/sponsor Tool / MCP Server side effect (read / write / irreversible), auth mode (MI / OBO), data classification, first- or third-party, pinned version/hash Knowledge Base sources, ACL mode (query-time filter / native propagation), freshness SLA, residency Guardrail intervention points (input / tool call / tool response / output), risks covered, action Trust boundary a group around elements sharing an identity and network boundary

Also tag relationships that carry untrusted content (web pages, customer emails, uploaded documents, third-party tool output).

A validation script checks the lethal trifecta per agent. If an agent has (private data) + (an untrusted-content inbound relationship) + (an external-communication tool), the build fails unless the agent element references a mitigation ADR.

Add a dynamic diagram for the incident workflow trajectory and a deployment diagram per environment.

docs.title: 8. Cloud-agnostic thinking: AWS and Google equivalents
docs.text:
An expert can explain the design without product names: a managed agent runtime, a retrieval service, a gateway, workload identity for agents, and policy enforcement. The mapping below is indicative and must be verified before teaching. Only the A2A integration of Bedrock AgentCore and Google ADK's native A2A support were verified in the research for this course.

Capability Azure AWS (verify) Google Cloud (verify) Model catalogue / serving Microsoft Foundry models (multi-vendor; Gemini not sold on Azure) Amazon Bedrock Vertex AI (Gemini) Managed agent runtime Foundry Agent Service (prompt and hosted agents) Bedrock AgentCore (A2A integrated — verified) Vertex AI Agent Engine (verify name) Agent framework MAF (connectors for Bedrock and Gemini too) Strands / Bedrock Agents (verify) ADK (native A2A — verified) Retrieval AI Search / Foundry IQ Bedrock Knowledge Bases / OpenSearch (verify) Vertex AI Search (verify) AI gateway APIM AI gateway API Gateway + custom (no direct equivalent verified) Apigee (verify AI features) Agent identity Entra Agent ID (federates to AWS/GCP) IAM roles / AgentCore identity (verify) Service accounts / workload identity Well-architected guidance WAF AI workload Well-Architected Generative AI Lens (unverified) Architecture Center GenAI guidance (unverified)

Portability seams are what keep exit cost low: - IChatClient and MEAI for model access; - MCP for tools; - A2A for agents; - OTel GenAI semantic conventions for telemetry; - agents-as-code (declarative YAML / MAF code) in Git; - evals in your own harness.

docs.title: Lab 1 — WAF AI assessment of your C17 deployment (≈3.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Produce an evidence-backed findings register for the current Fleet Ops Copilot.
  • Start state: branch a2/start (your G3 baseline deployed in your sandbox subscription) and architecture/waf/ templates.
  • Steps:
  • Run the WAF AI Assessment Review Tool for the workload and export the results.
  • For each of the 10 design areas, attach evidence. The evidence types are: a Bicep path, an Azure Resource Graph query result, a KQL query, an eval report, or a screenshot only as a last resort. Example Resource Graph query: 
    resources
| where type in~ ('microsoft.cognitiveservices/accounts','microsoft.search/searchservices','microsoft.documentdb/databaseaccounts')
| project name, type, publicNetworkAccess = tostring(properties.publicNetworkAccess),
          disableLocalAuth = tostring(properties.disableLocalAuth)
  • Diff your deployment against microsoft-foundry-baseline: ingress, egress, private endpoints, identities, standard setup, agents-as-code. List each difference as intentional (with an ADR) or a gap (with a finding).
  • Build the findings register (waf/findings.csv): ID, design area, pillar, severity (Critical / High / Med / Low), evidence, owner, remediation, target date.
  • Pick the top 5 findings and estimate remediation in t-shirt sizes with the uncertainty stated (A7 revisits estimation).
  • Break it: The instructor flips one Cosmos DB account to publicNetworkAccess: Enabled and adds a key-based connection in a Foundry project. Your Resource Graph checks must detect both, and the register must classify them as Critical.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • All 10 design areas have ≥ 1 evidence item.
  • The register passes the schema check.
  • The injected misconfigurations are detected by your queries (CI job waf-drift runs them).
  • Every "intentional deviation" links to an ADR.
  • Stretch: Turn your Resource Graph queries into PSRule custom rules and run them in CI on the Bicep before deployment, as a shift-left complement to post-deployment detection.

docs.title: Lab 2 — C4 with the AI profile, validated as code (≈3.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: A C4 model that a security reviewer, a customer's architect and a coding agent can all read, and that fails the build when the design is unsafe.
  • Start state: a2/lab2-start with architecture/c4/workspace.dsl skeleton, tag definitions and validate-ai-profile (.NET console).
  • Steps:
  • Model the System Context: Fleet Ops Copilot, the Trakia user personas, customer fleets (SaaS), the telematics provider, the parts supplier, M365/Teams and model providers through Foundry.
  • Model the Containers: web/Teams front ends, the agent API, the Fleet Assistant, Fleet Analyst and incident workflow agents, the MCP servers (tickets, scheduling, parts), the knowledge bases, model deployments, APIM, Cosmos DB, SQL TrakiaOps, and App Insights. Apply the AI profile tags with all mandatory properties.
  • Draw the trust boundaries: Trakia internal, the per-tenant boundary for SaaS, third-party tools, and model providers.
  • Mark untrusted-content relationships: customer emails into the incident workflow, supplier API responses, uploaded delivery notes.
  • Add a dynamic view of the incident workflow, from fault event through triage, diagnostics, policy check, booking with approval and customer notification. Add deployment views for dev and prod.
  • Run validate-ai-profile. It checks the mandatory properties, finds trifecta agents, flags Model Deployment elements whose retirement date falls within 6 months, and flags tools with irreversible side effects that lack a HITL point.
  • Break it: Add a "customer email auto-reply" tool to the Fleet Assistant (which already reads private incident data and ingests customer emails). The validator must fail with a trifecta violation. Fix it with one of two options, each with an ADR: (a) move email drafting to a separate agent with no private-data tools, or (b) require human approval before send.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • structurizr validate passes and validate-ai-profile exits 0.
  • The rendered diagrams are committed.
  • The trifecta break is detected and fixed with an ADR.
  • Every agent element names an Entra Agent ID or managed identity.
  • Stretch: Make the C4 DSL agent-readable context. Add it to AGENTS.md and have your coding agent answer "which agents can write to TrakiaOps?" from the model alone. Check the answer against the code.

docs.title: Lab 3 — Deploy an AI application landing zone and break its network (≈5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Land Fleet Ops Copilot in a governed landing zone and learn the failure signatures of private networking.
  • Start state: a2/lab3-start contains:
  • a fork reference to Azure/AI-Landing-Zones pinned at a course-tested SHA;
  • a platform-hub stub (Firewall, Bastion, DNS resolver, Log Analytics);
  • parameter files for trakia-prod-weu (or a course-assigned EU region).
  • Steps:
  • Deploy the hub stub, then the AI Foundry Landing Zone and the AI Gateway Landing Zone with your parameters (EU region, private endpoints on, public access off, standard agent setup, BYO VNet).
  • Add your overlays as separate Bicep modules, not upstream edits:
    • per-component managed identities;
    • project-level connections only;
    • diagnostic settings to central Log Analytics;
    • delete locks on Cosmos DB and the Foundry resource.
  • Wire the private DNS zones to the hub resolver. Verify name resolution from the agent subnet and the jump box: nslookup <search>.search.windows.net must return a private IP. Verify Foundry hostnames against the docs.
  • Configure the Firewall application rules: allow-list the supplier API, the telematics provider and the required Microsoft FQDNs (document each with its reason).
  • Assign the policy initiative: deny public network access, require private endpoints, disable local auth (definitions in policy/; A6 extends them).
  • Redeploy Fleet Ops Copilot into the landing zone via azd and run the C14 smoke eval suite through App Gateway.
  • Break it: Run these three induced faults one at a time and record symptom → diagnosis → fix in runbooks/network-faults.md:
  • (a) delete the DNS zone link for AI Search. The agent's retrieval fails with timeouts or name-resolution errors. Find it via the dependency failures in App Insights.
  • (b) remove the supplier FQDN from the Firewall. The parts tool fails with a 403/connection error. Find it in the Firewall logs.
  • (c) attempt to deploy a Storage account with public access. Azure Policy must deny it, and you capture the deny event.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • PSRule for Azure passes on the overlays with no Critical findings.
  • The policy compliance scan shows 100% compliance on the AI resources.
  • The smoke eval suite passes through the private path.
  • All three faults are diagnosed in the runbook with the KQL used.
  • az resource list shows no AI resource with public access enabled.
  • Stretch: Run Terraform from the same repo as a parallel deployment in a second resource group. Write a half-page "Bicep vs Terraform for Trakia" ADR that weighs team skills, AVM parity and state management.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Identity and the BOLA hole (≈3.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Prove the per-user conversation authorization gap exists, close it, and move agents to first-class identities.
  • Start state: a2/lab4-start. The agent API accepts conversationId from the client (the deliberately naive C9 shape).
  • Steps:
  • Exploit. As user mechanic-varna-02, obtain conversationId values: they are logged in a debug header and are guessable from a sequential test fixture. Call the API with another user's ID and read that conversation. Write the exploit as an xUnit security test that currently passes.
  • Fix. Add a conversation ownership store (Cosmos container conversationOwnership, partition key /tenantId, keyed by conversation ID → {tenantId, userObjectId, createdAt}). Enforce it in middleware before any agent call. Return 404, not 403, to avoid leaking existence. Use non-guessable IDs. 
    app.Use(async (ctx, next) =>
{
    if (ctx.Request.RouteValues.TryGetValue("conversationId", out var id))
    {
        var principal = ctx.User; // Entra token: oid + tid (+ app role)
        var owner = await ownership.GetAsync(principal.TenantId(), (string)id!);
        if (owner is null || owner.UserObjectId != principal.ObjectId())
        { ctx.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes.Status404NotFound; return; }
    }
    await next();
});
  • Flip the exploit test to assert 404. Add a cross-tenant variant using the SaaS tenant claim.
  • Agent identity. Register the Fleet Assistant and the incident workflow agents with Entra Agent ID (blueprint wizard in preview; scripted path if available, otherwise portal; verify). Grant least-privilege roles (ticket MCP: write; TrakiaOps: none for the assistant). Apply a Conditional Access template that blocks high-risk agent identities.
  • OBO path. The "my upcoming shifts" tool calls the scheduling API on behalf of the user. Verify in the logs that the downstream call carries the user's identity and the agent's identity, and that a disabled user cannot be impersonated.
  • Break it: Grant the Fleet Assistant identity Contributor on the resource group "to fix a permission error". Your access review query must flag it. Write the finding and revert.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The BOLA tests (same-tenant and cross-tenant) pass in CI.
  • No agent identity holds roles beyond the least-privilege matrix (identity/matrix.yaml, checked by a script that reads role assignments).
  • Sign-in and audit logs show the agent identity for agent actions.
  • The OBO evidence is captured.
  • Stretch: Register each MCP server as a protected resource with distinct scopes. Show that the incident agent's token cannot call the HR knowledge MCP server.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Orchestration pattern spike and portability map (≈4.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Choose the incident workflow's orchestration pattern from measured evidence, and show the design survives a cloud change on paper.
  • Start state: a2/lab5-start with your C12 multi-agent workflow, the C14 trajectory and outcome eval suite (60 incident scenarios, incl. 10 adversarial customer emails) and the τ-bench-style end-state checks.
  • Steps:
  • Implement three variants behind one interface:
    • (A) a single agent with all tools and an iteration cap of 12;
    • (B) a deterministic sequential workflow (MAF WorkflowBuilder) with an LLM step only at triage and drafting;
    • (C) a handoff multi-agent design (triage → diagnostics → policy → scheduling → notification) with per-agent tool scopes.
  • Run the suite 4× per variant (pass^4 for reliability). Collect task success, the trajectory evaluators (tool-call accuracy), tokens and cost per task (A1 model), p95 latency, the injection ASR on the adversarial emails, and the number of identities holding write tools.
  • Fill the decision matrix and write ADR-A2-003 "Incident orchestration pattern". Expected insight (do not assume it, measure it): (B) usually wins on cost, latency and reliability for a known process, while (C) or a B/C hybrid may be justified only by the security boundary around customer-email handling.
  • Portability map: annotate your C4 containers with the AWS and Google equivalents (Concepts §8 table, verified where you can). List every non-portable dependency with an exit cost estimate.
  • Break it: Add a fourth "group chat with 5 agents" variant because "the business liked the demo". Measure it. Then write the two-sentence answer to the sponsor explaining why it doesn't ship. Microsoft's guidance keeps group chat at ≤ 3 agents.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • Eval reports for all variants are committed.
  • The ADR cites the measured pass^4, cost and ASR.
  • The chosen variant meets the G3 thresholds.
  • The portability map lists ≥ 6 dependencies, each with seam/no-seam status.
  • Stretch: Re-implement variant B's triage step as a Copilot Studio agent that calls the rest via A2A. Measure the added latency and the governance implications.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text:
"Reference architecture gap hunt" (30 min, repeat with variations).

You get a one-page architecture description and diagram. Within 30 minutes, list the top 7 gaps against the baseline Foundry chat RA and the WAF AI design areas. For each gap, name the risk, the evidence that would confirm it, and the fix.

Variations: - a public-endpoint RAG app with API keys; - a multi-tenant agent passing threadId from the browser; - a hosted agent with unrestricted egress and a web-browse tool; - a "multi-region" design whose second region has no model quota; - a design on Global Standard deployments for EU personal data; - a 6-agent group chat for invoice approval.

The score is the share of reference gaps found, plus a bonus for gaps the reference missed and you justified.

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text:
Fleet Ops Copilot now runs in an AI application landing zone that has:

  • private networking;
  • Firewall egress allow-listing;
  • policy-enforced private endpoints and keyless auth;
  • per-component managed identities;
  • agents registered with Entra Agent ID;
  • the BOLA gap closed for users and tenants.

It is described by a validated C4 model with the AI profile, assessed with a WAF AI findings register, and the incident workflow's orchestration pattern is chosen by ADR from measured evidence.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text:
• Architecture-as-code gates in CI:
  • structurizr validate;
  • validate-ai-profile (trifecta, HITL on irreversible tools, model retirement horizon);
  • PSRule on Bicep;
  • waf-drift Resource Graph checks after deploy.
  • An "architecture reviewer" custom agent (.github/agents/arch-reviewer.agent.md or a Claude Code subagent). It reads PR diffs plus the C4 DSL and flags drift: a new outbound dependency missing from the model, a tool added without a side-effect tag, a public endpoint. It comments only; humans decide.
  • Security regression tests (BOLA) in the default test suite.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert WAF AI assessment Questionnaire answered without evidence Evidence for some areas All 10 areas evidenced; prioritised register; deviations vs baseline classified Plus automated drift detection, and findings tied to business impact and A1 costs Reference architecture fluency Copies the baseline Explains components Explains limits (no DR, no native LB, BOLA, single-region standard) and adapts them with ADRs Plus anticipates SaaS-specific gaps and designs mitigations before they are asked for Network & identity design Public endpoints / keys Private endpoints, some MI Landing zone, policy-enforced, per-component MI, Agent ID, OBO, BOLA fixed and tested Plus fault diagnosis runbook, least-privilege matrix enforced by script, cross-tenant tests Orchestration choice Picks multi-agent by default Justifies by intuition Measured spike (pass^k, cost, ASR, latency) and ADR Plus security-boundary reasoning, hybrid designs, explicit "when to revisit" triggers Architecture communication (C4 + portability) Boxes and arrows C4 levels correct AI profile complete; validated as code; dynamic view Plus portability seams and exit costs quantified; the model is used by agents and reviewers

Auto-checked: - Structurizr and AI-profile validation; - PSRule; - policy compliance; - waf-drift queries; - BOLA tests; - identity matrix script; - eval reports and thresholds for the spike; - ADR linter.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Treating the baseline as complete: no built-in DR, no native load balancing, multi-region out of scope.
  • Passing client-supplied conversation IDs to Agent Service (BOLA), or forgetting the tenant dimension of the check.
  • Public access left on "for the portal".
  • Private endpoints without DNS: everything deploys, nothing resolves.
  • Editing upstream landing-zone modules instead of overlaying, or upgrading a preview repo without pinning.
  • One shared identity for all agents.
  • Multi-agent for modularity's sake; group chats with more than 3 agents.
  • C4 diagrams without models, tools and untrusted-content flows, which is exactly where the AI risks live.
  • Unverified AWS/Google equivalence claims.

docs.title: A3 — Enterprise knowledge & data architecture for AI
docs.text: Level: Expert — AI Solution Architect track · Duration: 16h (theory 30% / labs 70%) · Prerequisites: A2; C6, C7, C10, C13 (vector search, permission-aware RAG, text-to-SQL, Foundry IQ/GraphRAG) · Volatility: High (AI Search agentic retrieval, knowledge sources, permission propagation and Purview integration are moving GA/preview lines)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
What separates an expert architect from a proficient one here: a proficient architect can build a good RAG pipeline for one application. An expert designs a knowledge platform: many sources, many consumers (agents, apps, tenants), one set of guarantees about permissions, freshness, residency and isolation. They know precisely which guarantees are GA, which are preview, and which the application must enforce itself.

In C7 you built permission-aware RAG for Trakia's ~1,500 documents. Enterprise rollout and SaaS change the problem in kind, not just in size:

  • Sources multiply. SharePoint HR libraries, workshop manuals in blob storage, incident history in SQL, telematics at ~5M rows, and per-customer contracts.
  • Consumers multiply. The Fleet Assistant, the Fleet Analyst, the incident workflow, Copilot Studio agents and customer fleets' own agents via A2A.
  • Tenants appear. A SaaS fleet's documents and telematics must never reach another fleet's answers, embeddings, caches, memories or eval datasets.

Most production RAG failures are data and retrieval failures, not model failures: stale versions, missing ACL filters, tables destroyed by naive parsing, distractors. In a multi-tenant platform each of these becomes a potential data breach.

Experts make the store choice an ADR backed by a bake-off. They treat ingestion as a product with SLAs. They default to the portable, GA permission pattern (query-time trimming on a filterable groups field) and adopt native ACL propagation only where it is available and tested. They design tenant isolation with tests that try to break it. They keep structured data behind governed tools rather than "RAG over rows". And they decide on GraphRAG with a cost model, not on hype.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Design a layered knowledge platform (sources → ingestion → enrichment → stores → retrieval APIs/knowledge bases → consumers) with explicit freshness, permission, residency and isolation guarantees per layer.
  2. Distinguish GA from preview in Foundry IQ and Azure AI Search agentic retrieval. Design production paths on GA features, with preview features behind flags.
  3. Choose and justify a vector store (AI Search vs Azure SQL / SQL Server 2025 vs Cosmos DB vs PostgreSQL) using a bake-off with recall, latency and cost at three scale points.
  4. Build an ingestion pipeline at scale with layout-aware parsing, contextual chunks, dedup, incremental updates and blue/green re-indexing via index aliases.
  5. Implement and test permission enforcement: query-time trimming (GA pattern) vs native ACL propagation (preview), including group-overage handling and Purview labels.
  6. Design EU data residency for every place data lands: model processing, indexes, caches, traces, memory and eval datasets.
  7. Decide when GraphRAG or LazyGraphRAG is warranted, and govern structured-data access (semantic layer, read-only text-to-SQL, RLS, query budgets).
  8. Design and verify multi-tenant data isolation with automated cross-tenant leak tests.

docs.title: 1. The knowledge platform as layers with guarantees
docs.text:
Layer Trakia components Guarantees to specify Sources SharePoint (HR, policies), Blob (manuals, scanned notes), SQL TrakiaOps, tenant uploads, web (regulation summaries) Owner, classification, residency, change feed Ingestion & enrichment Indexers / custom .NET pipeline (MEDI), Content Understanding / Document Layout skills, contextualisation, embeddings Freshness SLA (e.g., policy change visible ≤ 4h), parse quality, cost per 1k pages Stores AI Search indexes, SQL VECTOR, Cosmos DB Isolation model, ACL fields, encryption, backup / rebuild time Retrieval AI Search knowledge bases (agentic retrieval), Foundry IQ, MAF TextSearchProvider, SQL tools Permission enforcement point, latency p95, budgets Consumers Agents, Copilot Studio, A2A partners Which consumer may query which knowledge, under which identity

The platform owner publishes the guarantees, and each consumer's ADR states which guarantees it relies on. This is how the knowledge platform becomes a product (A4 operating model) instead of five teams each building their own RAG.

docs.title: 2. Foundry IQ and AI Search agentic retrieval: what is GA
docs.text:
• Foundry IQ knowledge bases are GA. Foundry IQ Serverless is preview. Foundry IQ is built on AI Search agentic retrieval and is described as turning enterprise content into reusable, permission-aware knowledge bases.
  • Agentic retrieval (knowledge bases orchestrating knowledge sources) is GA with API 2026-04-01 for extractive retrieval:
  • GA knowledge sources: search index, blob, OneLake, web (web needs a model reference).
  • Query planning, answer synthesis and reasoning effort remained preview at GA. The 2026-08-01-preview API adds retrievalReasoningEffort: "auto" (escalates to LLM planning only when needed), stored runtime and output budgets, per-source resultsProcessing: "none", neverQuerySource, SSE streaming and query hints.
  • Preview knowledge sources: File, Azure SQL, Fabric Data Agent/Ontology, MCP Server, Work IQ, and remote or indexed SharePoint.
  • Billing. From 2026-04-01, semantic ranker and agentic retrieval require separate billing consent (knowledgeRetrieval=standard). Model this in A1's cost model.
  • Index features that matter architecturally:
  • scalar (int8, ~4×) and binary (up to ~28×) quantization with rescoring;
  • Matryoshka truncation;
  • max 4,096 dimensions;
  • index aliases GA (Apr 2026), which enable blue/green re-indexing;
  • multivector fields (preview).
  • AI Search tiers. Tier choice determines partitions/replicas, storage, the maximum number of indexes per service and SLA eligibility. Tier limits are decisive for "index per tenant" designs. Verify current tier limits and prices before teaching; they are not reproduced here.

Design rule: build production retrieval on the GA extractive path. Put planning and synthesis behind a feature flag and admit them only when your C14 retrieval evals (recall@k, nDCG, the Foundry Document Retrieval evaluator's Fidelity/holes) show a gain that is worth the latency and cost.

docs.title: 3. Vector store selection
docs.text:
Criterion Azure AI Search Azure SQL DB / SQL Server 2025 Cosmos DB for NoSQL Azure Database for PostgreSQL (pgvector) Status GA (vector, hybrid, semantic ranker, KBs) VECTOR type GA everywhere; DiskANN index GA in Azure SQL DB / MI / Fabric, preview in SQL Server 2025 Vector + BM25 + hybrid RRF GA (May 2025) Not verified in course research — verify Retrieval sophistication Highest: hybrid, semantic rerank, agentic retrieval, skills, connectors Exact kNN (VECTOR_DISTANCE) recommended < ~50k vectors after predicates; ANN via SELECT TOP (N) WITH APPROXIMATE; hybrid = full-text + vector composed manually (verify) Hybrid RRF native Rich ecosystem; hybrid via tsvector/extensions Source of truth Copy (sync pipeline) Vectors next to rows; transactional; RLS reuse Next to documents/state Next to rows Permissions Filter fields (GA); native ACL propagation (preview) RLS (mature) Partition / filter RLS Cost model Fixed SU tiers Rides on existing DB capacity RU/s vCore Portability Azure-specific API (MEVD connector) T-SQL, MEVD MEVD Highest

Decision heuristics for Trakia:

  • Policy, manual and contract corpus (unstructured, multi-source, BG/EN, semantic rerank needed, SharePoint ACLs) → AI Search / Foundry IQ.
  • Incident history narratives that already live in TrakiaOps and must respect the same row-level security as the Fleet Analyst → SQL vectors next to the rows. No sync pipeline, one permission model.
  • Agent memory and conversation-adjacent semantic lookups → Cosmos DB, which already holds standard-setup state.
  • Use Microsoft.Extensions.VectorData (MEVD) so the bake-off runs the same code against each store. The connectors now ship under the CommunityToolkit.VectorData.* package names (verify per store).

Misconception to unlearn: "one vector database for everything". Multiple stores are fine if each has a clear reason, a single owner and evals. What you must not have is the same content in two stores with different permission models.

docs.title: 4. Ingestion pipelines at scale
docs.text:
• Parsing.
  • The Document Layout skill is GA (Sep 2025).
  • The Content Understanding skill is GA (Apr 2026): Markdown output, cross-page tables, image descriptions, semantic chunking. Content Understanding SDKs are GA including .NET.
  • The GenAI Prompt skill for image verbalisation is GA (Apr 2026).
  • For Trakia's maintenance manuals (tables, diagrams) and scanned delivery notes, naive text extraction is the leading root cause of wrong answers. Measure it in C7/C13 terms before scaling.
  • Contextual chunks. Prepending 50–100 tokens of LLM-written document context per chunk cut top-20 retrieval failures by 35% (embeddings), 49% (+ contextual BM25) and 67% (+ reranker) in Anthropic's study, at ~$1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching. Run it as a Batch job: Batch is ~50% cheaper, but verify the current Azure Batch discount and turnaround.
  • Dedup. No managed Azure feature was found. Use content hashing plus near-duplicate detection (MinHash or embedding similarity) in pipeline code. Duplicates and stale versions are the "distractors" that Chroma shows degrade answers.
  • Freshness. Use change feeds and incremental indexing. Freshness-aware retrieval and per-run incremental SharePoint ACL sync are preview. State a freshness SLO per source and monitor indexer lag.
  • Embedding model changes require full re-embedding. With index aliases (GA), you build manuals-v2 in parallel, run the retrieval eval suite against it, then switch the alias. One practitioner estimate puts re-embedding and re-indexing at ~20% of monthly inference spend (unverified). Calculate yours.
  • Scale arithmetic. Use it to sanity-check the design. For SaaS year 3, assume 40 tenants × ~3,000 documents × ~25 chunks ≈ 3M chunks, at 1,536 dimensions × 4 bytes ≈ 18 GB of raw vectors before quantization. Binary quantization brings that toward ~0.7 GB plus the full-precision copy if you keep originals for rescoring. This arithmetic decides tiers and whether discardOriginals is acceptable.

docs.title: 5. Permissions: query-time trimming vs native propagation
docs.text:
GA, portable pattern: query-time trimming. - Store a filterable allowed_groups (and tenant_id) collection on every chunk at ingestion. - At query time, the API derives the groups from the caller's Entra token and applies search.in filters. - Enforcement happens in your code path, which needs tests on every path (agents, tools, Copilot Studio via MCP, A2A).

Native propagation (preview). - ADLS Gen2 permissions with identity-based query filtering, the SharePoint indexer with ACLs (extended Jun 2026 to pages, lists, site groups and incremental sync), and blob/OneLake ingestionPermissionOptions. All are preview. - Elevated read for admin ACL debugging is preview. - Work IQ uses OBO with a customer-owned Entra app. - Benefit: no duplicated ACL logic. - Costs: preview SLAs, sync lag, and the need to verify behaviour per source.

Sharp edges you must design for:

  • Group overage. When a user belongs to many groups, the token may not carry them all (Entra overage behaviour; verify the current thresholds). Your trimming code must resolve groups through Graph and cache them with a TTL.
  • Revocation latency. A permission removed in SharePoint becomes effective in your index only after the next sync. You measured this in A1 Lab 4. State it as a guarantee ("≤ 1h") or design around it, e.g., re-check at citation time for sensitive collections.
  • Purview sensitivity labels. Label indexing is preview, and labels are returned in knowledge-base retrieve responses (sensitivityLabelInfo, preview). Use labels to exclude "Highly Confidential" content from agent-accessible indexes altogether, which is safer than trimming per query.
  • Never trim in the prompt. "Only use documents the user may see" in a system prompt is not access control.

docs.title: 6. Data residency in the EU
docs.text:
Residency must be designed for every place data lands or is processed. Index storage is only one of them:

  • Model inference. Global Standard deployments may process prompts in any region. Data Zone (EU) Standard/Provisioned keeps processing within the EU data zone. The model router runs on Global Standard and Data Zone Standard. Verify per model and region availability.
  • Indexes, Cosmos DB, SQL, Storage: in the EU region pair you chose (A5 for DR).
  • Semantic cache (Redis in the APIM gateway, A4): this is prompt and response content. It needs the same residency and tenant scoping.
  • Traces. OTel content capture is opt-in. Keep it off by default in EU production, redact in the Collector, and document the setting in the DPIA (A6).
  • Agent memory (Foundry memory is preview; MAF MemoryFileStore): per-user and per-tenant scope, TTL and "forget".
  • Eval datasets and red-team logs contain real questions. Classify them like production data.
  • Safety services. Content Safety groundedness detection is English-only and available only in some regions (France Central, Sweden Central, UK South among them). The AI Red Teaming Agent's agent-specific risk categories run cloud-only in 5 regions (incl. France Central, Sweden Central, Switzerland West). Region choice constrains which safety tooling you can use.

docs.title: 7. GraphRAG and LazyGraphRAG
docs.text:
• GraphRAG extracts entities and relations with an LLM, builds community summaries, and answers global, "sensemaking" questions ("what are the recurring themes across 3 years of incident reports?").
  • LazyGraphRAG defers the LLM work:
  • indexing cost ≈ vector RAG (~0.1% of full GraphRAG);
  • matched GraphRAG Global Search quality at >700× lower query cost;
  • a relevance-test budget acts as an explicit cost/quality dial;
  • available in Microsoft Discovery and Azure Local (preview); open-source availability not stated, so verify.
  • MAF exposes graph retrieval through a Neo4j GraphRAG provider.

Decision rule: - Use graph retrieval only for global/thematic or multi-hop entity questions that hybrid + rerank demonstrably fails on your eval set. - For Trakia that is "patterns across incidents by route, vehicle model and supplier part" for fleet managers and the SaaS analytics tier. It is not "what does policy 4.2 say".

docs.title: 8. Structured data: semantic layer and text-to-SQL governance
docs.text:
The Fleet Analyst (C10) answers questions over TrakiaOps. At enterprise and SaaS scale:

  • Semantic layer. Business metrics ("fuel efficiency", "unplanned downtime day", "on-time delivery") are defined once, as governed views or functions with descriptions, units and owners. The agent is grounded on the semantic layer's metadata, not on raw schema. Two analysts must get the same "downtime" number. This is a data-architecture deliverable, not a prompt.
  • Text-to-SQL is a tool, not RAG over rows:
  • read-only login;
  • an allow-listed schema (views only);
  • RLS with SESSION_CONTEXT carrying tenant and role, set by the tool host and never by the model;
  • parse and validate the SQL (single SELECT, no cross-tenant objects);
  • query timeout and row cap;
  • cost guard;
  • full audit (who, question, SQL, rows returned).
  • Evaluate with SQL metrics. RAGAS ships execution-based Datacompy and SQL-equivalence metrics. Your C10 golden queries become regression tests for every semantic-layer change.
  • AI Search's Azure SQL and Fabric knowledge sources are preview. That reinforces the tool approach for transactional data.

docs.title: 9. Multi-tenancy data isolation
docs.text:
Isolation models for the SaaS product:

Model Index SQL Cosmos When Pooled Shared index, mandatory tenant_id filter Shared DB + RLS on TenantId Shared container, partition key = tenant Standard tier, many small fleets Bridge Index per tenant on shared service Database per tenant (elastic pool) Container per tenant or hierarchical partition keys (verify) Mid-size fleets, per-tenant re-index and delete Silo Dedicated Search service Dedicated server Dedicated account Enterprise fleets with contractual isolation or residency demands

Microsoft's multitenant AI/ML guidance adds the model dimension:

  • Model tenancy options: tenant-specific, shared pre-trained, shared tenant-trained (needs consent and de-identification), and tuned shared per tenant.
  • Rule: treat models with the same sensitivity as their training data.
  • Noisy neighbours: per-resource limits may force scale-out across resources.
  • The page does not cover per-tenant grounding indexes or token quotas. Those come from your design and APIM (A4).

Isolation must extend to: - embeddings, which are derived personal and business data; - semantic cache keys; - memory stores; - trace content; - eval sets.

Tenant deletion must be complete and provable ("offboarding certificate"). This is easiest in bridge/silo designs.

Prove isolation with tests, not diagrams. Seed each test tenant with canary documents containing unique marker strings. Run every retrieval path (agent, tool, A2A, Copilot Studio via MCP, cache) as tenant B. Fail the build if any tenant-A marker appears in results, answers, cached responses or traces visible to B.

docs.title: Lab 1 — Vector store bake-off and knowledge platform ADR (≈4h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Choose stores per knowledge domain with measured recall, latency and cost at three scale points.
  • Start state: branch a3/start. Contains the C7 golden retrieval set (200 questions with qrels, stratified: factoid, table, multi-hop, BG, EN, abstention, permission-restricted), the MEVD harness and scale-gen (synthetic tenant corpora).
  • Steps:
  • Implement one IRetriever over MEVD with three backends:
    • AI Search (hybrid + semantic ranker);
    • Azure SQL (VECTOR + DiskANN, full-text composed);
    • Cosmos DB (hybrid RRF). 
      // Same record type, three stores (verify connector package names).
public sealed class ChunkRecord
{
    [VectorStoreKey] public string Id { get; set; } = default!;
    [VectorStoreData(IsIndexed = true)] public string TenantId { get; set; } = default!;
    [VectorStoreData(IsIndexed = true)] public string[] AllowedGroups { get; set; } = [];
    [VectorStoreData(IsFullTextIndexed = true)] public string Text { get; set; } = default!;
    [VectorStoreVector(Dimensions: 1536)] public ReadOnlyMemory<float> Embedding { get; set; }
}
  • Load three scale points: Trakia (~1,500 docs), SaaS year 1 (5 tenants), SaaS year 3 (40 tenants, ≈ 3M chunks via scale-gen). Use quantization where the store supports it.
  • Measure recall@10, nDCG@10, p50/p95 latency at 20 concurrent queries, and the monthly cost from the A1 cost model (fixed tier vs capacity-based).
  • Write ADR-A3-001 "Knowledge stores per domain": policies, manuals and contracts; incident narratives; memory. Include the "one content, one permission model" rule.
  • Break it: At year-3 scale, disable rescoring on binary-quantized vectors. Record the recall drop and decide whether discardOriginals is acceptable per domain.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • Bake-off report generated by dotnet run -- report with all metrics per store × scale.
  • The chosen design meets recall@10 ≥ 0.90 on the policy domain.
  • The ADR passes the linter and cites the report.
  • The cost figures reconcile with the A1 model (± 10%).
  • Stretch: Add a knowledge base (agentic retrieval, GA extractive) over the AI Search index. Compare against plain hybrid. Then flip to auto reasoning effort (preview API) behind a flag and record the latency and cost deltas.

docs.title: Lab 2 — Ingestion at scale with blue/green re-indexing (≈3.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Make ingestion a product with an SLA: parse quality, freshness and safe model changes.
  • Start state: a3/lab2-start. Contains 300 maintenance-manual PDFs (tables, diagrams), 200 scanned delivery notes and the policy library with versions.
  • Steps:
  • Build the pipeline: Content Understanding (Markdown, cross-page tables) → chunk → contextualise (Batch job, small model) → dedup (hash + embedding similarity) → embed → upsert into manuals-v1 behind alias manuals.
  • Add freshness metadata (sourceModified, ingestedAt, version) and an indexer-lag metric to App Insights. Define the SLO: policy change visible ≤ 4h.
  • Run the table-heavy subset of the golden set: naive extraction vs Content Understanding vs + contextual chunks.
  • Change the embedding model, which requires a full re-embed. Build manuals-v2 in parallel, run the retrieval eval gate, then switch the alias atomically. Keep v1 for rollback.
  • Break it: Change the embedding model in place (same index, new model for new chunks only). Observe the dimension mismatch, or worse, silently mixed vector spaces if the dimensions match. Your eval gate must catch the recall collapse before the alias switch.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • Table-question recall improves ≥ 15 points over naive extraction.
  • The alias switch is gated by CI on retrieval evals (fails below threshold).
  • Rollback works in < 5 minutes (timed).
  • The freshness dashboard shows the SLO.
  • Cost per 1k pages is computed and added to the A1 model.
  • Stretch: Process the scanned delivery notes with a Content Understanding prebuilt analyser into structured fields stored in SQL rather than the vector index. Justify why that is the right home for them.

docs.title: Lab 3 — Permission enforcement and revocation (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Prove that permissions hold on every retrieval path and that revocation latency is known.
  • Start state: a3/lab3-start. Contains an Entra test tenant with role groups (dispatcher, mechanic, HR, auditor), a user with 250+ groups (overage) and a SharePoint HR site.
  • Steps:
  • Implement query-time trimming: groups from the token, falling back to a Graph lookup on overage, cached with a 15-min TTL. Apply the filter in the retriever and assert that it cannot be bypassed: the filter is built server-side and the model never supplies it.
  • In parallel, configure the SharePoint knowledge source with ACL ingestion (preview) on a copy of the index.
  • Write a permission test matrix (role × document class × path: Fleet Assistant, MCP knowledge tool, Copilot Studio via MCP). Expect 0 leaks.
  • Revoke a user's access to an HR document. Measure the time until each path stops returning it: trimming path (your group-cache TTL) vs native ACL path (sync interval).
  • Exclude Purview "Highly Confidential" documents from agent indexes at ingestion (label indexing is preview; fallback: metadata from the SharePoint column).
  • Break it: The instructor adds a new "search_all_documents" diagnostic tool that calls the retriever without the trimming wrapper. Your matrix must fail. Then refactor so that the unfiltered retriever is not injectable outside the admin assembly (architecture test with NetArchTest/ArchUnitNET).
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The permission matrix passes with 0 leaks.
  • The overage user is resolved correctly.
  • Revocation latency per path is documented as a platform guarantee.
  • The architecture test prevents unfiltered retriever use.
  • Stretch: Compare answer quality between the two permission approaches on the HR subset. Write the go/no-go criteria for moving to native ACL when it reaches GA.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Multi-tenant isolation with canary leak tests (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Implement pooled and bridge isolation for SaaS and prove isolation across all data surfaces.
  • Start state: a3/lab4-start. Two synthetic tenants, rhodope-haulage and danube-logistics, each with documents, telematics and canary markers (CANARY-RH-7f3a…).
  • Steps:
  • Pooled: shared index with a mandatory tenant_id filter injected by the tenant-context middleware (from token tid → tenant registry), plus SQL RLS on TenantId: 
    CREATE FUNCTION sec.fn_tenant(@TenantId uniqueidentifier)
RETURNS TABLE WITH SCHEMABINDING AS
RETURN SELECT 1 AS ok WHERE @TenantId = CAST(SESSION_CONTEXT(N'TenantId') AS uniqueidentifier);
CREATE SECURITY POLICY sec.TenantPolicy
  ADD FILTER PREDICATE sec.fn_tenant(TenantId) ON dbo.Incidents,
  ADD BLOCK PREDICATE  sec.fn_tenant(TenantId) ON dbo.Incidents
  WITH (STATE = ON);
    The tool host sets SESSION_CONTEXT from the validated tenant claim, read-only, before running model-generated SQL.
  • Bridge: index per tenant for a "Premium" tenant. The tenant registry maps tenant → index name, and the retriever resolves the index from the registry, never from input.
  • Extend isolation to the APIM semantic cache key (tenant-scoped), memory store partition and trace content.
  • Build isolation-tests: for every path (retrieval, Fleet Analyst SQL, cache, memory, A2A endpoint), run the canary queries as the other tenant and assert that no foreign marker appears anywhere, including in the trace attributes visible to that tenant.
  • Implement tenant offboarding: delete the index or documents, SQL rows, cache entries, memory, eval data. Produce an offboarding certificate (JSON with counts before/after per store).
  • Break it: Remove the tenant_id filter from one code path, the "similar incidents" helper. Isolation tests must fail. Then make the pooled filter structurally unavoidable: tenant-scoped retriever factory plus architecture test.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • Isolation tests pass on all paths and run in CI on every PR.
  • The offboarding certificate shows zero residual records.
  • The ADR "Tenant isolation tiers" maps pooled/bridge/silo to SaaS plans with costs from A1.
  • Stretch: Add a "silo" deployment via the A2 landing-zone parameters for an enterprise tenant demanding contractual isolation. Estimate the cost to serve it.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Graph and structured knowledge decisions (≈2.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Decide on GraphRAG for global incident questions, and govern metric definitions for the Fleet Analyst.
  • Start state: a3/lab5-start. Contains 3 years of incident narratives (~9k) and the C10 analyst with raw-schema grounding.
  • Steps:
  • Build 30 "global" questions ("top recurring failure themes on the Plovdiv–Kulata route by vehicle model") with SME reference answers.
  • Compare hybrid + rerank vs graph retrieval: the MAF Neo4j provider, or LazyGraphRAG if available to you (verify access). Measure answer quality (rubric judge), indexing cost and query cost.
  • Write ADR-A3-004 "Graph retrieval for incident analytics" with explicit "revisit when" triggers.
  • Define a semantic layer: views and functions for DowntimeDays, FuelPer100Km and OnTimeDeliveryRate, with descriptions, units and owner. Re-ground the analyst on the semantic-layer metadata. Re-run the C10 golden queries plus 20 new metric questions.
  • Break it: Two analysts ask "downtime last quarter for Sofia depot" in different words. Before the semantic layer, show the divergent SQL and numbers. After it, show consistent results.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The graph decision is backed by measured cost and quality.
  • Semantic-layer metric questions reach ≥ 95% execution-match on the golden set.
  • The text-to-SQL tool enforces read-only access, allow-listed views, timeout, row cap and RLS (security tests pass).
  • Stretch: Expose the semantic layer to Copilot Studio through the C8 MCP server for a "fleet manager self-service" agent, inheriting the same RLS.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text:
"Where does this byte live?" (25 min, repeat with variations).

Given one user interaction, trace every place the data lands or is processed. Example: a Danube Logistics dispatcher asks the Fleet Assistant about a late shipment, attaching a customer email. For each location, state:

  • region and residency;
  • tenant scoping;
  • retention;
  • permission enforcement point;
  • deletion mechanism on offboarding.

Locations to cover: gateway logs, semantic cache, prompt to model (deployment type), retrieved chunks, tool calls, SQL, Cosmos conversation, memory, traces, eval sampling, red-team corpus.

Variations: - a Copilot Studio agent calling via MCP; - an A2A call from the customer's own agent; - a Bulgarian-language query with groundedness evaluation (English-only service, so what is your fallback?); - a user exercising GDPR erasure; - an embedding-model migration.

The score is locations found out of the reference list, plus correct enforcement points.

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text:
The product now sits on a knowledge platform:

  • stores chosen per domain by ADR;
  • a Content Understanding ingestion pipeline with freshness SLOs and blue/green index aliases;
  • permission enforcement tested on every path, with known revocation latency;
  • EU residency mapped for every data surface;
  • a governed semantic layer for the Fleet Analyst;
  • a graph-retrieval decision for incident analytics;
  • pooled and bridge tenant isolation proven by canary leak tests and a provable offboarding process.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text:
• Retrieval eval gate on index changes: any change to chunking, embedding model, analyser or alias target runs the retrieval suite (recall@k, nDCG, Document Retrieval evaluator) before the alias switch.
  • Isolation and permission suites run on every PR. They are non-negotiable gates and cannot be skipped by agents. A hook blocks PRs that modify the test filters without a CODEOWNERS approval.
  • Architecture tests (NetArchTest/ArchUnitNET) prevent unfiltered retrievers and tenant-unscoped data access from compiling into product assemblies.
  • A data-classification skill for coding agents: when an agent adds a new store, cache or log field, the skill prompts for tenant scope, residency, retention and deletion path, and updates the "where does this byte live" register.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Platform design & GA/preview judgement Single RAG app Layers named Layers with guarantees; production on GA, preview behind flags Plus published platform guarantees consumed by ADRs; upgrade criteria for preview features Store selection Preference Feature comparison Bake-off at 3 scale points with recall, latency, cost; per-domain ADR Plus quantization trade-offs measured, "one content, one permission model" enforced Ingestion Naive chunks Layout-aware parsing Contextual chunks, dedup, freshness SLO, blue/green aliases gated by evals Plus cost per 1k pages in the business model; rollback timed Permissions & residency Prompt-based trimming Filter on one path Matrix on all paths, overage handled, revocation latency measured, residency map Plus labels excluded at ingestion, architecture tests, region constraints on safety tooling handled Tenant isolation & structured data Shared everything Tenant filter Pooled/bridge designs, canary leak tests across cache/memory/traces, offboarding certificate, governed semantic layer Plus isolation tiers priced in SaaS plans, graph retrieval decided by cost/quality evidence

Auto-checked: - bake-off report; - retrieval eval thresholds and alias gate; - permission matrix; - isolation tests; - architecture tests; - offboarding certificate; - SQL tool security tests; - semantic-layer execution-match; - ADR linter.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Building the SaaS on preview-only features (planning, synthesis, native ACLs) without a GA fallback.
  • Trimming in the prompt, or building filters from model-supplied parameters.
  • Forgetting group overage and revocation latency.
  • Re-embedding in place without aliases, which mixes vector spaces.
  • Duplicated content across stores with different permission models.
  • Residency designed for indexes only, while caches, traces, memory and eval sets leak elsewhere. Using Global deployments for EU personal data without a decision.
  • Tenant filters "everywhere except one helper". Prove isolation with canaries and architecture tests.
  • GraphRAG because it is fashionable. Without global questions, hybrid + rerank wins on cost.
  • Text-to-SQL on raw schema with model-chosen tenant context.
