docs.title: A6 — AI governance, risk & compliance architecture
docs.text:
Level: Expert — AI Solution Architect track · Duration: 16h (theory 35% / labs 65%) · Prerequisites: A1–A5; C16 (threat model), C18 (AI Act classification, transparency, human oversight) · Volatility: High (EU AI Act guidance and national implementation, Digital Omnibus follow-ups, Azure Policy definitions, Agent 365/Purview features)

Not legal advice. This module teaches architects to build the technical and organisational system that makes compliance demonstrable. Classification decisions, legal bases and contractual positions must be confirmed by qualified counsel and the data protection officer. Article references are given for orientation; verify them against the consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
What separates an expert architect from a proficient one here: a proficient architect can classify one AI system and write a transparency notice (C18). An expert designs the governance system for the whole portfolio. That system has five parts:

  • an inventory that is always current;
  • risk-tiered approval workflows;
  • controls enforced as code;
  • evidence generated by the delivery pipeline as a by-product;
  • an audit trail that reconstructs who, which agent version, which model, which data and which approval produced any action.

The expert also knows how the obligations shift when the company moves from using AI internally to selling it to other companies.

Trakia's two decisions make governance a design problem:

  • Internal rollout. It reaches drivers, which is employment territory. The deferred "driver-behaviour scoring" feature from A1 evaluates the performance and behaviour of workers, which places it squarely in Annex III high-risk territory.
  • SaaS. It changes Trakia's role. Trakia becomes the provider of an AI system placed on the market, and each customer fleet becomes a deployer with obligations of its own that Trakia must enable: instructions for use, logging, human-oversight design.

The regulatory calendar also moved. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and pushed Annex III obligations to 2 December 2027. That is a design window, not a reprieve. Customers' procurement teams are already asking for evidence.

Teams without this skill fall into one of three patterns:

  • Paper governance: policies in a wiki that nobody's pipeline checks.
  • Freeze: "legal hasn't approved AI".
  • Surprise: a works council injunction or a customer audit finding.

Experts map regulation to controls, controls to automated checks, and checks to evidence. They make the compliant path the easiest path through the factory.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Build an AI system inventory/registry that records risk class, provider/deployer role per relationship, models, data, tools, owners and evidence links, with machine-checkable completeness.
  2. Classify Trakia's systems under the EU AI Act as amended (prohibited, Annex III high-risk, Art. 50 transparency, minimal), applying the current dates. Defend the reasoning, including the Art. 6(3) derogation and profiling (verify article references).
  3. Analyse how obligations change between internal use and SaaS: provider vs deployer, Art. 25 role shifts, and the deployer-support pack Trakia must ship.
  4. Conduct a GDPR DPIA for an AI feature that monitors employees, including retention and erasure across traces, memory, indexes and eval sets.
  5. Design an AI management system aligned with ISO/IEC 42001 and map it to the NIST AI RMF (Govern/Map/Measure/Manage) and the Generative AI Profile.
  6. Implement policy-as-code: Azure Policy for platform controls and CI checks for agent manifests, risk tier gates and evidence completeness.
  7. Design tamper-evident audit logging that reconstructs agent actions and supports AI Act record-keeping and GDPR rights.
  8. Operate a risk-tiered governance board with approval workflows, model and system cards, and evidence packs generated by the pipeline.

docs.title: 1. The EU AI Act timeline after the Digital Omnibus
docs.text:
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 was published 24 July 2026 and entered into force 27 July 2026. Dates an architect plans against:

Obligation Applies from Prohibited practices (Art. 5); AI literacy (Art. 4) 2 Feb 2025. Literacy is now softened to a duty to support literacy measures GPAI model obligations; governance and penalties framework 2 Aug 2025 (legacy GPAI models until 2 Aug 2027) Art. 50 transparency (AI interaction disclosure, synthetic content marking, deepfake labelling) 2 Aug 2026. Generative systems already on the market before then have until 2 Dec 2026 for Art. 50(2) machine-readable marking New prohibition: AI generating non-consensual intimate imagery / CSAM (or lacking reasonable safeguards against it) 2 Dec 2026 Annex III high-risk (incl. employment and workers management) 2 Dec 2027 (was 2 Aug 2026) Annex I product-embedded high-risk 2 Aug 2028 National regulatory sandbox (at least one per Member State) by 2 Aug 2027

Other omnibus changes relevant to Trakia:

  • Small mid-caps (new Art. 3(14b)) get SME-style privileges: simplified technical documentation, proportionate QMS, lower fine caps. Check whether Trakia qualifies.
  • High-risk EU database registration is reinstated in streamlined form.
  • New Art. 4a permits strictly necessary processing of special-category data for bias detection and correction under safeguards, now extending beyond high-risk systems.
  • The AI Office gets exclusive supervision of AI systems built on GPAI models by the same provider or group.
  • The broader "Digital Omnibus" (GDPR, NIS2, Data Act changes) was still in the legislative process as of July 2026. Track it.

Bulgaria. National competent-authority designation is thinly documented. One law-firm tracker names the Commission for Personal Data Protection (КЗЛД / CPDP) as the primary authority, with the Executive Agency for Accreditation for notified bodies. This is unverified. Point learners to the State Gazette (Държавен вестник) and CPDP for authoritative updates. Do not build governance processes that hard-code an authority until it is confirmed.

docs.title: 2. Classifying Trakia's portfolio
docs.text:
Apply a decision sequence for each system:

  1. Is it an AI system?
  2. Prohibited practice (Art. 5)?
  3. Annex I product safety component?
  4. Annex III use case?
  5. If Annex III, does the Art. 6(3) derogation apply? It is unavailable when the system performs profiling of natural persons (verify).
  6. Art. 50 transparency duties?
  7. GDPR overlay.
System Indicative classification (to be confirmed by counsel) Key reasoning Fleet Assistant (policy/manual Q&A, maintenance booking with approval) Not high-risk; Art. 50 disclosure of AI interaction Assists staff; no decisions about persons Fleet Analyst (telematics NL queries) Not high-risk as designed; becomes sensitive if used to rank individual drivers Purpose and use constraints must be written into instructions for use and enforced (no per-driver ranking views) Incident workflow (triage → booking → customer notification) Not high-risk; Art. 50 for AI-generated customer messages where applicable Human approval on bookings; customer comms disclosure Driver-behaviour scoring / coaching Annex III point 4 (employment, workers management), likely high-risk: monitoring and evaluating performance and behaviour of workers; profiling makes the Art. 6(3) derogation unavailable (verify) Annex III obligations from 2 Dec 2027; DPIA now; works council Driver fatigue detection from cabin camera (D3 idea) Check Art. 5 workplace emotion-recognition prohibition and its medical/safety exception (verify); biometric GDPR special category Design as a safety system with minimal data; legal review mandatory HR policy Q&A via M365 Copilot (A1 buy decision) Trakia is deployer of Microsoft's system; minimal risk Literacy support, transparency, data protection configuration

Misconception to unlearn: "we only use OpenAI/Anthropic models, so the AI Act is their problem". GPAI model providers carry GPAI obligations. Trakia, which builds an AI system on those models and puts it into service or places it on the market under its own name, is the provider of that system.

docs.title: 3. Provider vs deployer when selling SaaS
docs.text:
Internal use. Trakia is provider and deployer of its own system (it puts it into service for its own use).

SaaS to fleets. Trakia is the provider. Each customer fleet is a deployer.

For high-risk systems, providers carry: - risk management (Art. 9); - data governance (Art. 10); - technical documentation (Art. 11); - record-keeping and automatic logging (Art. 12); - transparency and instructions for use (Art. 13); - human-oversight design (Art. 14); - accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Art. 15); - a QMS (Art. 17); - conformity assessment, registration and post-market monitoring.

Deployers carry: - use according to instructions; - human oversight by competent people; - input-data relevance; - log retention (at least six months is the commonly cited minimum; verify Art. 26); - informing workers' representatives and affected workers before putting a high-risk system into service at the workplace (verify Art. 26(7)); - an FRIA for public bodies and certain private deployers (Art. 27).

Art. 25 role shifts. A deployer becomes a provider on substantial modification or rebranding under its own name. That is relevant if a large customer white-labels Fleet Ops Copilot, or if Trakia lets tenants upload custom agents that change the intended purpose. Contracts and product configuration limits are architecture.

Architectural consequence: the deployer-support pack. For every SaaS feature Trakia ships: - instructions for use; - the system card; - a logging and export API (so deployers can meet their log retention); - oversight configuration (approval steps a tenant can't switch off for high-risk features); - transparency notice templates in Bulgarian and English; - a works-council information template; - data-processing terms.

Customers will ask for this in procurement. Build it once, generate it per release.

docs.title: 4. GDPR and the DPIA for AI features
docs.text:
A DPIA is required for systematic monitoring of employees and for large-scale or innovative processing. The driver-behaviour feature needs one regardless of AI Act timing. Architectural content of a good AI DPIA:

  • Data flow map. Reuse the A3 "where does this byte live" register: prompts, retrieved chunks, tool outputs, traces, memory, eval sets, red-team corpora, gateway logs, semantic cache.
  • Lawful basis and purpose limitation per flow. Telematics collected for fleet operations is not automatically lawful to reuse for individual performance scoring.
  • Minimisation:
  • pseudonymised driver IDs (already in TrakiaOps);
  • aggregation thresholds (no per-driver views below N events);
  • OTel content capture off in production, redaction in the Collector.
  • Retention:
  • per store, with deletion jobs;
  • prompts and traces with the shortest feasible retention;
  • eval datasets classified as production data.
  • Data-subject rights. Access and erasure across all stores, including memory ("forget"), indexes, traces and eval samples. Design an erasure orchestrator, not a manual checklist.
  • Processors and sub-processors.
  • Microsoft (Foundry, Azure);
  • model providers offered through Foundry (verify the data-processing terms per model family);
  • Trakia as processor for SaaS customers, who are controllers of their drivers' data.
  • Residency and transfers. Data Zone EU deployments, EU regions and failover pairs (A3, A5).
  • Risks and mitigations, including model-specific ones: inference of special categories (MEAI's UngroundedAttributes evaluator is useful), hallucinated statements about people, memory poisoning.

docs.title: 5. Management systems and frameworks
docs.text:
• ISO/IEC 42001 is the certifiable AI management system (AIMS) standard. Plan-do-check-act structure, AI policy, roles and responsibilities, AI risk assessment and treatment, AI system impact assessment, Annex A reference controls, statement of applicability, internal audit, management review, continual improvement. Companions: ISO/IEC 23894 (AI risk management) and ISO/IEC 42005 (AI impact assessment). A Trakia AIMS scopes "design, development, operation and provision of Fleet Ops Copilot (internal and SaaS)". Certification is a commercial lever for SaaS sales.
  • NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Jan 2023) remains current; there is no "2.0". Functions: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. The Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024) lists GenAI-specific risks and actions. CSA published a draft Agentic NIST AI RMF Profile (Mar 2026). NIST runs an AI Agent Standards Initiative via CAISI.
  • Mapping is the architect's job. One control, many frameworks. Example: the "eval gate on release" control satisfies:
  • AI Act Art. 9/15 (risk management, accuracy, robustness);
  • ISO 42001 operational controls (verify the Annex A control IDs);
  • NIST Measure.

Build a control catalogue with one row per control, linked to frameworks, implementation and evidence.

docs.title: 6. Inventory, model cards and system cards
docs.text:
AI inventory record (extends the A4 agent registry; one record per AI system, linking to its agents):

  • system ID, name, purpose, intended users;
  • provider/deployer role per relationship (internal, each SaaS tenant);
  • risk class and rationale, with reviewer and date;
  • Art. 50 duties;
  • DPIA reference;
  • models (role, version, retirement date from A5);
  • data sources and classification;
  • tools and side-effect classes;
  • human-oversight points;
  • eval suite and last results;
  • red-team ASR;
  • incidents;
  • owner/sponsor;
  • status;
  • next review.

Model card (per model role as used by Trakia, not the vendor's card): - intended use; - evaluation results on Trakia's suites, including Bulgarian strata; - known failure modes from error analysis; - limitations (e.g., groundedness detection English-only → custom judge); - version and lifecycle.

System card (per AI system): - architecture summary (C4 extract); - capabilities and limitations; - oversight design; - safety evaluations; - data handling; - residency; - intended and prohibited uses; - contact.

The system card is the backbone of the Art. 13 instructions for use and the customer due-diligence response.

docs.title: 7. Governance boards and approval workflows
docs.text:
Tier the process by risk. A single heavyweight board for everything creates the "freeze" pattern.

Tier Examples Approval Evidence required T0 Internal productivity with bought SaaS (M365 Copilot) Product owner + IT security checklist Inventory entry, data config T1 Internal custom assistants, read-only tools Platform architect + security Eval report, threat model delta, DPIA screening T2 Agents with write actions, customer-facing, SaaS features Governance board (architecture, security, DPO, product) Full evidence pack, red-team scorecard, oversight design T3 Annex III / high-risk, employee monitoring Board + legal + management sign-off + works-council process T2 + DPIA, FRIA-style impact assessment, conformity plan

Workflow mechanics: - the request is a PR adding or changing an inventory record; - CI computes the tier from the manifest (a classification decision table) and requires the corresponding evidence and approvers (CODEOWNERS / environment protection rules); - the decision is recorded as an ADR; - re-approval triggers: model migration (A5), new tools, new data sources, new tenant category, incidents.

docs.title: 8. Policy-as-code
docs.text:
Platform controls (Azure Policy). Assign an initiative at the AI landing-zone scope: - deny public network access on AI services, Search, Cosmos and Storage; - require private endpoints; - disable local (key) auth; - require diagnostic settings to central Log Analytics; - allowed locations limited to EU regions; - required tags: ai-system-id, risk-tier, data-classification, tenant/stamp.

Built-in definitions exist for several of these. Verify names and effects, and whether model-deployment-level policies, such as allowed models or deployment types, are available for Foundry.

Delivery controls (CI). - An agent manifest schema (agent.yaml) must reference an inventory ID. CI fails if: - risk tier evidence is missing; - an irreversible tool lacks a HITL point; - a model role has a retirement date inside the release window without a migration ticket; - the content-capture flag is on for production; - the deployment region is outside the EU. - Evals, red-team ASR and isolation suites are gates (C14, A3).

Runtime controls. Guardrails (input / tool call / tool response / output, with tool controls preview), the gateway content-safety policy, Conditional Access for agents and lifecycle suspension (A4).

docs.title: 9. Audit logging
docs.text:
What to log for every agent action: - timestamp; - tenant; - user (pseudonymous ID); - agent ID and version; - model deployment and gen_ai.response.model; - prompt and instructions version; - retrieved document IDs (not content); - tool calls with arguments (redacted per classification); - guardrail decisions; - approval events: approver, what they saw (the raw action, per OWASP guidance), decision; - outcome.

Use trace correlation (gen_ai.conversation.id, trace IDs).

Properties: - Tamper-evident. Use immutable storage (WORM/immutability policies on Blob) or hash-chained records. - Separated from operational telemetry that engineers can purge. - Retention per policy: AI Act record-keeping for high-risk systems (Art. 12, plus deployer retention under Art. 26; verify periods) balanced against GDPR minimisation. - Access-controlled: the auditor role (A2 personas). - Exportable per tenant for SaaS deployers.

Reconstruction test. Given a booking made 3 weeks ago for Danube Logistics, reconstruct who and what caused it in under 15 minutes. If you can't, your audit design has failed.

docs.title: Lab 1 — AI inventory and classification as code (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Every Trakia AI system is inventoried, classified with recorded reasoning, and tiered automatically.
  • Start state: branch a6/start. Contains the A4 agent registry and governance/inventory/schema.json.
  • Steps:
  • Create inventory records for all systems in Concepts §2, plus the SRE agent and the coding agents of the factory. Are coding agents in scope of your AI policy? Decide, and record why.
  • Encode the classification decision sequence as a reviewed decision table (classification.yaml) and a small .NET evaluator. Example: 
    - id: annex3-employment
  when: { affects_workers: true, evaluates_performance_or_behaviour: true }
  result: { class: high-risk-annex-iii, derogation_6_3: unavailable_if_profiling, applies_from: 2027-12-02 }
  citation: "Annex III pt 4; Art. 6(2)-(3) — verify against consolidated text"
  • Record the provider/deployer role per relationship: internal, and each SaaS tenant category.
  • Generate the tier (T0–T3) and the required-evidence list per system. CI fails on missing evidence for the current status (e.g., "pilot" T2 requires an eval report and threat model).
  • Break it: A product manager adds "monthly driver ranking leaderboard" to the Fleet Analyst's purpose field. Re-classification must flip the system to T3 / Annex III, block its promotion, and open a governance-board issue.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The inventory schema validates and the classification evaluator's tests (≥ 12 cases incl. edge cases) pass.
  • Every record has a reviewer and date.
  • The leaderboard change is caught by CI.
  • Classification rationales cite articles marked "verify".
  • Stretch: Generate a portfolio dashboard showing systems by tier, open evidence gaps and upcoming dates (2 Dec 2026 Art. 50(2) marking; 2 Dec 2027 Annex III).

docs.title: Lab 2 — DPIA and impact assessment for driver coaching (≈3.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Decide how (and whether) Trakia offers driver-behaviour features, with a DPIA and design alternatives.
  • Start state: a6/lab2-start. Contains the A3 data-location register, telematics schema and persona notes from the A1 works-council representative.
  • Steps:
  • Describe three design alternatives:
    • (a) individual driver scores visible to managers;
    • (b) private coaching: each driver sees only their own feedback, managers see only depot-level aggregates above a minimum group size, no ranking, no HR use;
    • (c) fleet-level safety analytics only (no individual processing beyond what operations already needs).
  • For each, run the DPIA: data flows, lawful basis, necessity and proportionality, risks to drivers (incl. inference errors, chilling effects), mitigations, residual risk. Also run an impact assessment in the spirit of ISO/IEC 42005 (fairness across routes and vehicle types: are drivers on mountain routes scored unfairly?).
  • Re-run the AI Act classification per alternative. Note which remain Annex III (evaluating behaviour of workers may persist even in coaching designs; counsel must decide).
  • Specify the technical controls for the chosen design:
    • aggregation thresholds enforced in SQL views (A3 semantic layer);
    • no per-driver API for manager roles (authorization tests);
    • retention;
    • an erasure orchestrator covering index, memory, traces and eval samples;
    • a fairness evaluation in CI (score distributions by route type with tolerance).
  • Draft the worker information notice (BG/EN) and the works-council briefing outline (used in A7).
  • Break it: A developer adds a "top 10 safest drivers" endpoint for a depot-motivation campaign. Authorization and aggregation tests must fail. Explain in the DPIA addendum why "positive" rankings still evaluate behaviour.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The DPIA template is complete (linter).
  • The chosen design's controls are implemented as tests and pass.
  • The erasure orchestrator removes a test driver's data from all registered stores, with a report.
  • The fairness check is in CI with a documented threshold.
  • Stretch: Write the deployer-facing instructions-for-use section for SaaS customers who enable the coaching feature, including their own works-council duties (verify Art. 26).

docs.title: Lab 3 — Policy-as-code across platform and pipeline (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Make the compliant path the only deployable path.
  • Start state: a6/lab3-start. Contains A2 policy definitions and agent manifests from A4.
  • Steps:

  • Extend the Azure Policy initiative:

    • allowed EU locations;
    • deny public network access;
    • disable local auth;
    • require diagnostic settings;
    • required tags ai-system-id, risk-tier, data-classification.

    Assign it at the AI landing-zone management group/subscription. Run a compliance scan. 2. Write agent-manifest CI validation: - inventory ID exists; - tier evidence present; - irreversible tools have HITL; - content capture off for prod; - model roles have no retirement inside the release window without a migration ticket (reads the A5 register); - deployment type is Data Zone EU or regional EU for personal data. 3. Gate releases with environment protection: T2/T3 releases require board approvers; the evidence pack (Lab 4) must exist. 4. Document each policy in the control catalogue with its AI Act / ISO 42001 / NIST mapping. - Break it: Run three violations one at a time: - (a) deploy a Global Standard model deployment for the Fleet Analyst (personal data); - (b) a new Search service in a non-EU region; - (c) an agent manifest enabling content capture in prod.

Each must be blocked at the right layer (policy deny / CI fail) with a clear message. - Acceptance criteria: - The policy compliance report shows 100% on AI resources. - All three violations are blocked with evidence (deny event, CI log). - Every control in the catalogue maps to ≥ 1 framework and links an automated check or a named manual review. - Stretch: Assess ASSERT / the Agent Control Specification (open-sourced at Build 2026): generate adversarial tests from Trakia's AI policy text and compare them with your C14 red-team set. Report the overlap and new findings.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Audit trail and evidence pack generation (≈3.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Any action is reconstructable, and every release produces the evidence a regulator, auditor or customer will ask for.
  • Start state: a6/lab4-start.
  • Steps:
  • Implement an audit event emitter in the agent middleware and tool hosts, following the Concepts §9 schema. Write to an append-only store with immutability, plus hash chaining per tenant per day. Keep it separate from operational telemetry.
  • Build the reconstruction query: given a booking ID, return the full causal chain (event → triage agent version → model → retrieved doc IDs → tool calls → approval by whom, seeing what → outcome).

  • Build the evidence pack generator in the release pipeline. It produces:

    • system card;
    • model cards per role;
    • eval report (dotnet aieval);
    • red-team scorecard (ASR);
    • threat model delta (C16);
    • isolation and permission test results (A3);
    • DPIA reference;
    • control-catalogue status;
    • SBOM plus an AI bill of materials (models, MCP servers with hashes, datasets).

    All are signed, versioned and attached to the release. 4. Produce a traceability matrix: AI Act Arts. 9–15 (and deployer support items) → controls → evidence artefacts for the driver-coaching feature (T3), even though obligations apply from 2 Dec 2027. - Break it: The instructor edits an audit record in storage. Hash-chain verification must detect it. Then reconstruct a 3-week-old Danube Logistics booking within 15 minutes. - Acceptance criteria: - Tamper detection test passes. - Reconstruction completes in ≤ 15 min with all chain links. - The evidence pack is generated automatically for the release and is complete per tier (checker). - The traceability matrix has no unmapped article for the T3 feature. - Stretch: Expose a per-tenant audit export API for SaaS deployers, with tenant isolation tests (A3 canaries).

docs.title: Lab 5 — Governance board simulation and customer due diligence (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Run the tiered approval process end to end and answer a customer's AI due-diligence questionnaire from generated evidence.
  • Start state: Outputs of Labs 1–4. The instructor provides a 40-question SaaS customer questionnaire (residency, sub-processors, model lifecycle, evals, red-teaming, human oversight, logging, incident response, AI Act role).
  • Steps:
  • Submit two requests via PR: (a) promote the Fleet Analyst to SaaS GA (T2); (b) pilot driver coaching internally (T3).
  • Run the board: architecture, security, DPO and product (rotated roles; the instructor plays legal). Decide approve / approve with conditions / reject. Record ADRs with conditions and re-approval triggers.
  • Draft the ISO/IEC 42001 AIMS skeleton:
    • scope;
    • AI policy (1 page);
    • roles;
    • risk assessment method (reuse A1 scoring);
    • statement of applicability outline;
    • internal audit plan;
    • management review cadence;
    • the NIST AI RMF function mapping.
  • Answer the customer questionnaire. ≥ 80% of answers must link to generated evidence (system card, evidence pack, policy compliance, DR test report from A5), not prose.
  • Break it: Mid-board, a severity-2 incident is reported: the incident agent drafted a customer email containing another customer's shipment reference (an isolation failure in a template cache). Apply your incident process: containment, notification assessment (GDPR breach evaluation), inventory update, re-approval trigger, corrective action.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • Board decisions are recorded with conditions and triggers.
  • The AIMS skeleton covers all mandatory clauses listed in the course template.
  • The questionnaire is ≥ 80% evidence-linked.
  • The incident record is complete, with a root cause and a new automated check.
  • Stretch: Estimate the effort and cost of ISO/IEC 42001 certification for Trakia (A1 model, people family) and its expected impact on SaaS sales cycles. Treat the result as a business-case line, not a compliance cost.

docs.title: Kata
docs.text:
"Classify in 20 minutes" (repeat with variations).

Given a one-paragraph feature description, produce: - the AI Act class with articles (marked verify); - provider/deployer roles internal vs SaaS; - Art. 50 duties; - whether a DPIA is needed; - the governance tier; - the three controls you would automate first.

Variations: - AI-drafted customer delay notifications; - a voice assistant for drivers; - a tenant-uploaded custom agent; - a white-labelled reseller deal (Art. 25); - synthetic training images of damaged trucks (Art. 50(2) marking); - route optimisation that assigns shifts based on driver history (Annex III task allocation; verify).

The score is agreement with the reference classification plus the quality of the control choices.

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text:
Fleet Ops Copilot now has an ISO/IEC 42001-style governance system:

  • a complete AI inventory with classification-as-code and risk tiers;
  • a DPIA-backed decision on driver coaching with enforced aggregation, authorization and fairness checks;
  • Azure Policy and CI policy-as-code;
  • a tamper-evident audit trail with a 15-minute reconstruction;
  • evidence packs and system/model cards generated per release;
  • a deployer-support pack for SaaS customers;
  • a running governance board with recorded decisions.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text:
• Agent-manifest and inventory validators in CI. Tier-based required approvers via CODEOWNERS and environment protection.
  • Evidence pack generator as a release stage. The release fails if evidence is incomplete for the tier.
  • Governance skill for coding agents: when an agent's change touches tools, data sources, models or purpose fields, the skill updates the manifest, flags re-classification and drafts the DPIA screening delta for a human.
  • Coding agents themselves are inventoried (T1). The factory's own permissions, sandbox and data policies (A7) are referenced from the AI policy.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Regulatory analysis Generic "AI Act applies" Correct classes for obvious systems Correct post-omnibus dates; Annex III and Art. 5 edge cases; provider/deployer per relationship; Art. 25 risks Plus design alternatives that change classification, deployer-support pack, uncertainty flagged for counsel Data protection Privacy notice only DPIA for one flow DPIA covering all data surfaces, erasure orchestrator, residency, retention per store Plus fairness evaluation, worker-information materials, special-category inference controls Controls as code Policies in a wiki Some Azure Policy Policy initiative + CI manifest validation + release gates, all mapped in a control catalogue Plus re-approval triggers automated from model/tool/data changes; negative tests for each control Audit & evidence App logs Structured logs Tamper-evident audit with reconstruction ≤ 15 min; evidence pack per release; traceability matrix Plus per-tenant export, AIBOM, questionnaire ≥ 80% evidence-linked Governance operation Single approver Board exists Risk-tiered workflow, recorded decisions, AIMS skeleton, NIST/ISO mapping Plus incident-to-governance loop and certification business case

Auto-checked: - inventory and classification tests; - leaderboard re-classification; - DPIA linter; - authorization, aggregation and fairness tests; - erasure report; - policy compliance and deny events; - manifest validation; - audit tamper detection; - reconstruction timing; - evidence pack completeness; - traceability matrix coverage.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Using pre-omnibus dates (Annex III from 2 Aug 2026), or treating the 2027 deadline as a reason to wait.
  • "The model vendor is responsible", which ignores Trakia's provider role for its own system and SaaS.
  • Positive rankings ("safest drivers") treated as harmless. They still evaluate worker behaviour.
  • A DPIA that covers the database but not traces, caches, memory and eval sets.
  • Governance as one heavyweight board for everything (freeze), or as wiki policies nobody checks (theatre).
  • Audit logs in the same mutable store engineers purge for cost.
  • Hard-coding a Bulgarian authority that isn't confirmed.
  • Shipping SaaS without instructions for use and log export for deployers.
  • Treating this module as legal advice. Escalate classification calls to counsel.

docs.title: A7 — The architect's craft in AI programmes
docs.text: Level: Expert — AI Solution Architect track · Duration: 14h (theory 30% / labs 70%) · Prerequisites: A1–A6; C19 (automated SDLC); your factory from C4–C19 · Volatility: Med (the craft is durable; tool landscapes, radar placements and productivity evidence change every few months)

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
What separates an expert architect from a proficient one here: a proficient architect produces good designs. An expert produces good decisions in a programme: decisions that are recorded, testable, communicated so each audience can act on them, estimated honestly under uncertainty, and continuously verified by fitness functions. The expert also leads the team and the agentic factory that implement those decisions, measuring outcomes rather than output and governing what the agents may do. In AI programmes the gap between the two shows quickly, because:

  • the technology changes quarterly;
  • quality is statistical;
  • costs scale with behaviour;
  • stakeholders range from the CFO to a works council that worries about drivers being watched.

Trakia is now an AI programme, not a project. It runs an internal rollout across three depots, a SaaS business with prospects asking for proposals, a governance board, a platform team and a product team whose code is mostly written by agents. The architect's week has five different jobs in it:

  • an ADR on whether to adopt a preview feature;
  • an architecture review where a team claims its design "meets the quality bar";
  • an executive steering meeting about a delayed milestone;
  • a works-council session about the driver-coaching pilot;
  • a pre-sales workshop with a 120-truck fleet in the Rhodopes.

There is also the agentic factory to govern. DORA 2025 found about 90% AI adoption among developers and describes AI as "a mirror and a multiplier": it amplifies whatever discipline exists. METR's early-2025 trial found experienced developers 19–20% slower with AI while they believed they were faster. METR's February 2026 update says developers are probably sped up now, but calls its own evidence "very weak" on the size. An architect who governs the factory on vibes will get vibes.

This closing module of the architect track (not to be confused with the joint capstone) trains the craft: ADRs for AI, fitness functions with evals at their core, communication by audience, estimation under uncertainty, pre-sales solution design, governing AI-augmented teams, an organisational technology radar and a personal system for keeping current.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
1. Write ADRs for AI decisions that record evidence, volatility, reversibility, cost of change and review triggers tied to model lifecycles and preview status.
  2. Define and automate architecture fitness functions (quality evals, cost per task, latency, ASR, isolation, dependency rules) and run an architecture review that uses them as evidence.
  3. Communicate one architecture to executives, legal/DPO, a works council and engineers, adapting content, risk framing and asks to each audience.
  4. Estimate AI work under uncertainty with ranges, reference classes, spikes and eval-gated milestones, and explain estimates to sponsors without false precision.
  5. Lead pre-sales solution design: discovery, a solution blueprint, PoC/pilot design with success criteria, and a priced proposal with stated assumptions and risks.
  6. Govern the agentic factory: permission and sandbox policies, model and data policies, DORA plus AI-specific metrics, and an operating model with clear roles.
  7. Build and maintain an organisational technology radar with evidence-based placements and a quarterly cadence aligned to vendor event cycles.
  8. Operate a personal and team system for keeping current that distinguishes signal (lifecycle notices, GA changes) from noise (leaderboards, launch hype).

docs.title: 1. ADRs for AI decisions
docs.text:
No authoritative standard for "AI ADRs" exists, so the format here is a course convention built on the classic ADR shape (context, options, decision, consequences), with ≥ 3 options considered (incl. "do nothing / status quo" where meaningful); the ADR linter enforces this. It adds fields that AI decisions specifically need:

Field Why AI needs it Example (Trakia) Evidence Statistical quality claims need eval reports, not opinions "pass^4 = 0.86 vs 0.71 (report link)" Volatility Preview features and model versions change under you "Depends on AI Search 2026-08-01-preview (query planning)" Reversibility / cost of change Some choices are config (model role), some are migrations (embedding model, vector store) "Embedding change = full re-index, ~6h at year-1 scale" Review triggers Decisions expire with model retirements, GA moves and cost thresholds "Revisit at GA of knowledge-source ACLs, or if cost/task > €0.06, or at retirement of model X (date)" Assumptions & owners Business-case assumptions (A1) drive design "Adoption ≥ 60% (owner: product)" Compliance impact Changes can re-tier a system (A6) "No change to risk tier"

ADRs as agent context. An ADR-driven repo (docs/adr/, C4 DSL, architecture.md) doubles as context for coding agents. Agents read the decisions, and architecture tests (ArchUnitNET/NetArchTest) catch drift. Keep ADRs short, link evidence, and supersede them rather than edit them.

docs.title: 2. Architecture reviews and fitness functions
docs.text:
A fitness function is an objective, automated check that an architectural characteristic holds. For AI systems, evals are fitness functions for quality:

Characteristic Fitness function Where it runs Answer quality Failure-mode pass rates with judges validated by TPR/TNR (C14) PR (cached), nightly (uncached) Agent reliability pass^k on τ-bench-style scenarios; tool-call accuracy Nightly Safety Red-team ASR ≤ threshold (C16/A6) Weekly / release Isolation & permissions Canary leak tests, permission matrix (A3) Every PR Cost Cost per successful task ≤ budget (A1/A5) Nightly from telemetry Latency TTFT p95 under load (A5) Release Structure Dependency rules: no unfiltered retriever; agents only call tools via gateway (ArchUnitNET/NetArchTest) Every PR Lifecycle No model role retiring within the release window without a migration ticket (A5/A6) Every PR

Running an architecture review:

  • Bring evidence, not slides. The package contains the WAF AI assessment (A2), C4 with the AI profile, ADRs, fitness-function results, the cost model and the DR test report.
  • Review the decision record and the risks, not the diagram aesthetics.
  • Outcome: approve / approve with conditions / rework, with conditions written as new fitness functions where possible.
  • Watch for "reviewer always finds something". Anthropic notes that review agents asked to find gaps will always find some, which pushes toward over-engineering. The same holds for human boards. Weigh findings by risk and cost.

docs.title: 3. Stakeholder communication by audience
docs.text:
The same architecture is presented to each audience as different arguments:

Audience What they decide What they need Trakia example Executives / steering Funding, priorities, risk appetite Outcome vs plan, P50/P90 ranges, top risks with mitigations, explicit asks "Pilot met 7 of 9 gates; cost/task 18% over; ask: approve 6-week extension for adoption work" CFO Investment, pricing Unit economics, margin per tenant tier, sensitivity A5 price floor per isolation tier Legal / DPO Lawfulness, contracts, regulatory exposure Data flows, roles (provider/deployer), DPIA, residency, sub-processors, evidence A3 data-location register + A6 evidence pack Works council / employee representatives Consent or consultation on monitoring and workplace technology Purpose, what is not done (no rankings, no HR use), data minimisation, who sees what, retention, worker rights, oversight, how to complain, the trial and review plan Driver-coaching pilot: private feedback, depot aggregates ≥ N, no individual manager view Engineers / product teams How to build ADRs, paved road, fitness functions, examples Golden agent template, gateway onboarding Customers (SaaS) Buy / trust System card, security and residency, SLOs, roadmap, AI Act role split Deployer-support pack (A6)

Communication rules:

  • Lead with the decision you need.
  • Express uncertainty as ranges and probabilities, never as unearned precision.
  • Show what the system will not do. This is especially powerful with works councils and legal teams.
  • Separate facts, estimates and opinions.
  • Bring evidence links.

For driver monitoring, labour-law consultation duties (and Art. 26(7)-style worker information for high-risk systems; verify) make the works council a gate, not a courtesy. Plan it into the timeline.

docs.title: 4. Estimation under uncertainty
docs.text:
AI work carries unknowns that conventional estimation ignores:

  • Reachability of the quality bar. You do not know whether 90% groundedness on Bulgarian table questions is achievable until error analysis.
  • Data readiness surprises (A1 Lab 2).
  • Model behaviour changes across migrations.
  • Adoption.
  • Preview feature timing.

Techniques:

  • Ranges and reference classes. Estimate P50/P90 from your own history of similar work (the C-track increments are your first reference class), not from bottom-up optimism.
  • Spikes as uncertainty purchases. A 3-day spike that answers "can we reach 85% on table questions?" is worth more than 3 weeks of detailed planning. Price the spike against the value of the information.
  • Eval-gated milestones. Plan in stages that end with a measurable eval result: "M2: error analysis complete, failure taxonomy, baseline pass rates". Re-estimate at each gate. Commit to the next gate firmly and to the whole programme only in ranges.
  • Monte Carlo on task ranges (reuse A1's engine) to produce delivery-date distributions.
  • Make the cone of uncertainty visible to sponsors. Report "P(done by date)" and what would move it.
  • Agent-augmented estimates. Agent speed-ups vary by task type and team discipline (DORA "amplifier"; METR's evidence is mixed). Calibrate from your factory metrics (§6), not vendor claims.

docs.title: 5. Pre-sales and solution design
docs.text:
The architect in pre-sales converts a prospect's ambiguity into a credible, bounded proposal:

  1. Discovery. Run A1's workshop, compressed into 1–2 days. Assess data readiness and constraints (residency, isolation demands, integration with the prospect's telematics provider and TMS).
  2. Solution blueprint. Context diagram, tenant tier (pooled/bridge/silo), integration points (MCP/A2A), oversight design, AI Act role split, SLOs.
  3. PoC vs pilot vs MVP:
  4. A PoC answers one technical question (time-boxed, disposable).
  5. A pilot tests value with real users under production-like controls.
  6. An MVP is the first sellable increment.

Never let a PoC become production by drift. Avoid the demo trap, where a scripted happy path sets expectations the eval suite will not support. Demo against the prospect's own sampled data with eval scores shown. 4. Success criteria agreed in writing: eval thresholds on the prospect's golden set, adoption, cost per task, SLOs. 5. Proposal. Scope, assumptions (each with an owner), exclusions, risks, a pricing basis from A5 unit economics, a ranged timeline, and the change process.

docs.title: 6. Leading AI-augmented teams and governing the factory
docs.text:
Evidence to calibrate expectations:

  • DORA 2025: ~90% AI adoption. AI use is linked to higher throughput, but ensuring software works before delivery remains a challenge. The AI Capabilities Model names seven practices:
  • clear AI policy;
  • healthy data ecosystem;
  • accessible internal knowledge;
  • strong version control and code review;
  • user-centric focus;
  • platform engineering;
  • small batches.

Larger changesets raise instability. - Thoughtworks Radar Vol. 34 (Apr 2026): - Caution: coding throughput as a productivity measure, agent instruction bloat, coding agent swarms, "MCP by default", codebase cognitive debt. - Adopt: DORA metrics ("lines of code generated is misleading; rework rate exposes blind spots"), context engineering, curated shared instructions. - Trial: mutation testing, feedback sensors, sandboxed execution as default. - Slopsquatting. 19.7% of 2.23M AI code samples referenced hallucinated packages, and 43% of the hallucinated names recurred on every run. That makes package allow-lists a governance must.

The factory governance policy (one document, enforced by configuration):

  • Permissions and sandboxing:
  • coding agents run in sandboxes/devcontainers with egress allow-lists;
  • cloud agents push only to agent branches;
  • CI on agent PRs needs human approval;
  • production credentials are never available to coding agents.
  • Model and data policy:
  • approved models and providers for coding agents (BYOK to Foundry where required);
  • what code and data may leave the tenant;
  • no production personal data in agent contexts.
  • Supply chain:
  • package allow-lists;
  • lockfiles with hash verification;
  • new-package age rules;
  • skills, plugins and MCP servers vetted and pinned (A4 registry applies to the factory too).
  • Quality gates: human-owned acceptance tests, mutation score, eval gates, AI review plus human review. "Explain the diff" is required for high-risk changes.
  • Accountability: a human is accountable for every merged line. Agent-authored changes are attributable (assess Agent Trace-style attribution).

Metrics. Pair the DORA keys (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore; plus rework rate) with factory-specific measures:

  • first-pass acceptance rate of agent PRs;
  • iterations per PR;
  • mutation score;
  • escaped defects;
  • eval regression rate;
  • agent cost per merged PR;
  • review time per PR (a cognitive-load signal).

Reject lines of code, PR counts and "% code written by AI" as goals.

Operating model. The roles: - product teams owning agents and evals; - the platform team owning the paved road (A4); - governance owning tiers and boards (A6); - the architect owning decisions and fitness functions.

Add deliberate-practice rituals against skill atrophy: unaided katas, and diff-defence reviews where the human explains the agent's change.

docs.title: 7. A technology radar for your organisation
docs.text:
A radar records your organisation's positions, with evidence. It is not a copy of an industry radar.

  • Rings:
  • Adopt: default, paved road.
  • Trial: use on real work with an owner and exit criteria.
  • Assess: spike only.
  • Hold: don't start new work.
  • Quadrants for Trakia: platforms, tools, techniques, protocols/standards.
  • Every blip has: an owner, evidence (spike report, eval delta, cost), the date, the status of the underlying feature (GA/preview), and a review trigger.
  • Cadence: quarterly, plus extra passes after Microsoft Build (May/June) and Ignite (November), when previews typically move. Ignite 2026 is imminent at the time of writing.
  • Seed blips, from this course:
  • Adopt: MAF 1.0; APIM AI gateway policies; AI Search GA extractive KBs; failure-driven evals; mutation testing.
  • Trial: Foundry hosted agents (GA 9 Jul 2026); Foundry Toolboxes (GA); MCP C# SDK 2.0 (experimental APIs).
  • Assess: Foundry memory / Routines (preview); AI Search query planning (preview); ASSERT / Agent Control Specification; agentgateway; Spec Kit / OpenSpec.
  • Hold: Assistants API (retired); MCP sessions/SSE/sampling patterns; coding agent swarms.

docs.title: 8. Keeping current without drowning
docs.text:
• Signals that demand action:
  • model lifecycle notices (A5 watcher);
  • GA/preview transitions of features you depend on;
  • SDK major versions;
  • protocol revisions (MCP deprecation windows end ≥ 28 Jul 2027);
  • regulatory dates and guidance (A6);
  • security advisories.
  • Noise: leaderboards (saturating and largely vendor-run), launch-day benchmark claims, "X is dead" posts.
  • System:
  • an automated watch for lifecycle and release notes;
  • a monthly 2-hour "currency review" with the team;
  • quarterly radar updates;
  • nightly lab and product CI against live models (the course itself does this) to detect real breakage;
  • a personal reading list of primary sources: Learn "What's new" pages, the Architecture Center, protocol changelogs, the Hamel/Shankar evals FAQ, Anthropic engineering posts, DORA, Thoughtworks Radar.
  • Credentials as a forcing function. AB-100 for architects and AI-103 for developers both changed in 2026. Use them to check breadth, not as proof of depth.

docs.title: Lab 1 — ADR set and an ADR-driven change through the factory (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Write AI ADRs that hold up under review, then have an agent implement one under an architecture fitness gate.
  • Start state: branch a7/start. Contains all ADRs from A1–A6, the ADR linter with AI fields, and ArchUnitNET test project skeleton.
  • Steps:
  • Audit your existing ADRs against the AI fields (evidence, volatility, reversibility, review triggers). Fix the three weakest.
  • Write ADR-A7-001 "Adopt AI Search query planning for the manuals domain?" (preview). Use the A3 evidence and decide: assess / trial behind a flag / hold. Set triggers (GA date, eval delta ≥ X, latency budget).
  • Write ADR-A7-002 "Coding agents may not access production data stores". Encode it as fitness functions: an ArchUnitNET rule that no factory tool assembly references production connection configuration, plus a CI check on agent sandbox network policy.
  • Hand ADR-A7-003 ("move the 'similar incidents' helper behind the tenant-scoped retriever factory", from A3) to a coding agent (Copilot cloud agent or Claude Code headless). The agent must read the ADR, implement, and pass the fitness functions. Review and defend the diff yourself.
  • Break it: Instruct the agent (in a separate run) to "make the test pass quickly". Observe whether it weakens the architecture test or adds an exception. Your CODEOWNERS and hook configuration must block changes to fitness-function files without architect approval.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • All ADRs pass the linter.
  • The agent PR passes all fitness functions without modifying them.
  • The tamper attempt is blocked.
  • Your diff-defence note explains every changed line.
  • Stretch: Have an agent propose an ADR from an issue (context + options + evidence links) for a human to decide. Measure how often its option analysis misses a constraint you consider essential.

docs.title: Lab 2 — Fitness functions and an architecture review board (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Turn the A-track's quality bars into continuously evaluated fitness functions, and run a review with them.
  • Start state: a7/lab2-start.
  • Steps:
  • Create fitness.yaml with all functions from Concepts §2, each with a threshold, source, frequency and owner. Wire them into CI (PR, nightly, release) and a single dashboard.
  • Prepare an architecture review package for the SaaS GA release: WAF AI assessment delta, C4, ADR index, fitness status, cost model, DR report, evidence pack (A6).
  • Run the ARB for another team's package (peer exchange, as in peer review of 3 projects). Use the WAF AI assessment and the fitness dashboard. Produce findings classified by risk, with conditions written as new or tightened fitness functions.
  • Receive your own review and respond with accept/rebut per finding.
  • Break it: The instructor slips a "quality claim without evidence" into one package: "Bulgarian groundedness meets bar" with no judge validation. Reviewers must catch it. The rebuttal must not rely on unvalidated judge scores.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • Every fitness function runs automatically at its declared frequency.
  • The dashboard shows status.
  • Review findings are risk-rated with ≥ 2 conditions turned into fitness functions.
  • The evidence-free claim is caught.
  • Stretch: Compute the "fitness debt": functions failing or missing per characteristic. Present it as a single page for the steering committee.

docs.title: Lab 3 — One architecture, four audiences (≈3h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Communicate the driver-coaching pilot and the SaaS GA decision to executives, legal/DPO, the works council and engineers.
  • Start state: a7/lab3-start. Contains A6 DPIA, A5 unit economics, A2 C4 and the persona cards (CFO, DPO, works-council representative, lead engineer) with hidden concerns.
  • Steps:
  • Executive one-pager: decision asked, P50/P90 outcomes, top risks, asks.
  • Legal/DPO brief (2 pages): roles (provider/deployer), data flows, DPIA status, residency, sub-processors, open legal questions for them.
  • Works-council session (10 slides max, BG or EN): purpose, what the system will not do, who sees what, aggregation thresholds, retention, worker rights and complaint path, oversight, trial period and joint review. Prepare answers for "can managers see my score?" and "will this be used in dismissals?".
  • Engineering briefing: ADRs, paved-road changes, fitness functions.
  • Present to role-played stakeholders (instructor + peers, or the A1 persona simulator agents loaded with the new cards). Capture objections and update the artefacts.
  • Break it: The "CFO" asks to add per-driver insurance-risk scores to the pilot "since the data is there anyway". Respond in writing within 10 minutes, covering purpose limitation, A6 classification change, works-council impact and the alternative you can offer.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • All four artefacts are in architecture/comms/.
  • The audience rubric is ≥ Proficient for each.
  • Every factual claim links evidence.
  • The works-council deck has an explicit "will not do" section mirrored by enforced controls (A6 tests).
  • Stretch: Run the works-council deck through a Bulgarian-language readability and terminology review with an LLM judge calibrated on your glossary. Fix flagged jargon.

docs.title: Lab 4 — Pre-sales: Rhodope Haulage proposal (≈2.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Turn a prospect's RFP into a bounded, priced, honest proposal.
  • Start state: a7/lab4-start. RFP from Rhodope Haulage (fictional): 120 trucks, cross-border to Greece, wants incident triage and Bulgarian/Greek driver Q&A, insists on "dedicated data" and a 4-week go-live. Includes a 200-document sample corpus and 2 weeks of telematics.
  • Steps:
  • Run a compressed discovery with the simulated customer personas (A1 simulator). Assess data readiness on the sample: language mix and token counts. Note that Greek language support affects your Bulgarian-calibrated judges and the English-only safety services.
  • Write the solution blueprint: tenant tier (bridge vs silo given "dedicated data"), integrations, oversight, residency, AI Act role split.
  • Run a 2-hour PoC spike on the sample corpus: retrieval quality on 30 SME questions (prospect-provided reference answers). Report the eval scores honestly.
  • Estimate with ranges (Monte Carlo) and produce P(go-live in 4 weeks). Propose an eval-gated plan: a PoC gate, a pilot gate, and GA.
  • Write the proposal: scope, assumptions with owners, exclusions, risks, price from A5 unit economics plus onboarding effort, SLOs, change process.
  • Break it: The sales lead wants to promise "95% accuracy" in the proposal. Replace it with measurable, testable acceptance criteria tied to the prospect's golden set, and explain why in two sentences.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • The blueprint passes the AI-profile validator (A2).
  • PoC eval results are attached.
  • The estimate shows P50/P90 and P(4 weeks).
  • The proposal lists ≥ 8 assumptions with owners.
  • The price is traceable to the unit-economics model with margin shown.
  • Stretch: Prepare a one-page "why not 4 weeks" explanation for the prospect's CEO that keeps the deal alive. Offer a 4-week PoC/pilot milestone with what it will and won't deliver.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Govern the factory: policy, metrics, operating model and radar (≈2.5h)
docs.text:
• Goal: Put the agentic SDLC under explicit governance with measured outcomes, and publish Trakia's technology radar.
  • Start state: a7/lab5-start. Your C19 factory, GitHub/ADO access for metrics, and the radar template.
  • Steps:
  • Write factory-governance.md (Concepts §6) and enforce it:
    • devcontainer/sandbox egress allow-list;
    • agent branch protections;
    • required human approval for agent-PR CI;
    • package allow-list plus lockfile hash verification;
    • pinned MCP servers and skills;
    • prohibited production credentials (secret scanning plus environment rules).
  • Build the factory metrics dashboard from the GitHub/ADO APIs and telemetry: DORA keys, rework rate, first-pass acceptance of agent PRs, iterations per PR, mutation score, eval regression rate, escaped defects, agent cost per merged PR. Include 4 weeks of history from your own work.
  • Interpret the data: where does the factory amplify discipline, and where does it amplify chaos? Write three improvement actions tied to DORA AI Capabilities (e.g., smaller batches, better internal knowledge).
  • Define the operating model: roles and RACI (product, platform, governance, architect), rituals (currency review, radar review, diff-defence, unaided katas), escalation paths.
  • Publish Trakia Radar 2026-Q4: ≥ 16 blips across 4 quadrants, each with an owner, evidence, GA/preview status and a review trigger, plus the post-Ignite review date.
  • Break it: An agent run attempts to install a package not on the allow-list, with a plausible hallucinated name (slopsquatting drill). It must be blocked and logged, and the metrics must record the blocked event.
  • Acceptance criteria:
  • Policy enforcement is demonstrated by negative tests (egress, branch, package, credentials).
  • The dashboard renders from live data.
  • No vanity metric is used as a goal.
  • The radar passes the schema check (all fields) and is versioned in Git.
  • Stretch: Compare one month of agent cost per merged PR against first-pass acceptance by task type. Propose a routing policy (which tasks go to cloud agents, which to interactive work, which stay human-first).

docs.title: Kata
docs.text:
"30-minute AI ADR" (repeat weekly through the capstone).

You receive a decision prompt. Write a complete ADR in 30 minutes, with ≥ 3 options considered (incl. "do nothing / status quo" where meaningful), evidence needed (and what spike would produce it), volatility, reversibility, cost of change, review triggers and compliance impact.

Prompts rotate: - hosted agent vs self-hosted for a new SaaS feature; - adopt Foundry memory (preview) for driver preferences; - semantic cache for the analyst; - pin vs auto-upgrade for the judge model; - Bicep vs Terraform for tenant stamps; - A2A vs REST for a supplier integration; - move Fleet Analyst to a cheaper model role; - allow tenants to bring their own MCP servers.

A peer scores it with the ADR rubric in 5 minutes. Variation B ("estimation drill"): in 20 minutes, produce a P50/P90 range and the top 3 uncertainty drivers for a feature, plus the cheapest spike that would narrow the range most.

docs.title: Product increment — Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text:
The A-track deliverable set is complete: a defended architecture package for Fleet Ops Copilot's enterprise rollout and SaaS business:

  • business case (A1);
  • reference architecture and landing zone (A2);
  • knowledge platform (A3);
  • agent platform (A4);
  • reliability and FinOps (A5);
  • governance system (A6);
  • ADRs with AI fields, a continuously evaluated fitness-function suite, audience-specific communication artefacts, a priced pre-sales proposal template and the Trakia technology radar.

This package is the architect's half of the capstone baseline.

docs.title: Factory increment — your agentic SDLC
docs.text:
The architect now governs the factory:

  • an enforced governance policy (sandbox, egress, branches, packages, credentials, pinned skills and MCP servers);
  • a metrics dashboard combining DORA keys and AI-specific measures;
  • fitness functions protected by CODEOWNERS and hooks against agent tampering;
  • ADR-driven agent work;
  • a defined operating model with deliberate-practice rituals.

The factory is now an audited, measured system, and the A6 inventory references its coding agents.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient Expert Decision records Undocumented decisions ADRs with options ADRs with evidence, volatility, reversibility, review triggers Plus ADRs drive agent work and are enforced by fitness functions; superseded cleanly as evidence changes Fitness functions & reviews Manual checklist Some automated tests Full fitness suite incl. evals, cost, ASR, isolation, structure; risk-rated review with conditions Plus conditions automatically become fitness functions; "fitness debt" reported to steering Stakeholder communication One deck for all Adjusted tone Audience-specific artefacts with evidence links and explicit asks; works-council "will not do" backed by controls Plus handles live objections (e.g., scope creep into insurance scoring) with principled, documented responses Estimation & pre-sales Single-point estimates Ranges Monte Carlo, eval-gated milestones, PoC with honest scores, priced proposal with assumptions Plus value-of-information reasoning for spikes; proposal keeps the deal and the integrity Factory governance & currency Tool enthusiasm Some rules Enforced policy, outcome metrics (DORA + AI-specific), operating model, evidence-based radar Plus improvement actions linked to DORA capabilities; currency system with automated signals; radar used in decisions

Auto-checked: - ADR linter; - fitness-function wiring and frequency; - agent PR fitness pass and tamper block; - dashboard data freshness; - policy negative tests (egress, branches, packages, credentials); - slopsquatting block; - radar schema; - proposal traceability (price → unit-economics model); - PoC eval report presence.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• ADRs that record the decision but not the evidence, or that never expire. AI decisions need review triggers.
  • Quality claims without validated judges ("the LLM judge says 94%").
  • One presentation for every audience. Treating the works council as a formality.
  • Single-point estimates for AI work. Promising accuracy percentages instead of testable criteria.
  • PoCs that drift into production. Demos on curated happy paths.
  • Measuring the factory by lines of code, PR counts or "% AI-written". Ignoring rework and review load.
  • Agents allowed to edit the tests and fitness functions that judge them.
  • Copying an industry radar instead of recording your own evidence.
  • Chasing every launch; missing the one lifecycle notice that matters.
