docs.title: Assessment and gates
docs.text:
Release: 2026.11 · Duration: 6 h learner effort per gate (incl. oral) · Format: individual, practical, AI use expected · Assessed against: the Competency matrix (G1 and G2: Competent in their areas; G3: Proficient in at least 3 of 4 blocks with none below Competent, and all 12 areas evidenced through the blocks plus the G3 evidence pack, see §5)

This chapter tells you what each gate assesses, how it is run, how it is scored and what happens if you do not pass. It deliberately does not describe gate variants, test cases or planted faults: the gates measure how you handle work you have not seen.

docs.title: 1. Why gates, and what they measure
docs.text:
Gates turn the course into a mastery-learning system. You move to the next task class only after showing you can do the work at the required level, on cases you have not seen. Bloom's synthesis put feedback-corrective mastery learning alone at about 1 SD over conventional instruction. The gates are where that feedback and correction happen, so they report specific failure categories and include a resit path.

Because AI assistance is expected, a gate does not ask whether you can produce code. Agents produce code. A gate measures three things that agents do not supply on your behalf:

  1. Judgement. What to build, which failure matters, what to leave out, and which trade-off to accept.
  2. Verification. Whether your evals, tests and traces actually catch what's wrong. The hidden suites check your system, and a gate-sensitivity check tests your own gates.
  3. Explanation. Whether you can explain, predict and safely modify what you submitted. This is checked in the oral and the written explanation.
Gate After Task class Centre of gravity G1 C0–C5 Prompt feature + first tool + evals Build a feature through the Factory and prove it with failure-driven evals G2 C6–C11 RAG + tools + single agent + SQL + test automation Debug and extend a system you did not write, then defend a design decision G3 C12–C19 Production multi-agent system on Azure Operate, attack, migrate and redesign a running system under time pressure

Before G1, C0 includes a short, auto-marked gate-readiness quiz (pass 5/6, retake allowed) on the rules in this chapter. Use it to check that you understand the assessment components, the unaided segment, the ownership rule and the gate-sensitivity check before you need them.

docs.title: Environment and what is provided
docs.text:
• A private gate repository per candidate. It is created for you from the gate's start state. You get write access to your own gate repo only.
  • Bring your Factory. In the first 15 minutes you may copy your own Factory assets into the gate repo: AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md, .github/copilot-instructions.md, .github/agents/*.agent.md, skills, hooks, custom commands, CI templates and eval helpers. Product code from your own repo may not be copied. This tests whether your Factory is portable and whether it helps you.
  • Model access goes through the course AI gateway with a per-candidate key. It exposes the roles chat-fast, chat-reasoning and embedding (plus chat-local via Foundry Local on your machine) and enforces a per-candidate token quota, published in the brief and set at about 3× the reference solution's consumption. Exceeding it ends model access, not the gate. Cost discipline is part of the assessment.
  • Coding agents: any agent is allowed (Copilot, Claude Code, Codex or others). Internet access is allowed for documentation and package registries.
  • Visible vs hidden evals. Each gate ships a small visible smoke suite. The hidden suite runs in the grader pipeline after submission and is never shown. Results come back per stratum and per failure category, never per case.
  • Submission is a tag submit on your gate repo before the time box ends. The grader pipeline checks out that tag, so commits after the deadline are ignored.

docs.title: Required submission artefacts (all gates)
docs.text:
1. Code and Factory changes on the submit tag, with CI green on that commit.
  2. GATE-REPORT.md, using the template for the gate.
  3. Agent session evidence: exported transcripts or logs from your coding-agent sessions. Use the tool's export or your Factory's logging hook; the exact mechanism depends on the tool, so verify the current export options against current documentation. Session logs are not graded for style. They are used in the oral and to resolve integrity questions.
  4. A cost line: tokens consumed per role, taken from the gateway's per-key metrics.

docs.title: Scoring model
docs.text:
Every gate combines three elements:

  • Hard gates (must-pass, binary). Failing any hard gate means failing the gate, whatever else scores well. They protect non-negotiables: safety, security, honesty, a working build.
  • Hidden-eval thresholds, expressed relative to the reference solution run on the same day with the same pinned models, plus an absolute floor. Example: "≥ 90% of reference field accuracy and ≥ 0.85 absolute". Relative thresholds absorb model drift. Floors stop the bar falling when the reference has a bad day. The floors below are initial values and may be recalibrated for each course release.
  • Rubric (Novice / Competent / Proficient / Expert) on 5 criteria per gate, scored by two assessors from the artefacts and the oral.

Handling nondeterminism. The hidden suite runs 3 times. Quality metrics use the mean of the 3 runs. Hard-gate safety items use pass^3: they must pass in all three runs, because a safety property that holds two times in three does not hold.

Gate-sensitivity check. After submission the grader mutates your system in known ways, such as degrading the prompt, removing a validation step or disabling a filter. It then reruns your own CI eval gate. A gate that stays green under a mutation that breaks the hidden suite indicates hollow evals, and this feeds the "Evals & verification" rubric row. This is mutation testing applied to evals.

docs.title: Oral defense protocol (all gates)
docs.text:
• G1 runs 20 minutes and G2 and G3 run 30 minutes. Orals happen within 3 working days of submission, with two assessors, and are recorded for moderation (retained for 90 days; consent required).
  • Explain: the assessors pick 3 diff hunks from your submission at random (a script picks them, so the selection is not cherry-picked). For each, you explain what it does, why it is there, and what breaks if it is removed.
  • Predict: the assessor proposes a change, such as "set max iterations to 1", "remove this filter" or "swap to a model without tool calling". You predict the effect on behaviour, evals and cost before running anything.
  • Modify: you make one small, specified change live, with or without your agent, while narrating how you verify it.
  • Challenge: one or two questions on your report (G1, G2) or design (G2 defense, G3 Block D).
  • Ownership rule: if you cannot explain code you submitted, the "Directing & verifying agents" criterion is scored Novice, whatever the hidden-eval score. You own what you merge.

docs.title: Integrity stance
docs.text:
AI use is expected and does not need to be declared beyond the session evidence. What is not allowed:

Not allowed How it is detected or prevented Help from another human during the time box (including asking another person to prompt for you) Light proctoring of the unaided segment, oral consistency checks, and comparison of session logs with the commit history Sharing gate content or hidden-eval results with other learners Variants rotate, hidden cases are regenerated for each cohort, and leaked content is detectable in later submissions and public repos Eval gaming: special-casing hidden or visible cases, or detecting the grader Hidden cases are fresh paraphrases of the visible distributions; a grader check looks for case-specific branches and literal case strings; gaming is an automatic fail and an integrity review Copying product code from your own or others' earlier repos Repo provenance check against course repos (similarity scan); Factory assets are exempt Misrepresenting understanding The oral defense

What is not policed: which agent you use, how you prompt it, whether you read documentation, or whether you use an agent during the oral's "modify" step, as long as you narrate verification.

Proctoring is deliberately light. Only the short unaided segments are proctored (screen share or in-room). The rest relies on assessment design: hidden suites, the gate-sensitivity check, session logs and the oral. Recordings are processed as personal data under the cohort privacy notice.

docs.title: Accommodations
docs.text: Learners with documented needs receive up to +25% time on the practical blocks (institutional policy governs the exact amount). They can also choose an alternative oral format: written questions answered live in chat with follow-up, or more time to think. The constructs assessed do not change. Raise accommodation needs with the course team well before your gate week.

docs.title: 3. Gate G1 — Build a feature through the Factory, prove it with evals
docs.text: Prerequisites: C0–C5 complete and module acceptance checks green. Assesses: K1, K2, K7 and K8 at Competent, with K3 and K4 lightly.

docs.title: Format and time box (6 h total)
docs.text: Time Block Mode 0:00–0:15 Briefing, repo creation, bring-your-Factory copy — 0:15–0:45 Unaided segment. Read a set of provided traces and the baseline's prompt; answer short questions: predict behaviour and name failure modes No AI, proctored 0:45–4:15 Build: spec → tests → agent implementation → error analysis → evals → CI gate AI expected 4:15–4:50 Write GATE-REPORT.md (eval report + explanation) AI allowed; you are accountable for every claim 4:50–5:00 Tag submit — within 3 days Oral, 20 min (+ ~20 min prep) —

docs.title: What is provided
docs.text:
• A standard Fleet Ops Copilot at C5 level (streaming API, IChatClient pipeline, one tool, golden set v1, eval project, CI). It is not your own product, so everyone starts from the same baseline and you must work in code you did not write.
  • BRIEF.md: a one-page feature brief written as a business request, with acceptance criteria and non-functional requirements (latency, cost per request, BG/EN).
  • pilot-traces/: unlabelled traces from a synthetic "pilot", in OTel JSON plus readable Markdown.
  • evals/visible/: a small set of example cases for the feature.
  • Gateway key with token quota; Foundry Local available.

Each candidate receives one feature from a rotated set of variants. All variants sit in the Fleet Ops domain and exercise the same skills: typed extraction or grounded answering, tool calls, abstention or clarification, Bulgarian and English input, and resistance to instructions embedded in untrusted input.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
1. Specify before building. Update SPEC.md for the feature. Write human-owned acceptance tests (xUnit) before implementation: schema validity, tool-call expectations, and abstention behaviour. No exact-string assertions on model output.
  2. Build through the Factory. Direct your coding agent through plan → implement → verify. The commit history should show this shape, for example a plan commit or plan file, followed by implementation commits that turn tests green. Update AGENTS.md if you learn something the next agent session needs.
  3. Error analysis. Run the feature over the pilot traces' inputs. Open-code the first failure in each failing trace. Axial-code the notes into a taxonomy of ≥ 3 failure modes, with counts, in evals/error-analysis.md.
  4. Failure-driven evals. For each failure mode, write at least one evaluator, code-based where possible. Use an LLM judge only if no code check is possible, and say how you would validate it. Extend the golden set to ≥ 25 cases, including ≥ 5 BG and ≥ 3 abstention or clarification cases. Wire the evals into CI with response caching and a threshold that fails the build.
  5. Explain. GATE-REPORT.md (≤ 2 pages) covers the taxonomy, eval results, what you fixed, what you chose not to fix and why, cost per request measured, and one risk you see for production.

docs.title: What the hidden suite covers (G1)
docs.text:
The hidden suite is stratified so that a feature tuned only to the visible cases does not pass. Strata include typical English and Bulgarian input, Latin-script Bulgarian, missing or ambiguous fields, unknown entities, adversarial embedded instructions, out-of-scope requests, tool failures and long inputs.

Metrics: schema validity; field-level accuracy or citation correctness (depending on the variant); abstention correctness; tool-call correctness; leakage checks where customer-facing text is produced; p95 latency and cost per request on chat-fast.

docs.title: G1 hard gates
docs.text:
# Hard gate H1 submit builds, all your tests green in CI, no secrets (gitleaks), and the eval CI gate is present and enforced H2 Hidden schema validity ≥ 98% (mean of 3 runs) H3 Safety item, pass^3: the safety property stated for your variant holds in all three runs (for example a high recall on safety-critical items, no unsupported answers to dangerous requests, or zero customer-facing leaks of internal or driver data) H4 No exact-string assertions on model output in tests, and no case-specific branches (static check) H5 Oral completed, and the ownership rule not triggered

Hidden-eval thresholds (initial floors, may be recalibrated per release): primary accuracy metric ≥ 90% of reference and ≥ 0.80 absolute. Abstention correctness ≥ 0.80. Cost per request ≤ 1.5× reference.

docs.title: G1 rubric
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent (pass level) Proficient Expert Problem framing & spec Builds from the brief without a spec; acceptance criteria are implicit Spec and human-owned tests precede implementation and cover the brief's criteria Spec makes non-obvious decisions explicit (abstention policy, enum boundaries, BG handling); tests cover edge strata Spec anticipates failure modes later confirmed by the hidden suite and scopes them deliberately Directing & verifying agents Accepts agent output; can't explain parts of the diff Plan → implement → verify visible; tests and evals run before "done"; diff fully explained in the oral Constrains the agent effectively (memory-file updates, hooks, small batches); catches and corrects at least one agent error, with evidence in the logs Factory assets measurably sped up or de-risked the work, e.g. a reusable skill or check that a peer could adopt Error analysis & evals Generic metrics; evals written before looking at traces Taxonomy from traces; one evaluator per failure mode; CI gate works Code-based checks preferred and justified; golden set stratified; gate-sensitivity check catches ≥ 2 of 3 grader mutations Gate-sensitivity check catches all mutations; report quantifies residual risk per failure mode Engineering quality, security & cost Works on the happy path only Handles tool errors and unknown entities; keyless auth; cost per request measured Prompt laid out for caching; budgets or limits respected; injection-in-input handled by design (not "please ignore") Measurable cost and latency optimisation at equal quality, with the trade-off documented Explanation (written + oral) Describes what was done, not why Explains decisions and limitations correctly; predictions mostly right Predictions right, including cost effects; states what was deliberately not fixed and why Teaches: clear causal explanations a peer could act on; spots a weakness in their own design unprompted

Pass: all hard gates, every criterion ≥ Competent, hidden thresholds met.

docs.title: 4. Gate G2 — Debug and extend a RAG + agent system you did not write
docs.text: Prerequisites: G1 passed; C6–C11 acceptance checks green. Assesses: K2, K3, K4, K5, K7, K8, K10 and K12 at Competent.

docs.title: Format and time box (6 h total)
docs.text: Time Block Mode 0:00–0:20 Briefing; read ARCHITECTURE.md, the user complaints and the bug-report template — 0:20–0:40 Unaided segment. From provided traces, write hypotheses for the complaints. No fixing. No AI, proctored 0:40–3:20 Debug: find, root-cause and fix injected defects, each with a regression test or eval AI expected 3:20–4:50 Extend: implement the new capability with evals AI expected 4:50–5:20 GATE-REPORT.md: bug table + one ADR — within 3 days Design defense, 30 min (+ ~10 min prep) —

docs.title: What is provided
docs.text:
• Fleet Ops Copilot at C11 level. It includes BG/EN policy RAG (hybrid + rerank + allowed_groups), a Trakia MCP server, the Fleet Assistant agent (MAF, approval for actions), the Fleet Analyst text-to-SQL agent, the test pyramid, a mutation gate and Playwright tests.
  • A shared read-only AI Search index, plus local SQL Server 2025 (TrakiaOps small profile).
  • complaints/: user complaints written as support tickets.
  • traces/: production-like traces, some showing the injected defects.
  • The visible eval suite. Warning given in the brief: "the eval suite itself may not be trustworthy".

docs.title: Debug task
docs.text: The system contains several injected defects; the brief tells you that there are "at least five". They span retrieval, security, agent and tool behaviour, and verification (including the Factory's own gates). Root-cause each one from evidence, fix it, and protect the fix with a regression test or eval. Fixing every security-category defect is a hard gate.

docs.title: Extension task
docs.text: You also implement one new capability on the same system, with evals for its failure modes. The capability is specified in your brief and varies by variant. Expect it to involve consequential actions behind approval, cross-lingual retrieval, or multi-turn analytics, and to require that existing guarantees (permissions, read-only access, approvals, idempotency) still hold.

docs.title: Bug table (in GATE-REPORT.md)
docs.text: Symptom Evidence (trace id, query, metric) Root cause Fix (commit) Regression test / eval How I would have prevented it

docs.title: Design defense (30 min)
docs.text: You present one ADR from the gate, chosen from: retrieval fix approach, tool or approval design, or the eval-trust fix. The board probes it with changed constraints, for example a much larger corpus, an additional language, a model without tool calling, a new legal restriction on what may be indexed, or a halved cost budget. You must adapt the decision or explain why it holds.

docs.title: What the hidden suite covers (G2)
docs.text:
• Retrieval: BG/EN queries; recall@10 and nDCG@5.
  • Groundedness and citation correctness: a course judge, pinned and validated against human labels (TPR/TNR ≥ 0.85 on the course's labelled set).
  • Permission matrix: every role × restricted documents, through every endpoint.
  • SQL safety: write attempts, multi-statement batches, cross-scope access under RLS, prompt-injected SQL.
  • Tool-call accuracy on a set of tasks.
  • Approval enforcement: attempts at state change without approval.
  • Budget behaviour when a tool keeps failing.
  • Per-defect regression probes: hidden tests that fail if a defect is still present.
  • Extension suite for the new capability.

docs.title: G2 hard gates
docs.text:
# Hard gate H1 Build and CI green; no secrets; eval and mutation gates enforced (thresholds > 0) H2 Permission matrix: 0 leaks, pass^3, across all endpoints H3 SQL safety: 0 write or cross-scope statements executed, pass^3 H4 Approval: 0 unapproved state-changing tool calls, pass^3 H5 All security-category defects root-caused and fixed, each with a regression test H6 Design defense completed; ownership rule not triggered

Thresholds (initial floors): - ≥ 5 defects correctly root-caused and fixed, including all security ones. - Retrieval recall@10 and groundedness ≥ 90% of the reference. - Extension suite ≥ 85% of the reference. - The agent terminates within budget on 100% of the budget probes.

docs.title: G2 rubric
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent (pass level) Proficient Expert Diagnosis from evidence Changes code until symptoms vanish Each fix tied to trace or metric evidence and a stated root cause Uses traces, the eval breakdown and the permission matrix systematically; distinguishes symptoms that share a cause Finds all defects, including the eval-trust defect, and explains how each escaped the existing gates Fix quality & regression protection Fixes break other things; no tests Every fix has a regression test or eval; no new hidden-suite regressions Fixes address the class, not the instance (e.g., the filter enforced centrally for all endpoints) Adds a fitness function or gate that would have caught the class earlier (architecture test, policy check) Extension design Feature works on the happy path Meets the extension suite; approval and idempotency correct Tool design follows the course guidance (consolidated, paginated, actionable errors); evals cover the new failure modes Extension design is reusable as a pattern with documented trade-offs Verification & Factory use Trusts the visible suite Notices that the suite may lie and verifies it independently Repairs the eval harness and the CI gates; the gate-sensitivity check passes Uses agents in parallel effectively (e.g., one agent per hypothesis in worktrees), with evidence of verification discipline Design defense Restates what was built Justifies the ADR with alternatives and consequences Adapts correctly to 2 or more changed constraints with quantified reasoning (cost, recall, risk) Identifies the constraint that would flip the decision before being asked

Pass: all hard gates, all criteria ≥ Competent, ≥ 2 criteria at Proficient, thresholds met.

docs.title: 5. Gate G3 — Operate, attack, migrate, redesign
docs.text:
Prerequisites: G2 passed; C12–C19 acceptance checks green; a G3 evidence pack submitted 48 h before the gate. The pack links ADR-0012 (topology), ADR-0013 (retrieval choice), ADR-0014 (memory design), ADR-0015, ADR-0017, ADR-0018 and ADR-0019; the C13 context budget (docs/context-budget.md) with the context-rot and compaction results; the C14 eval report and judge cards; the C16 threat register and ASR report; the C18 risk file, DPIA delta, fairness report and FairnessGateTests output; and the C19 factory scorecard and agent policy. The pack is not scored on its own; the board uses it for Block D questions, and the bring-your-Factory rule (§2) applies to Blocks A–C.

Assesses: the pass decision follows the block rubric and pass rule below (≥ Proficient in 3 of 4 blocks). The 12 competency areas are evidenced across the blocks and the pack as mapped in the next table. An area not shown at Proficient does not fail a candidate who meets the pass rule, but it is recorded on your competency record as a remediation item before track entry. This is the last common gate before the tracks diverge.

How G3 evidences the 12 areas

Area Primary evidence in G3 K1 AI foundations Block C (token and cost-per-task deltas); Block A when the scenario involves cost K2 Prompting & structured I/O Block C (structured-output and tool-calling behaviour of the candidate model) K3 Retrieval & knowledge Block A when the scenario involves retrieval; otherwise ADR-0013, the C14 eval report's retrieval slices plus the Block D tenancy question on index isolation K4 Tools & MCP Block B (tool scope, MCP descriptions) K5 Agents & orchestration Block A (workflow behaviour); ADR-0012 K6 Context & memory Pack (ADR-0014, context budget, context-rot/compaction results) + mandatory Block D board question; Block B where memory is in scope K7 Evaluation Block C (pairwise per-failure-mode); Block A postmortem eval action K8 Testing & SDLC automation Factory use in Blocks A–C; C19 scorecard K9 Operations, observability & cost Block A K10 Security Block B K11 Responsible AI & governance Block D (AI Act classification); pack (risk file, DPIA delta, fairness report) + mandatory Block D board question on fairness K12 Architecture & business Block D

docs.title: Format and time box (6 h, one day, four blocks)
docs.text:
Time Block Mode 0:00–0:15 Briefing; access to your pre-provisioned Azure environment — 0:15–1:45 Block A — Production incident (90 min) AI expected; Azure SRE Agent (Reader mode) allowed 1:45–2:00 Break — 2:00–3:15 Block B — Red team (75 min) AI expected; [Python] PyRIT / AI Red Teaming Agent 3:15–4:30 Block C — Model migration (75 min) AI expected 4:30–4:45 Break — 4:45–5:45 Block D — Design review (20 min prep unaided, 40 min board) Prep proctored, no AI after Environment teardown (automated) —

The environment contains Fleet Ops Copilot at C19 level:

  • the multi-agent incident workflow
  • Container Apps and a Foundry hosted agent
  • the APIM AI gateway (PTU-style priority pool simulated with two backends, plus circuit breaker)
  • AI Search
  • App Insights with dashboards and KQL workbooks
  • guardrails
  • the CI/CD pipeline
  • a synthetic traffic generator running throughout

docs.title: Block A — Production incident (90 min)
docs.text:
At T0 an alert fires. Each candidate gets one incident scenario, drawn from a pool covering cost, latency and throttling, answer quality, security and model-lifecycle failures. The cause is planted; your job is to contain it and prove it.

Tasks: 1. Declare severity and impact within 15 minutes, as a status note in the incident channel file. 2. Mitigate first: feature flag, rollback, quota, block or failover. Record the time to mitigate. 3. Find the root cause from traces and KQL. SRE Agent hypotheses must be verified, not pasted. 4. Write a blameless postmortem (postmortems/G3.md) with timeline, impact, root cause, contributing factors, and action items. The action items must include a new eval or alert that would have caught this earlier and a Factory change if relevant.

Hard gate: the mitigation contains the impact within the block, and no destructive action is taken outside scope (no data deletion, no disabling of security controls as a "fix").

docs.title: Block B — Red team (75 min)
docs.text:
Target: a red-team variant of the environment with planted weaknesses that you are not told about.

Tasks: 1. Run an automated scan with the AI Red Teaming Agent or PyRIT [Python]. Note the region and feature limitations: agent-specific risk categories are cloud-only in five regions, and some agent types are not supported as targets, so manual attacks fill the gaps. 2. Write manual attacks in BG and EN. Content Safety classifiers are not validated for Bulgarian, so language-specific attacks matter. 3. Produce a scorecard with ASR per category, the top findings with reproduction steps, each mapped to OWASP LLM / ASI IDs, and mitigations ranked architecture-first. 4. Implement one architectural mitigation, such as removing a trifecta leg, constraining the action space or isolating a shared component, and re-measure ASR.

Hard gate: at least one valid, reproducible finding, plus a measured ASR before and after the mitigation.

docs.title: Block C — Model migration (75 min)
docs.text:
Notice: "The model behind chat-reasoning retires in 60 days. Candidate replacement: <model-X>." The candidate model is chosen to differ from the current one in a way that matters; finding out how is part of the task.

Tasks: 1. Swap by configuration only. Any code change must be justified. 2. Run the production eval suite pairwise. Report per-failure-mode pass rates, cost per task and p95 latency deltas, and the changes in caching behaviour. 3. Find the behaviour difference and decide whether to adapt the prompt or tool layer, choose a different candidate, or route by task. 4. Write a go/no-go memo: decision, evidence, a canary plan (APIM weighted backends: stages, metrics, rollback triggers), a PTU consideration (provisioned deployments are not auto-upgraded) and owner sign-offs.

Hard gate: the decision is supported by per-failure-mode data. A "go" based on aggregate scores alone, or with no rollback criteria, fails.

docs.title: Block D — Design review (60 min)
docs.text:
You receive a change request from Trakia's leadership that extends the product's business scope.

Prep (20 min, unaided): write a one-page design note on paper or in a plain editor with no AI.

Board (40 min): present for 10 minutes, then 30 minutes of questions.

The board probes your design but does not prompt you towards the issues. Expect to be asked about the architectural, regulatory and sequencing consequences of the request: what changes in the system, what the change means under the EU AI Act and GDPR (with legal questions flagged for counsel rather than answered as a lawyer), what to build first, what not to build, and what evidence each step requires.

Evidence-pack questions (mandatory, within the 30 min of questions). The board always asks at least two questions adapted to your own pack: one on your context and memory design (C13: ADR-0014 and docs/context-budget.md), and one on your fairness evidence (C18: the fairness report and its gate rule). Answer them from your own data.

Hard gate: you identify the principal architectural risk and the principal regulatory-classification implication of the change request without being prompted.

docs.title: G3 rubric (per block, plus one overall)
docs.text:
Criterion Novice Competent Proficient (pass level) Expert A — Incident Root-causes before mitigating; impact grows Mitigates within the block; root cause found Mitigation in under 30 min; root cause proven from traces; postmortem actions include an eval or alert and a Factory change Finds contributing factors beyond the planted cause (e.g., the missing gate that let the change ship) and fixes the class B — Red team Runs the scanner, reports raw output Valid findings with repros; ASR measured Findings mapped to OWASP; architectural mitigation reduces ASR measurably; BG attacks included Finds planted weaknesses the scanner misses; the mitigation generalises; residual risk is stated honestly C — Migration Aggregate score comparison only Pairwise per-failure-mode comparison; decision stated Finds the behaviour difference and handles it; the canary plan has metrics and rollback triggers; cost per task considered Proposes a durable migration process (eval set, routing, lifecycle watch) beyond this one swap D — Design review Describes features, not design Identifies the key architectural and regulatory issues when prompted Identifies both unprompted; sound design for the change; correct classification reasoning with obligations; answers the context/memory and fairness pack questions from their own data Reshapes the request (scope, intended purpose, sequencing) to reduce risk while preserving business value, with clear trade-offs Overall — Operational judgement Unsafe actions or unsupported claims Safe, but slow or unverified Safe, verified, communicates status clearly under time pressure Calm prioritisation; communication others could act on

Pass: all block hard gates, ≥ Proficient in at least 3 of the 4 blocks, none below Competent, and "Overall" at Proficient or above.

docs.title: 6. How hidden eval suites are kept fair
docs.text:
• Access. Hidden suites are held privately and are readable only by the grader pipeline and the gate owners. Your gate repo is checked out read-only by the grader.
  • Origin. Cases are written from failure modes observed in earlier cohorts, which is failure-driven evaluation applied to the course itself. Each cohort gets freshly paraphrased, human-reviewed cases, labelled by stratum.
  • Judges. Course LLM judges are pinned (model deployment plus judge prompt version) and validated against human-labelled examples per failure mode, with TPR and TNR ≥ 0.85 on a held-out split (course-designer threshold). A judge that drifts after a model change is re-validated before grading resumes.
  • Calibration. Before each release and after any pinned-model change, thresholds are checked against the reference solution so that the bar stays stable.
  • Determinism for appeals. Responses are cached so that a graded run can be re-run exactly for re-grading and appeals. The 3 graded runs themselves are uncached.
  • Feedback. You receive per-stratum scores, the failure categories hit, and which gate-sensitivity mutations your CI missed. You do not receive cases.
  • Retirement. A case that leaks is retired immediately, and its variant is rotated out.

docs.title: 7. Retake and appeal policy
docs.text:
Situation Policy G1 or G2 not passed Remediation plan agreed with a mentor (targeted labs and katas mapped to the failed criteria and strata). Resit with a different variant no earlier than 2 weeks later. G3: 1–2 blocks below Competent, or a block hard gate failed Block-level resit of the failed blocks only, within 3 weeks, with a different scenario. G3: 3 or more blocks failed Full G3 resit after remediation. Attempts Up to 3 attempts per gate per enrolment. After the third, you transfer to the next cohort at the start of the corresponding level, keeping the module credits already earned. Integrity breach The gate is void. An integrity review is held with the course lead, and the outcome may include removal. Not counted as an attempt if you are cleared. Appeals Within 5 working days, in writing, against specific rubric rows or hard-gate results. A second assessor who did not grade the attempt reviews the recording and artefacts; cached responses allow an exact re-run of the hidden suite. Technical failure (gateway outage, Azure incident) Time is extended by the outage duration, or a free resit is granted; the decision is logged.

Failing a gate is not a failure of the course design. It is the feedback-corrective loop working, and the resit path is part of the design.

docs.title: Competency matrix
docs.text:
AI Solution Developer & AI Solution Architect

Purpose: the single definition of what learners must be able to do at each stage, used for self-assessment, lab rubrics, gate rubrics, capstone grading and portfolio statements. · Release: 2026.11 · Owner: course lead (changes go through the quarterly course review)

docs.title: 1. How to read this matrix
docs.text:
Twelve competency areas (K1–K12) cover the AI-specific part of the job. General software engineering (Git, testing basics, HTTP, SQL) is an entry prerequisite and is not repeated here.

Four levels, each defined by observable behaviour. Every cell describes what an assessor can see in a repo, a trace, a CI run, a document or an oral answer. Knowledge alone ("knows what RAG is") never qualifies.

Level General meaning Typical point in the course SFIA-style analogue (course-designer inference) Novice Follows a worked example. Can name the concept and reproduce the happy path with guidance. Doesn't yet see failure modes. During Level 1 Level 2 (assist) Competent Builds the thing independently from a spec, recognises the common failure modes when shown evidence, and fixes them with standard techniques. Required at G1 (L1 areas) and G2 (L2 areas) Level 3 (apply) Proficient Chooses among alternatives with measured trade-offs, anticipates failure modes before they happen, verifies systematically and explains decisions in writing. Evidenced at G3 in all core areas (blocks + evidence pack; pass rule and area mapping in Assessment and gates §5) Level 4 (enable) Expert Designs the verification and the system together, handles novel situations and conflicting constraints, teaches and sets standards for others, and defends decisions under questioning. The Expert level is split by role. Required at capstone in the learner's track-critical areas Developer: Level 4–5 · Architect: Level 5–6

Expert is split by role. At Expert level the Developer and the Architect are expected to do different things, not more or less of the same thing. The Developer goes deeper into engineering (implementing, measuring, hardening). The Architect goes broader in judgement (deciding, constraining, governing across systems and teams). Both must still meet Proficient everywhere.

Graduation requirements: - Proficient in all 12 areas. - Expert in the 6 track-critical areas for your track, marked ● in §3. - No area below Proficient at the capstone defense.

Evidence rules: 1. A behaviour counts only if there is an artefact or an observation: a commit, a CI run, an eval report, a trace, a document, or an oral answer recorded on the assessor's sheet. 2. AI assistance is expected. The learner must be able to explain and modify the evidence (see the integrity stance in Assessment and gates). 3. A single observation of a behaviour is enough to reach Novice or Competent. Proficient and Expert need consistency across at least two different contexts, such as a lab and a gate, or the product and the capstone.

docs.title: K1 · AI foundations (models, tokens, economics, limits)
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Calls a model from code. Can state that tokens, not words, are billed and limited. Repeats a lab measurement when given the script. Competent Predicts and then measures token counts and cost for EN vs BG text. Handles finish_reason=length and context overflow. Demonstrates that temperature 0 is not deterministic and stops asserting exact strings in tests. Picks a model role (fast-small / workhorse / frontier reasoning) for a task and states why. Proficient Builds a quality × cost × latency table for one task across ≥ 3 models, including a local one, and a reasoning-effort sweep. Recognises cases where an LLM is the wrong tool (tabular prediction, high-volume deterministic classification, fixed-layout extraction) and proposes the alternative with evidence. Distinguishes per-token price from per-task cost. Expert — Developer Diagnoses quality regressions to their mechanism (context position, tokenisation, sampling, effort, cache-busting prompt layout) from traces. Runs model bake-offs as reproducible eval jobs. Sizes local or self-hosted models (memory by total parameters, compute by active parameters for MoE, quantisation trade-offs). Expert — Architect Sets model-selection policy by capability class rather than by name. Writes the "LLM vs classical ML vs specialised service" decision as an ADR that survives model churn. Explains these trade-offs to non-technical stakeholders without overstating capability. Treats vendor benchmarks as saturating and mostly vendor-run, and requires domain evals.

Typical evidence: C1 measurement notebook, C1/C2 explanation write-ups, D1 sizing sheet, A1 portfolio memo.

docs.title: K2 · Prompting & structured I/O
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Writes a system prompt and few-shot examples from a template. Uses structured output when told to. Competent Defines JSON-Schema-constrained outputs mapped to C# types. Measures schema-failure rate vs free-text parsing. Versions prompts in the repo. Writes tool descriptions that a reviewer finds unambiguous. Proficient Lays out prompts for caching (static prefix first) and verifies cache hits in telemetry. Designs abstention ("not in sources") and clarification paths. Handles BG/EN mixed input. Writes prompt changes as reviewable diffs with eval deltas. Expert — Developer Builds prompt and schema middleware (validation, repair, retry with budget) in the MEAI pipeline. Detects prompt brittleness with perturbation evals. Treats prompts, tool schemas and judge prompts as versioned, tested artefacts with owners. Expert — Architect Sets organisation-wide conventions for prompt and schema management (registry, versioning, review, ownership). Decides where structured contracts sit between systems, and when to use typed decision models or classifiers instead of free generation.

Typical evidence: C3 labs, prompts/ history, C15 prompt registry, A7 standards document.

docs.title: K3 · Retrieval & knowledge
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Embeds documents and runs a vector query following a lab. Explains chunks and similarity in their own words. Competent Builds hybrid retrieval (BM25 + vectors with RRF) plus a reranker, with citations. Implements security trimming from identity claims (allowed_groups) and proves that no out-of-role document is returned. Knows that switching embedding models means re-embedding the corpus. Proficient Evaluates retrieval (recall@k, nDCG) separately from generation (groundedness, completeness) on a stratified golden set that includes abstention, permission and injection cases. Compares parsing options on tables and scans. Chooses a vector store via an ADR. Applies contextual chunking or quantisation where measurements justify it. Expert — Developer Climbs the retrieval ladder empirically (vector → hybrid → rerank → contextual → agentic retrieval) and stops where the evals plateau. Implements blue/green re-indexing with index aliases. Tunes BG/EN retrieval with language-specific analysers and evals. Decides on GraphRAG against measured global-question performance. Expert — Architect Designs the enterprise knowledge platform: source-of-truth ownership, data readiness, index lifecycle, permission propagation (GA pattern vs preview native ACLs), residency, cost model (fixed search units vs database capacity), and multi-tenant index strategy. Decides "no RAG" when the corpus fits in a cached prompt (roughly < 200k tokens).

Typical evidence: C6/C7 ADR and eval report, C13 GraphRAG decision, A3 knowledge-platform design.

docs.title: K4 · Tools & MCP
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Registers a C# method as a tool with AIFunctionFactory and observes the model calling it. Can explain that the model requests tool calls and the application executes them. Competent Designs consolidated, namespaced tools with pagination, truncation and actionable errors, and shows they beat CRUD-style tools on an eval set. Ships an MCP server with the C# SDK on the 2026-07-28 spec, consumed by the app and a coding agent. Proficient Proves statelessness (several replicas behind round-robin). Applies Entra OAuth to MCP. Propagates trace context via _meta. Recognises outdated 2025-era MCP patterns (handshake, sessions, SSE, sampling) and migrates them. Picks a hosting model (Functions vs ACA vs APIM export) with justification. Expert — Developer Builds code-as-tool-interface variants and measures the token savings. Implements tool-definition pinning and hashing against rug pulls. Writes MCP Apps or Tasks-extension features where they fit. Builds tooling for coding agents, such as an MCP server over the project's own schema and tickets. Expert — Architect Designs the tool and MCP topology for an organisation: a gateway (APIM / toolbox) with per-tool policy via Mcp-Method/Mcp-Name headers, a server registry, approval and pinning, identity (on-behalf-of vs agent identity), and the seams with low-code (Copilot Studio) and A2A peers. Rejects "MCP by default" when a direct API call is simpler.

Typical evidence: C3/C8 labs, C16 poisoned-MCP lab, A4 integration design.

docs.title: K5 · Agents & orchestration
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Runs a MAF agent with tools from a template. Distinguishes a workflow (predefined code paths) from an agent (model-directed). Competent Writes a tool loop by hand and ports it to MAF. Adds explicit termination: max iterations, token and cost budgets, timeouts, a final-answer schema, repetition detection. Adds human approval for consequential actions. Proficient Chooses the lowest rung on the complexity ladder (direct call → workflow → single agent → multi-agent) using eval, cost and latency evidence. Implements checkpointed, resumable workflows with HITL. Explains when multi-agent helps (read-heavy, parallel) and when it hurts (write-heavy, coupled), with the ~15× token cost in view. Expert — Developer Builds durable, long-running agents (persisted sessions, HITL waits without compute). Hosts them (Foundry hosted agents / Container Apps). Engineers reliability (pass^k, simulators, fault injection). Builds custom harnesses with the Copilot SDK or Claude Agent SDK where they fit. Expert — Architect Defines the agent platform: which agent types are allowed where (prompt, hosted, low-code), registry and lifecycle (agents as code, immutable versions), inter-agent trust boundaries (A2A, signed agent cards), and an autonomy policy that ties levels of agency to risk class and oversight.

Typical evidence: C9/C12 labs and ADRs, D2/D7 reliability report, A4 platform design.

docs.title: K6 · Context & memory
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Keeps chat history in a session. Can explain why the context window is a budget. Competent Demonstrates context rot and "lost in the middle" with a lab measurement. Implements tool-result clearing and summarisation-based compaction. Scopes session memory per user. Proficient Chooses between compaction, structured notes, sub-agents and just-in-time retrieval for a long-horizon task on measured outcomes. Designs memory with TTL, GDPR "forget", write-time validation against poisoning, and multi-session evals. Decides what goes in memory files vs skills vs hooks for coding agents. Expert — Developer Builds context-assembly pipelines with explicit token budgets per section and tests them. Implements procedural memory distilled from trajectories, with evaluation of the gain. Diagnoses agent failures caused by context composition from traces. Expert — Architect Sets memory and retention policy across products (what may be remembered, where, for how long, under whose control). Aligns that policy with the DPIA, residency and the AI Act logging requirements. Decides platform memory (preview) vs owned memory stores with lock-in and audit in view.

Typical evidence: C13 labs, C4/C19 Factory memory files, A6 retention policy.

docs.title: K7 · Evaluation
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Runs a provided eval suite and reads its report. Competent Reads ≥ 30 real traces before writing evaluators. Open-codes failures and builds a golden set from them. Writes binary, code-based checks where possible. Gates CI on eval thresholds with response caching. Proficient Builds a failure taxonomy through axial coding. Writes one judge per failure mode, validated against human labels with TPR and TNR on separate dev and test splits. Builds trajectory evals from spans. Runs a pairwise model-migration comparison per failure mode. Refreshes the eval set from new traces on a schedule. Expert — Developer Builds evaluators for others' systems (the "green agent"). Builds simulated-user harnesses (τ-bench style) reporting pass^k. Calibrates judges for Bulgarian where vendor classifiers are English-only. Detects eval overfitting and leakage. Keeps eval cost under control. Expert — Architect Defines the organisation's evaluation policy: which evidence is required for release, migration and risk files, who owns golden sets, how evals feed AI Act technical documentation and ISO/IEC 42001 evidence, and the acceptance thresholds tied to business risk. Rejects generic "helpfulness" scores as release criteria.

Typical evidence: C5/C14 eval reports, G1–G3 hidden-eval results, capstone eval report, A6 evidence pipeline.

docs.title: K8 · Testing & SDLC automation (the Factory)
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Uses a coding agent in chat or agent mode to scaffold and explain code, and reviews the diff before committing. Competent Maintains short, curated AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md files. Runs plan → implement → verify. Writes failing acceptance tests that the agent must satisfy. Configures permissions and a format/build hook. Requires the agent to run tests and evals before claiming done. Proficient Runs test-first specs with a mutation-score gate and E2E test agents, and audits healer changes. Picks the right spec ceremony for the change size. Runs parallel agents in worktrees. Puts AI review and CodeQL autofix in CI under branch protection. Can explain every merged line. Expert — Developer Builds custom agents, skills, plugins and harnesses (Copilot SDK / Claude Agent SDK). Runs unattended agents safely: sandboxes, least-privilege tokens, egress allow-lists, package allow-lists against slopsquatting. Measures first-pass acceptance, rework and cost per merged PR, and improves them. Expert — Architect Governs the Factory across teams: agent permission and sandbox policy, required gates, data and model choices for coding agents, Azure Repos vs GitHub capability differences, DORA plus AI-specific metrics, an operating model, and a review practice that prevents codebase cognitive debt.

Typical evidence: Factory repo history, agent session logs, C11/C19 labs, G1 oral, A7 governance policy.

docs.title: K9 · Operations, observability & cost
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Turns on OTel in MEAI and finds a model call in the Aspire dashboard. Competent Traces a request across app, agent, tools and MCP server. Writes KQL for latency, errors and token usage. Sets budgets and TPM limits and keeps lab spend within them. Proficient Attributes cost per task, per feature and per tenant. Keeps trace content capture off by default and documents why. Versions prompts and models with canary promotion. Rehearses a model migration with a go/no-go memo. Diagnoses an incident from traces within a time box. Expert — Developer Engineers cost and latency down (caching, routing and cascades, batch, semantic cache where safe) at equal eval scores. Load-tests 429 behaviour and failover. Pins semconv versions and maps attributes in the Collector. Writes runbooks and postmortems that others can execute. Expert — Architect Designs the AI gateway (quotas, chargeback, priority pools PTU → PAYG, circuit breaking), the FinOps model (PTU vs PAYG break-even, showback), the model-lifecycle process (retirement watch, 60-day plan, PTU not auto-upgraded), SLOs and DR by reconstruction. Checks cost models against actuals.

Typical evidence: C15/C17 dashboards, G3 incident block, D5 cost report, A5 lifecycle and FinOps plan.

docs.title: K10 · Security
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Keeps secrets out of the repo and uses keyless auth. Can state that prompt injection is unsolved at the model level. Competent Identifies the lethal trifecta in a design and removes one leg. Implements least-privilege tools, approval for state changes and conversation-ownership checks (BOLA). Runs safety evaluators in CI. Proficient Threat-models with STRIDE mapped to OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025) and Agentic Top 10 (ASI01–ASI10). Applies injection design patterns (plan-then-execute, dual LLM, action selector, context minimisation). Runs red-team scans and reports attack success rate (ASR) before and after fixes. Uses Foundry guardrails as a second layer, not the first. Expert — Developer Builds and runs attack suites (PyRIT / AI Red Teaming Agent [Python], custom attacks in BG/EN). Implements sandboxed code execution with egress blocks. Implements MCP pinning, memory-poisoning defences and package allow-lists. Fixes classes of vulnerability, not single instances. Expert — Architect Designs agent identity and access (Entra Agent ID, Conditional Access, OBO vs app identity), network isolation (private endpoints, egress firewall), trust boundaries between agents and tenants, and the security review process. Applies the Agents Rule of Two in design reviews.

Typical evidence: C16 threat model and ASR report, capstone red-team swap, G3 red-team block, A4/A6 designs.

docs.title: K11 · Responsible AI & governance
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Adds an AI disclosure to the UI. Knows the EU AI Act exists and has risk tiers. Competent Classifies a feature under the AI Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, identifying prohibited, high-risk (Annex III), transparency (Art. 50) and minimal-risk cases. Recognises the provider vs deployer role. Writes a DPIA-relevant data flow. Recognises that Trakia's driver monitoring touches Annex III employment use cases. Proficient Produces a risk file: intended purpose, classification rationale, data governance, logging, human-oversight design, accuracy and robustness evidence from evals, and transparency notices. Designs oversight that works (interrupt and override, not rubber-stamping). Knows the current dates (Art. 50 from 2 Aug 2026; Annex III from 2 Dec 2027; Annex I from 2 Aug 2028) and that the Bulgarian implementing details need checking at source. Expert — Developer Implements oversight, logging and transparency mechanisms as tested features. Produces evidence (eval reports, red-team scorecards, model and system cards) automatically from the pipeline. Builds bias and performance-disparity evals, e.g. BG vs EN users. Expert — Architect Designs the AI management system (ISO/IEC 42001-style): inventory, risk classification process, roles, controls mapped to the AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001, an evidence pipeline and change control. Shapes the intended purpose to avoid unnecessary high-risk classification where that is legitimate. Advises leadership on the regulatory timeline and where legal counsel is required.

Typical evidence: C18 risk file, capstone AI Act risk file, A6 governance design.

docs.title: K12 · Architecture & business
docs.text:
Level Observable behaviours Novice Draws a context diagram of the product and writes a first ADR from a template. Competent Writes ADRs with real alternatives and consequences. Maintains C4 context and container diagrams as text. Estimates the monthly cost of a feature from token measurements. Proficient Deploys with IaC behind a gateway with private networking. Writes a cost model that matches actuals within an agreed tolerance. Writes a DR plan for components without native DR (reconstruction from agents as code) and runs a drill. Runs a WAF AI assessment and acts on findings. Expert — Developer Shapes technical architecture from below: proposes ADRs backed by measurements, prototypes risky decisions as spikes with evals, enforces architecture with fitness functions (ArchUnitNET/NetArchTest) and explains trade-offs to architects and product owners. Expert — Architect Moves from business problem to a scored use-case portfolio, ROI and TCO, build/buy/extend (least operational responsibility first), reference architecture and landing zone, multi-tenancy, a roadmap and an operating model (CoE). Defends these decisions to a review board and to non-technical stakeholders. Keeps the design simple enough to operate.

Typical evidence: ADR log, C17 deployment, A1–A7 deliverables, capstone architecture package and defense.

docs.title: 5. Using the matrix
docs.text:
• Self-assessment. At the start, at each gate and before the capstone, learners rate themselves per area and attach one evidence link per rating. Mentors compare the ratings with gate results. Large gaps in either direction, particularly over-confidence, are discussed in mentor sessions. The METR finding that developers felt ~20% faster while measuring ~19% slower is the motivating example of why self-perception is not evidence.
  • Rubric derivation. Every module rubric (Novice / Competent / Proficient / Expert) is derived from the relevant cells here. If a module rubric contradicts the matrix, the matrix wins and the module is fixed in the next release.
  • Portfolio statements. Graduates describe themselves by area and level with linked evidence, e.g. "Evaluation: Expert (Developer) — built a calibrated BG groundedness judge, TPR 0.91 / TNR 0.88 on held-out test split; capstone eval report link". Graduates do not use generic claims like "experienced in GenAI".
  • Hiring-side reading. Employers should read the Expert level as "demonstrated on realistic, assessed tasks with synthetic data", not as years of production ownership.

docs.title: Course overview
docs.text:
AI Solution Developer & AI Solution Architect — from developer to expert

Course release: 2026.11 (content as of October 2026) · Total effort: ≈ 475 h per learner (core 274 h + one expert track ≈ 120 h + joint capstone 80 h) · Stack: Azure + .NET 10 first, with bounded Python and Node.js · Format: learning by doing on one evolving product, gated by hidden eval suites, code review and design defense

docs.title: The promise, stated plainly
docs.text:
You are a working software developer who is new to AI. Over about 475 hours of deliberate practice you will build, test, secure, ship, operate and govern one realistic LLM and agentic product, Fleet Ops Copilot for the fictional logistics company Trakia Freight. You will build it through your own agentic delivery pipeline (the Factory), where coding agents do most of the typing and you specify, constrain and verify their work. You then go deeper in one of two expert tracks, Developer or Architect, and defend a team capstone for a new client in a different domain in front of a review board. "Expert" here means demonstrated, assessed competence on expert-level tasks. You will diagnose failures from traces, design verification before implementation, choose the lowest-complexity architecture that passes the evals, and defend each decision with evidence about cost, risk and quality. It does not mean seniority. Seniority still comes from years of running production systems. What the course gives you is the habits, the portfolio and the judgement that make those years count, plus an honest record of what you can and cannot do yet.

What the course is not: a tour of Azure products (they will be renamed again), a prompt-tricks course, an ML-research course (you will not train foundation models), or a certification cram. Certification alignment is mapped below, but passing a vendor exam is a side effect and not the goal.

docs.title: 1. Who it is for
docs.text:
Entry profile: a working developer in any language who is comfortable with Git (branches, PRs, rebase), HTTP/REST and JSON, SQL (joins, aggregation, indexes), a unit-test framework, and containers at the "run a compose file" level. No prior AI or ML knowledge is assumed. If you don't know C#, C0 teaches enough to start, and the language grows with the labs.

Not a fit (yet): people who have never shipped code to a shared repository, people who want a no-code path (Copilot Studio is covered as an architecture option, not as a learning medium), and ML researchers who want model training (see the AWS AIP-C01 boundary below: this is an AI-engineering course, not ML engineering).

docs.title: Entry check (≈ 2–3 h, self-administered, honour-based)
docs.text:
Complete all four without an AI assistant. The point is to calibrate your fundamentals, because the course later depends on your ability to judge code you did not type.

  1. Build: in any language, implement GET /vehicles/{id}/trips?from=&to= over the provided SQLite file entry/trakia-mini.db. Return 404 for unknown vehicles and 400 for an invalid date range, and paginate. Write at least 5 unit or integration tests. Open a PR against your own fork.
  2. Query: write one SQL query that returns, for each depot, the 3 vehicles with the highest harsh-braking events per 100 km in the last 30 days, ties broken by vehicle id.
  3. Read: given a 150-line C# file and a 100-line Python file (entry/read/), answer 6 questions about behaviour, including one that hides an off-by-one error and one that hides an async/await mistake.
  4. Operate: run the provided docker compose up, find why the API container restarts (the cause is in the logs), and fix it.

Pass indicator: all four done in under 3 hours, tests green. If you need more than about 5 hours, close the gap first (Git, SQL and testing fundamentals). The course will not teach them and the gates assume them.

Hardware and accounts: 16 GB RAM minimum and 32 GB recommended (Foundry Local models plus Docker plus SQL Server; exact model memory needs vary, so verify against current documentation (the Foundry Local model list)). Docker or Codespaces, a GitHub account, an Azure subscription where you can create resource groups (Section 8), and access to at least one coding agent (GitHub Copilot with agent mode and/or Claude Code).

docs.title: 2. Exit competencies
docs.text:
A graduate can do the following, and every item is assessed by a gate, a lab acceptance check or the capstone (see Competency matrix for the full framework):

  1. Explain and predict model behaviour in engineering terms. Covers tokens and their cost (including token-heavier Bulgarian text), sampling nondeterminism (temperature 0 is not deterministic in production serving), reasoning effort, context budgets and when not to use an LLM.
  2. Build provider-agnostic AI features in .NET on Microsoft.Extensions.AI, where swapping a model (cloud ↔ Foundry Local ↔ any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) is a configuration change followed by a green eval run.
  3. Design retrieval that is hybrid, reranked, permission-trimmed and multilingual, and measure retrieval and generation separately.
  4. Design tools and MCP servers for agents (consolidated, paginated, actionable errors). Ship a stateless MCP server on the 2026-07-28 spec.
  5. Choose the lowest-complexity architecture that passes the evals: prompt → workflow → single agent → multi-agent. Implement it with Microsoft Agent Framework with budgets, checkpoints and human approval.
  6. Run failure-driven evaluation: error analysis on real traces, a failure taxonomy, binary evaluators per failure mode, LLM judges calibrated against human labels (TPR/TNR), trajectory evals and CI gates.
  7. Operate AI systems: end-to-end OpenTelemetry traces, cost per task, model migration with a go/no-go based on per-failure-mode evals, and incident diagnosis from traces.
  8. Secure agentic systems architecturally: lethal-trifecta analysis, least agency, agent identity, guardrails as a second layer, MCP supply-chain controls, and red teaming with measured attack success rate.
  9. Govern: classify a system under the EU AI Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, produce the risk file, design human oversight and map practice to NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001.
  10. Deliver through agents: run a governed agentic SDLC (repo memory, skills, hooks, test-first specs, mutation and eval gates, cloud agents from issues to PRs, AI review, SRE agent) and be able to explain and defend every merged line.
  11. Developer track: engineer for performance, cost, durability and reliability (pass^k, simulators, fault injection), customize models when evals justify it, and build your own agent tooling.
  12. Architect track: move from business problem to portfolio, business case (ROI and TCO, build/buy/extend), reference architecture and landing zone, multi-tenant gateway, model-lifecycle and DR plan, FinOps, a governance system and a programme operating model, and defend all of it in front of a review board.

docs.title: 3. Two roles, one technical core
docs.text:
The 2026 job market and the 2026 certification overhaul describe two related roles. Analyses of US postings (one recruiter-analytics source, so treat as directional) show the AI engineer as an applied builder: Python 62%, cloud 55%, foundation models 51%, with RAG and observability in the core stack. The AI architect appears as "a design role with a build component, not the reverse": cloud platforms 60.9%, Python 43.9%, observability 38.9%, foundation models 37.8%, RAG 28.1%, CI/CD 26.2%, Azure named in 42.5% of postings, and typically about 7 years of experience. Microsoft's certifications split the same way: AI-103 (AI Apps and Agents Developer) and AB-100 (Agentic AI Business Solutions Architect; "Expert" suffix in the title: verify against current documentation).

AI Solution Developer AI Solution Architect Primary output Working, evaluated, observable, secure AI features and agents in production Decisions and the structures that make many teams' AI features safe, affordable and sustainable Owns Implementation, eval suites and judges, tool and MCP design, performance and cost per task, reliability engineering, the team's Factory Use-case portfolio and business case, reference architecture and landing zone, gateway and tenancy model, model-lifecycle and DR strategy, governance system, ADRs, review process Typical artefacts Code, evals, traces, red-team fixes, runbooks, postmortems ADRs, C4 models, threat models, cost models, DR plans, AI Act risk files, WAF AI assessments, stakeholder memos Decides How (within constraints): retrieval strategy, agent loop design, prompt and context layout, which failure deserves an evaluator Whether and what (setting constraints): build/buy/extend, which models and regions, risk appetite, tenancy, SLOs, budgets, oversight design Success measured by Hidden-eval scores, pass^k, mutation score, cost per task, escaped defects Review-board outcomes, cost-model accuracy vs actuals, DR drill results, audit readiness, adoption and ROI evidence Target level at exit (SFIA-style, course-designer inference) Level 4–5 ("enable", "ensure and advise") Level 5–6 ("ensure and advise", "initiate and influence")

Overlap is deliberate. Both roles take the same 274-hour core, and architects build everything developers build in the core. An architect who cannot read a trace, run an eval or spot a lethal trifecta in a design produces slideware. A developer who cannot write an ADR, estimate cost per task or explain the AI Act classification of a feature cannot be trusted with autonomy. The tracks differ in depth of engineering (D) versus breadth of judgement (A), and they meet again in the capstone, where mixed teams must make both work together.

docs.title: 4. Course structure
docs.text: The core is sequential because each module adds a product increment that the next one builds on. Inside the Developer track the order is recommended, not enforced (D5 recommends D1; D7 recommends D2 and D5). The Architect track is effectively sequential, because each module's prerequisites name its predecessors (A3 needs A2; A4 needs A2–A3; A5 needs A1, A2 and A4; A6 needs A1–A5; A7 needs A1–A6). Learners may take both tracks (+≈ 120 h). The capstone requires G3 and at least 4 of the 7 modules of one track, with the remaining track modules allowed to run in parallel (see pacing).

docs.title: 5. The running product and the Factory
Trakia Freight and Fleet Ops Copilot
docs.text:
Trakia Freight is a fictional mid-size logistics company headquartered in Plovdiv, Bulgaria. It has about 400 trucks, about 600 drivers, three depots (Plovdiv, Sofia, Varna) and cross-border EU routes. All data is synthetic and GDPR-safe, and it is generated by seeded tools in the lab repo (trakia-fleetops, /data):

  • SQL Server 2025 database TrakiaOps: vehicles, pseudonymized drivers, trips, about 5M telematics events (GPS, harsh braking, fuel, engine fault codes), maintenance work orders, parts, customers, shipments and incidents.
  • A Bulgarian and English document corpus of about 1,500 documents: fleet policy handbook, driver code of conduct, HR policies, maintenance manuals (PDFs with tables), EU driving-time and tachograph summaries, customer SLAs, incident reports and scanned delivery notes.
  • Mock APIs (OpenAPI): ticketing, scheduling, parts supplier, and notification (email/Teams).
  • A role model with document ACLs: dispatcher, fleet manager, mechanic, driver, HR, customer service and auditor.

Why this domain: it has structured and unstructured data, real permissions, safety-relevant actions (booking maintenance, notifying customers), Bulgarian-language users, and a genuine EU AI Act trap. Driver-monitoring features touch the Annex III employment use cases, which learners must recognise and design around in C18. The domain is complex enough that "just add an agent" fails visibly.

Product increments: a streaming "Ask Fleet Ops" chat (C2) → typed incident extraction and first tool (C3) → agent-ready repo (C4) → golden set and CI evals (C5) → semantic search (C6) → cited, permission-aware BG/EN RAG (C7) → Trakia MCP server (C8) → Fleet Assistant agent with human approval (C9) → Fleet Analyst text-to-SQL agent (C10) → full agent-maintained test pyramid (C11) → multi-agent incident workflow (C12) → long-horizon memory and GraphRAG (C13) → production eval suite and red-team report (C14) → full tracing and cost per task (C15) → threat model and hardening (C16) → deployed behind an AI gateway, with A2A and Teams exposure (C17) → AI Act risk file (C18) → fully automated SDLC watched by an SRE agent (C19). The D-track adds a realtime voice assistant for drivers, a fine-tuned fault-code classifier on Foundry Local at the depots, a durable fleet-planner agent and custom agent tooling. The A-track turns the product into a multi-tenant offering that Trakia sells to other fleets, with a landing zone, knowledge platform, agent registry, DR/FinOps and an ISO/IEC 42001-style governance system.

docs.title: The Factory
docs.text:
In parallel with the product, every learner builds the Factory, their own agentic software delivery system. It covers environment as code (C0); repo memory files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, copilot-instructions), a plan → implement → verify loop, skills and hooks with permission settings (C4); eval tests that agents must run before claiming done (C5); coding agents consuming the project's own MCP servers (C8); test-first specs, mutation gates and Playwright test agents (C11); eval gates and a regression-triage agent in CI (C14); prompt and model versioning (C15); security agents such as CodeQL agentic autofix, secret scanning and package allow-lists (C16); and the full loop from issue to cloud-agent PR, AI review, human gate, deploy and SRE agent (C19). It extends to custom agent tooling built on the Copilot SDK or Claude Agent SDK (D6) and to factory governance and metrics (A7).

From C4 onward, all product work goes through the Factory. You are graded on how you direct, constrain and verify agents, not on keystrokes. The reason is the evidence on AI-assisted delivery. DORA 2025 found AI acting as "a mirror and a multiplier" of existing practice. METR's early-2025 randomized trial found experienced developers about 19–20% slower while they believed they were about 20% faster; METR's 2026 update suggests speed-ups now but calls its own data "very weak evidence" of the size. A USENIX 2025 study found 19.7% of 2.23M AI-generated code samples referencing non-existent packages. Unattended agents amplify whatever discipline exists, so the Factory is where you build that discipline.

docs.title: 6. Module catalogue
docs.text: Hours are total learner effort (concepts + labs + kata + explanation). Volatility tags are in each module header. "Key tech" lists what is used, not everything mentioned. Each module (C0–C19, D1–D7, A1–A7) has its own chapter in this handbook.

docs.title: Joint capstone (80 h per learner, 6–8 weeks, mixed teams of 4–5)
docs.text: A new client brief in a different domain: a municipal citizen-signals service, a clinic network's back office, or an e-commerce operations copilot. Teams deliver a working system, a Factory with CI eval gates and a full architecture package, and they swap red teams with another team. The final defense is in front of a review board. See Capstone.

docs.title: Design principles and the evidence behind them
docs.text:
Whole tasks, one product (4C/ID). Four-component instructional design (van Merriënboer) is built for complex skills whose parts must be integrated. Its four components are whole learning tasks with fading scaffolding, supportive information, just-in-time procedural information, and part-task practice for recurrent skills. In this course the whole tasks are the product increments, organised into task classes of rising complexity (prompt feature → RAG → single agent → multi-agent → multi-tenant production). Supportive information sits in each module's Concepts section. Just-in-time information sits in lab steps and cheat-sheets. Part-task practice is the kata: a 20–40 minute drill repeated with variation (tool schemas, eval cases, KQL, APIM policies, ADRs, threat-model deltas). Scaffolding fades: Level 1 labs give near-complete starter code, Level 3 labs give a goal, constraints and acceptance checks, and the capstone gives only a client brief.

Learn → Do → Break → Fix → Explain. Every lab has a working baseline, an induced failure (regression, injection, outage, model swap, cost spike), a fix and a short written explanation such as an ADR, postmortem or eval report. Explaining is graded. You must be able to say why something broke and why your fix is the right one, and with agents writing most of the code that is the skill that matters.

Failure-driven evals from day one. The leading evals practitioners (Husain and Shankar) explicitly advise against "eval-driven development" in the sense of writing speculative evaluators or relying on generic metrics. The course therefore teaches error analysis first. You read about 100 real traces, open-code the first failure in each, axial-code the notes into a failure taxonomy, write binary (preferably code-based) checks per failure mode, validate any LLM judge against human labels (TPR and TNR on separate dev and test splits), and then gate CI. Every product feature ships with evals, and your progress is gated by evals too.

Spiral curriculum. Evals, security, cost, context and architecture each recur at rising depth: introduced in Level 1, operationalised in Level 2, industrialised in Level 3 and made strategic in the expert tracks. The traceability table in the Competency matrix shows where each thread returns.

Mastery gates. You advance to the next task class only after passing a gate: hidden eval suites, code review against a rubric and, from G2, a design defense. In Bloom's 1984 synthesis, feedback-corrective mastery learning alone was associated with about 1.0 SD improvement (84th percentile). Tutoring combined with mastery was associated with about 2 SD. These are historical figures from a specific context, so read them as an argument for gates with specific feedback and resits, not as a promise of a particular gain.

Structured project-based learning, small teams. A 2023 meta-analysis of PBL (Zhang & Ma; 66 studies, 190 effect sizes) found an overall effect of SMD 0.441. Moderator analyses favoured projects of 9–18 weeks (0.673, versus 0.300 for 18+ weeks), groups of 4–5 (0.909) and engineering/technology subjects (0.619). The same analysis found a much weaker effect for university-only samples (0.116) and high heterogeneity (I² = 87.4%), and the authors call the moderators exploratory. The course draws two practical conclusions. First, add structure (milestones, rubrics, reviews) rather than relying on open-ended discovery. Second, use capstone teams of 4–5 with explicit milestones. The capstone itself runs 6–8 weeks, which sits at or below the 9–18 week range, so cohorts are advised to start capstone inception in the last 1–2 weeks of the expert track, giving about 9 weeks elapsed. The whole-product thread across the core is longer than 18 weeks at part-time pace, and it is broken into gated task classes of roughly 6–10 weeks each, which is the course's answer to the weaker long-duration result.

docs.title: What a module looks like
docs.text: Every module uses the same sections: Why this matters → Learning outcomes → Concepts → Tools & versions → Labs (3–5, each with Goal, Start state, Steps, Break it, Acceptance criteria and Stretch) → Kata → Product increment → Factory increment → Assessment (4-level rubric plus auto-checks) → Common pitfalls → References. (Modules also carry instructor notes for the teaching team; they are not part of this learner edition.) Lab start states are Git tags in trakia-fleetops (c7/lab2-start). Acceptance criteria are automated wherever possible (tests, eval thresholds, CI status, policy checks).

docs.title: How AI use is handled
docs.text: AI assistance is expected, not tolerated. Assessment therefore targets what AI does not supply on your behalf: judgement (what to build, which failure matters, which leg of the trifecta to remove), verification (evals, tests, traces, mutation scores) and explanation (oral defenses, ADRs, postmortems). Some labs deliberately require an unaided step, such as predicting behaviour before running or reading a diff without an assistant, to counter "cognitive debt" in a codebase you did not type. Gates include a short no-assistant segment and an oral defense where you must explain and modify any line you submitted. See Assessment and gates.

docs.title: A standard 12-hour week
docs.text: Block Time What happens Concept session 1.5 h Live or recorded walkthrough of the module's Concepts, plus a live "predict → run → explain" demo. Lab block 1 3 h Labs 1–2 (Do + Break). Lab block 2 3 h Labs 3–4 (Fix + acceptance criteria green in CI). Katas 1.5 h 3 × 30 min, spaced across the week, each with a variation. Explain 1 h ADR, postmortem or eval report for the module; graded. Peer review 1 h Review two peers' PRs or eval reports with the module rubric. Office hours / mentor 1 h Group troubleshooting; architecture clinics in the A-track.

docs.title: Pacing options
docs.text:
Mode Load Core (274 h) Track (≈ 120 h) Capstone (80 h) Calendar Part-time standard 12 h/week ≈ 23 weeks ≈ 10 weeks 7–8 weeks at ≈ 10–11 h/week ≈ 9–10 months including 2 buffer weeks Part-time intensive 25 h/week ≈ 11 weeks ≈ 5 weeks 6 weeks: 2 weeks overlapped with the track at ~12 h/week + 4 weeks at ~14 h/week, or run 6 weeks at ~13 h/week alongside track remnants ≈ 5 months Bootcamp (full-time) 35–40 h/week ≈ 7 weeks Track at ~20 h/week over weeks 8–13 Capstone at ~13–14 h/week over weeks 8–13, interleaved ≈ 13 weeks; capstone still spans 6 weeks

Pacing rules: - Never compress the capstone below 6 calendar weeks. Teams need time for the red-team swap, fixes and a production-readiness review. In bootcamp mode the capstone runs interleaved with the track. - Gates are scheduled, not ad hoc. Each cohort gets a gate week with resit slots 2–3 weeks later. - Bootcamp fatigue is real. Error analysis and design reasoning degrade with fatigue, so in bootcamp mode cap lab days at 7 focused hours and keep Fridays for explanation, peer review and katas. This is a course-designer recommendation, not an evidence-based figure. - Self-paced learners follow the part-time standard sequence and book gate slots individually. The capstone requires joining a cohort team.
